cell_structure_interactions_medi2200.htm.title: MEDI2200 W2 · Cell Structure & Interactions
cell_structure_interactions_medi2200.htm.subject: Cell Biology
cell_structure_interactions_medi2200.htm.content: Cytoskeleton: actin microfilaments (7-9nm, ATP, polar, plus/barbed fast + minus/pointed, treadmilling, arrays: lamellipodium branched/filopodium parallel/stress fibre/cortex; toxins phalloidin/cytochalasin/latrunculin), microtubules (25nm, aB-tubulin, GTP, dynamic instability via GTP cap, MTOC anchors minus end, search-and-capture; taxanes stabilise, vinca destabilise, tau/Alzheimer's), intermediate filaments (10nm, antiparallel staggered tetramer -> non-polar, no nucleotide/motors, tension; keratin/vimentin/desmin/GFAP/neurofilament/lamin; epidermolysis bullosa). Motors: myosin (actin, to +), kinesin (MT, to + anterograde), dynein (MT, to - retrograde); all ATP. Whole-cell: division (spindle + actin contractile ring), migration (protrude/adhere/contract/release), cilia (9+2 axoneme, dynein arms; Kartagener). ECM: GAGs/proteoglycans (compression) + fibrous proteins (tension). GAGs unbranched, negative, draw Na+/water; hyaluronan (no sulfate/no core), chondroitin, heparan, keratan. Proteoglycan = GAGs on core (aggrecan on hyaluronan). Collagen triple helix Gly-X-Y (glycine at centre; vit C for cross-links -> scurvy), most abundant, types I skin/bone, II cartilage, IV basal lamina net. Elastin cross-linked stretch/recoil (aorta 50%, Marfan/fibrillin, emphysema). Fibronectin = glue (matrix to actin via integrin). MMPs degrade matrix (controlled; metastasis). Basal lamina: laminin + collagen IV + nidogen + perlecan (Goodpasture, Alport). Junctions apical->basal: tight->adherens->desmosome->gap->cell-matrix. Groups: occluding (tight), anchoring (adherens/desmosome/hemidesmosome/actin-linked), channel (gap). Cadherins (cell-cell homophilic, Velcro, cell-type specific), integrins (cell-matrix, RGD). Filament: adherens+actin-linked->actin; desmosome+hemidesmosome->intermediate filaments (keratin). Tight junction claudin/occludin seal (gate+fence -> directional transport, blood-brain barrier). Gap junction connexon (6 connexins, ~1.4nm/~1kDa, electrical+metabolic coupling). Integrins RGD outside + actin inside, focal adhesion mechanosensor, anoikis; hemidesmosome (a6b4, collagen XVII, keratin; bullous pemphigoid). E-cadherin loss -> metastasis; pemphigus (desmoglein).

questions.question: Which cytoskeletal filament's main job is pure mechanical (tensile) strength?
questions.explanation: Intermediate filaments (~10 nm) are non-polar ropes built for tensile strength. Actin shapes the surface; microtubules position organelles and transport cargo.

questions.question: The thickest and stiffest cytoskeletal filament is the:
questions.explanation: Microtubules are hollow 25 nm tubes — the thickest and stiffest. Actin microfilaments (7–9 nm) are the thinnest; intermediate filaments sit between.

questions.question: Actin filaments are built from globular subunits that each carry bound:
questions.explanation: Actin monomers bind ATP (hydrolysed to ADP once buried). Microtubules, by contrast, use GTP on their tubulin dimers.

questions.question: The plus (barbed) end of an actin filament is where subunits:
options: A. add fastest, extending the filament
B. leave fastest, shrinking the filament
C. are permanently locked in place
D. carry no bound nucleotide at all
questions.explanation: The plus (barbed) end grows fastest; the minus (pointed) end loses subunits. Net plus-end growth at the leading edge pushes the membrane forward.

questions.question: Treadmilling of an actin filament occurs when it:
options: A. grows at plus, shrinks at minus
B. grows at both its ends at once
C. shrinks entirely from both ends
D. stops all subunit exchange fully
questions.explanation: In treadmilling, ATP-actin adds at the plus end while ADP-actin leaves the minus end at the same rate — subunits flux through while the length stays constant.

questions.question: The branched actin network that pushes out the leading edge of a crawling cell forms the:
questions.explanation: The lamellipodium is a branched (dendritic) actin sheet whose plus-end growth pushes the membrane out. Filopodia are tight parallel bundles; stress fibres contract.

questions.question: Dynamic instability of a microtubule is controlled by:
options: A. a GTP cap at the plus end
B. an ATP cap at the plus end
C. the loss of all its tubulin
questions.explanation: GTP-tubulin adds at the plus end and its cap stabilises growth; when hydrolysis catches up and the cap is lost, the GDP core springs apart and it shrinks.

questions.question: Why is the instability of microtubules useful to a dividing cell?
options: A. it lets them search and capture targets
B. it permanently fixes them in place
C. it stops the spindle ever forming
D. it removes the need for an MTOC
questions.explanation: Growing and collapsing in all directions lets microtubules 'search and capture' — any that hit a kinetochore are stabilised, wiring the spindle without a blueprint.

questions.question: At the microtubule-organising centre (MTOC), which end of the microtubules is anchored?
questions.explanation: Minus ends are anchored at the MTOC with plus ends pointing outward — the fixed geometry that lets motor proteins deliver cargo directionally.

questions.question: Anti-cancer taxanes (paclitaxel) block mitosis by acting on microtubules to:
questions.explanation: Taxanes over-stabilise microtubules while vinca alkaloids destabilise them; either way a dividing cell can't build a working spindle and dies.

questions.question: Intermediate filaments lack polarity because they are assembled from:
questions.explanation: Two dimers align antiparallel and staggered into a tetramer, cancelling direction; the finished rope has no plus or minus end, so no motors and no treadmilling.

questions.question: Which statement about intermediate filaments is correct?
options: A. no motor proteins move along them
B. kinesin walks along them quickly
C. they treadmill just like actin does
D. they carry a GTP cap at one end
questions.explanation: Because they are non-polar and carry no nucleotide, nothing walks along intermediate filaments — their sole role is bearing tension.

questions.question: Mutations in keratin intermediate filaments cause skin to blister with minor friction in:
questions.explanation: Keratin gives basal skin cells their strength; mutations let them rupture under friction — epidermolysis bullosa simplex. The others involve different proteins.

questions.question: Myosin is the motor protein that walks along:
questions.explanation: Myosin walks along actin (usually toward the plus end). Kinesin and dynein are the microtubule motors; intermediate filaments have no motors.

questions.question: Which pairing of microtubule motor and its direction is correct?
options: A. kinesin to plus, dynein to minus
B. kinesin to minus, dynein to plus
C. both kinesin and dynein to plus
D. both kinesin and dynein to minus
questions.explanation: Kinesin carries cargo toward the plus end (outward/anterograde); cytoplasmic dynein carries it toward the minus end (inward/retrograde).

questions.question: During cytokinesis, the structure that pinches the cell into two is a ring of:
questions.explanation: An actin–myosin contractile ring forms around the equator and constricts to divide the cell. Microtubules meanwhile form the spindle that segregates chromosomes.

questions.question: The core of a cilium or flagellum, the axoneme, is arranged as:
options: A. nine doublets around a central pair
B. six connexin subunits around a pore
C. two protofilaments in a double helix
D. eight tetramers packed in a rope
questions.explanation: The '9+2' axoneme is nine outer doublet microtubules around a central pair; dynein arms slide the doublets, and because they're tethered, sliding becomes a bend.

questions.question: Immotile cilia in primary ciliary dyskinesia (Kartagener syndrome) result from defective:
questions.explanation: Without working dynein arms the cilia can't bend, so mucus isn't cleared (chest infections), sperm can't swim, and left–right asymmetry becomes random.

questions.question: The two great classes of extracellular matrix molecule are fibrous proteins and:
questions.explanation: The ECM combines gel-forming GAGs/proteoglycans (which resist compression) with fibrous proteins like collagen (which resist tension).

questions.question: Glycosaminoglycans let cartilage resist compression because their fixed negative charge:
options: A. draws in Na⁺ and then water
B. repels all water from the gel
C. binds collagen into stiff rods
D. blocks any ion from entering
questions.explanation: The dense fixed anionic charge pulls in cations (Na⁺), which osmotically draw in water; the trapped, near-incompressible water resists load as fluid pressure.

questions.question: Which glycosaminoglycan is unusual in being unsulfated and lacking a protein core?
questions.explanation: Hyaluronan is the exception — no sulfate and no core protein; it forms the long backbone onto which many proteoglycans dock to build a giant aggregate.

questions.question: A proteoglycan consists of:
options: A. GAG chains on a core
B. a triple helix of collagen
questions.explanation: A proteoglycan is one or more GAG chains covalently attached to a core protein; many dock onto hyaluronan to form aggregates such as aggrecan.

questions.question: Collagen's Gly-X-Y repeat requires glycine at every third position because glycine:
options: A. fits the crowded helix centre
B. is the largest available amino acid
C. carries a strong negative charge
D. binds calcium within the fibril
questions.explanation: Glycine's tiny H side-chain is the only one that fits the crowded centre of the triple helix; a bulkier residue kinks it — the lesion in osteogenesis imperfecta.

questions.question: Type I collagen, the body's most abundant collagen, predominates in:
questions.explanation: Type I is the fibrillar workhorse of skin, bone and tendon (~90% of body collagen). Type II is in cartilage; type IV forms the basal-lamina network.

questions.question: Vitamin C is needed for strong collagen because it is required to:
options: B. add glycine to every third slot in it
C. wind the three chains together tightly
D. cut collagen into short fibril lengths
questions.explanation: Vitamin C enables hydroxylation of proline/lysine, which cross-links neighbouring helices for strength; without it collagen is weak — the basis of scurvy.

questions.question: Elastin's role in the aorta and skin is to provide:
questions.explanation: Cross-linked elastin stretches under load and snaps back on release; the aorta is ~50% elastin, storing the pulse and releasing it between beats.

questions.question: Fibronectin functions in the ECM as the molecule that:
options: A. glues the matrix to cells
C. seals the epithelial cell gaps
D. forms the whole mitotic spindle
questions.explanation: Fibronectin binds both matrix components and cell-surface integrins, linking the ECM (via integrins) to the actin cytoskeleton — the matrix 'glue'.

questions.question: Matrix metalloproteases (MMPs) are kept on a tight leash mainly because:
options: A. uncontrolled digestion would destroy tissue
B. they build new collagen fibrils quickly
C. they generate the cell's whole ATP supply
D. they seal the gaps between epithelial cells
questions.explanation: MMPs degrade matrix, so unchecked they would dissolve tendons and vessel walls; they are secreted inactive, confined by receptors, and held by inhibitors.

questions.question: The two main structural builders of the basal lamina are:
options: A. laminin and type IV collagen
questions.explanation: Laminin organises the sheet and type IV collagen forms its felt-like network; nidogen ties them and perlecan adds charge for filtration.

questions.question: Reading an epithelial cell apical to basal, which junction is highest (most apical)?
questions.explanation: The tight junction sits highest so it can seal the gap around the apex; below it come adherens junctions, desmosomes, gap junctions and basal anchors.

questions.question: Which receptor superfamily mediates cell-to-cell adhesion?
questions.explanation: Cadherins mediate homophilic cell–cell adhesion; integrins bolt cells to the extracellular matrix.

questions.question: A desmosome differs from an adherens junction in that it anchors to:
questions.explanation: Both are cadherin-based, but desmosomes tie into keratin intermediate filaments (the tension-bearers), whereas adherens junctions link to actin.

questions.question: The tight junction enables directional (vectorial) transport across an epithelium because it:
options: A. blocks solutes leaking between cells
B. opens a pore between the cytoplasms
C. anchors the cell down to the matrix
D. contracts to change the cell shape
questions.explanation: As a gate it stops paracellular leakage (so transport goes through cells) and as a fence it keeps apical importers and basal exporters apart — glucose in apically, out basally.

questions.question: A gap junction's connexon channel allows the passage of:
options: A. ions and small molecules only
B. proteins and nucleic acids freely
D. nothing at all between the cells
questions.explanation: The ~1.4 nm pore (about a 1 kDa cut-off) passes ions and small metabolites — coupling cells electrically and metabolically — but excludes proteins and nucleic acids.

questions.question: Integrins anchor a cell to the matrix by binding ECM motifs such as RGD outside and linking inside to:
questions.explanation: Integrins bind ECM proteins (classically the RGD motif) outside and, via adaptors like talin, the actin cytoskeleton inside — the focal adhesion.

questions.question: Because integrin adhesion signals that a cell is anchored, cells that lose this grip may undergo:
questions.explanation: Integrin engagement permits survival signals; detached cells lose them and die by anoikis — a safeguard that cancer cells must overcome to metastasise.

musculoskeletal_system_mhhs2401.html.title: MHHS2401 W1 PI · Musculoskeletal Introduction
musculoskeletal_system_mhhs2401.html.subject: Musculoskeletal System
musculoskeletal_system_mhhs2401.html.content: Skeleton = bones+cartilage+ligaments; 206 bones; functions: support, protection, mineral/lipid storage, blood cell production, leverage. Axial vs appendicular. Bone tissue: compact (osteons: central Haversian canal, lamellae, lacunae, canaliculi) vs spongy (trabeculae). Cells: osteoprogenitor, osteoblast, osteocyte, osteoclast. Ossification: endochondral (cartilage model) vs intramembranous. Growth at epiphyseal plate. Joints: functional (syn/amphi/diarthrosis), structural (fibrous/cartilaginous/synovial). Muscle: fascicle arrangements, pennate=force, parallel=range; compartment syndrome->fasciotomy. Upper limb nerves from brachial plexus; carpal tunnel=median nerve. Development from mesoderm. Achondroplasia=FGFR3 AD.

questions.question: How many bones make up the adult human skeleton?
questions.explanation: The adult skeleton has 206 bones: 80 axial plus 126 appendicular.

questions.question: Which bone cell breaks down (resorbs) bone?
questions.explanation: Osteoclasts resorb bone; the suffix -clast means carve, while -blast builds and -cyte maintains.

questions.question: The femur and humerus are examples of which bone shape?
questions.explanation: Long bones have a shaft and two ends and act as levers; the femur and humerus are classic examples.

questions.question: Which joint type is freely movable and has a fluid-filled cavity?
questions.explanation: Synovial joints have a fluid-filled cavity and are the freely-movable family, such as the knee and shoulder.

questions.question: A structure that attaches a muscle to a bone is a:
questions.explanation: A tendon attaches muscle to bone; a ligament joins bone to bone.

questions.question: Which of these belongs to the axial skeleton?
questions.explanation: The axial skeleton is the skull, vertebral column, sacrum, coccyx and thoracic cage; limbs and girdles are appendicular.

questions.question: In compact bone, the central (Haversian) canal of an osteon carries:
questions.explanation: The central canal runs up the osteon core carrying blood vessels and nerves that feed the buried osteocytes.

questions.question: Osteocytes reside in small spaces within the bone matrix called:
questions.explanation: Osteocytes sit in lacunae; the tiny canaliculi connecting lacunae let them exchange nutrients and signals.

questions.question: Which type of ossification forms most long bones from a cartilage model?
questions.explanation: Endochondral ossification replaces a cartilage model with bone and forms most long bones; flat bones form intramembranously.

questions.question: Flat bones such as those of the skull form by which process?
questions.explanation: Flat bones form by intramembranous ossification, where osteoblasts deposit osteoid directly with no cartilage model.

questions.question: The shaft of a long bone is called the:
questions.explanation: The diaphysis is the shaft, compact bone around the medullary cavity; the epiphyses are the expanded ends.

questions.question: Which membrane covers the outer surface of a bone and carries its nerves?
questions.explanation: The periosteum covers the outer bone, is richly innervated and vascular, and is anchored by Sharpey's fibres.

questions.question: Growth in the length of a long bone occurs at the epiphyseal plate, made of:
questions.explanation: The epiphyseal plate is hyaline cartilage between diaphysis and epiphysis; it becomes the epiphyseal line when growth stops.

questions.question: A joint that permits no movement, such as a skull suture, is a:
questions.explanation: Functionally, a synarthrosis allows no movement, an amphiarthrosis slight movement, and a diarthrosis free movement.

questions.question: The shoulder and hip are examples of which synovial joint type?
questions.explanation: Ball-and-socket joints such as the shoulder and hip allow movement in all planes.

questions.question: The elbow, which moves in a single plane, is which type of synovial joint?
questions.explanation: The elbow is a hinge joint, allowing flexion and extension in one plane.

questions.question: Which fascicle arrangement packs many short fibres to maximise force?
questions.explanation: Pennate muscles angle many short fascicles onto a tendon, packing in more fibres for greater force at the cost of range.

questions.question: In muscle terminology, the insertion is the attachment to the:
questions.explanation: The insertion attaches to the movable bone (usually distal) and is pulled toward the origin on the fixed bone.

questions.question: In the cubital fossa, the brachial artery divides into the radial artery and the:
questions.explanation: The brachial artery splits in the cubital fossa into the larger ulnar and smaller radial arteries.

questions.question: The nerves of the upper limb arise from the brachial plexus, roots:
questions.explanation: The brachial plexus arises from spinal roots C5 to T1 and supplies the upper limb with mixed motor and sensory nerves.

questions.question: A broad, flat sheet that connects muscle to muscle or bone is a(n):
questions.explanation: An aponeurosis is a broad flat sheet; a tendon is a rope-like cord, and both attach muscle to its target.

questions.question: The formation of blood cells within red marrow is called:
questions.explanation: Blood cell production, or haematopoiesis, occurs in red marrow and is one of the five skeletal functions.

questions.question: The whole musculoskeletal system develops from which embryonic germ layer?
questions.explanation: The entire MSK system arises from mesoderm; its connective-tissue precursor is mesenchyme.

questions.question: The pubic symphysis, joined by fibrocartilage, is which structural joint?
questions.explanation: A symphysis is a secondary cartilaginous joint united by fibrocartilage; a synchondrosis uses hyaline cartilage.

questions.question: Stability of a synovial joint depends on articular shape, muscle tone and:
questions.explanation: Synovial stability rests on three things: the shape of the articular surfaces, the ligaments, and muscle tone.

questions.question: A fibrocartilage ring that deepens a socket, as at the shoulder, is a:
questions.explanation: A labrum is a fibrocartilage ring that deepens a socket; an articular disc lies between surfaces and a bursa cuts friction.

questions.question: Compression within the carpal tunnel affects which nerve?
questions.explanation: The carpal tunnel is a rigid space under the flexor retinaculum; swelling squeezes the median nerve, causing carpal tunnel syndrome.

questions.question: A strip of skin supplied by a single spinal nerve is called a:
questions.explanation: A dermatome is the skin strip of one spinal nerve; a myotome is the muscle group supplied by one spinal nerve.

questions.question: Which structure caps the limb bud and signals the mesoderm to keep growing?
questions.explanation: The apical ectodermal ridge caps the limb bud and signals the mesoderm beneath it to keep growing, driving outgrowth.

questions.question: Fingers and toes are separated during development by:
questions.explanation: Apoptosis deletes the tissue between the digital rays; if it fails, digits stay webbed, causing syndactyly.

questions.question: Achondroplasia, producing short limbs, results from a mutation in which gene?
questions.explanation: Achondroplasia is an autosomal dominant FGFR3 mutation that brakes endochondral ossification, so long bones cannot lengthen.

questions.question: Which mesoderm gives rise to the muscle that migrates into the limb?
questions.explanation: Paraxial mesoderm (somites) forms the limb muscle, while lateral plate mesoderm forms the skeleton and connective tissue.

questions.question: Rising pressure inside a closed fascial compartment after injury causes:
questions.explanation: Non-stretchy deep fascia lets pressure climb in a closed compartment until it chokes vessels and nerves, causing compartment syndrome.

arm_elbow_forearm_mhhs2401_wk2.html.title: MHHS2401 W2 · Arm, Elbow & Anterior Forearm
arm_elbow_forearm_mhhs2401_wk2.html.subject: Musculoskeletal System
arm_elbow_forearm_mhhs2401_wk2.html.content: Distal humerus: capitulum (lateral, radius head), trochlea (medial, ulnar trochlear notch); radial+coronoid fossae anterior, olecranon fossa posterior. Elbow = hinge; anular ligament at proximal radioulnar pivot joint. Epicondyle-olecranon triangle preserved in supracondylar fracture, lost in dislocation. Pulled elbow = anular ligament tear. Arm anterior (musculocutaneous: biceps, brachialis=pure flexor, coracobrachialis), posterior (radial: triceps). Pronation/supination = radius over ulna. Anterior forearm flexors median except FCU + medial half FDP (ulnar). Extrinsic hand muscles = remote control. Golfer's elbow = medial epicondylitis (flexor-pronator).

questions.question: The rounded lateral surface of the distal humerus that articulates with the radius is the:
questions.explanation: The capitulum is the lateral rounded surface that caps the radius head; the medial trochlea takes the ulna.

questions.question: The elbow is classified as which type of synovial joint?
questions.explanation: The elbow is a synovial hinge joint, allowing only flexion and extension; forearm rotation happens at the radioulnar joints.

questions.question: Which muscle is the chief extensor of the forearm?
questions.explanation: Triceps brachii, in the posterior compartment, is the chief extensor of the forearm and inserts on the olecranon.

questions.question: In the anatomical position, the radius lies on which side of the forearm?
questions.explanation: The radius is the lateral bone of the forearm and the ulna is the medial bone.

questions.question: Golfer's elbow is inflammation at which bony landmark?
questions.explanation: Golfer's elbow is medial epicondylitis, overuse of the common flexor tendon at the medial epicondyle; tennis elbow is lateral.

questions.question: The trochlea of the humerus articulates with which part of the ulna?
questions.explanation: The spool-shaped trochlea runs in the trochlear notch of the ulna, forming the hinge of the elbow.

questions.question: The olecranon fossa on the posterior humerus receives the olecranon during:
questions.explanation: The posterior olecranon fossa receives the olecranon in extension; the anterior fossae receive the radius head and coronoid in flexion.

questions.question: The biceps brachii tendon inserts onto which feature of the radius?
questions.explanation: Biceps inserts on the radial tuberosity; because it pulls on the rotatable radius, it both flexes the elbow and supinates.

questions.question: The triceps brachii inserts onto which part of the ulna?
questions.explanation: Triceps inserts on the olecranon, a long lever behind the elbow axis, giving a strong extension moment.

questions.question: The fibrous capsule of the elbow is weakest in which locations?
options: C. only on the medial side
D. only on the lateral side
questions.explanation: The capsule is weak anteriorly and posteriorly to allow flexion and extension, but thickened at the sides into collateral ligaments.

questions.question: Which ligament rings the head of the radius at the proximal radioulnar joint?
questions.explanation: The anular ligament forms a fibrous collar around the radius head, holding it against the radial notch of the ulna.

questions.question: Pronation and supination of the forearm occur at which joints?
questions.explanation: Rotation happens at the proximal and distal radioulnar joints together, as the radius rolls over the fixed ulna.

questions.question: The anterior (flexor) compartment of the arm is supplied by which nerve?
questions.explanation: The musculocutaneous nerve supplies the anterior arm flexors; the radial nerve supplies the posterior extensors.

questions.question: Which muscle is the chief flexor of the forearm and inserts on the ulna?
questions.explanation: Brachialis runs from the humeral shaft to the ulnar tuberosity; because the ulna cannot rotate, it is a pure, reliable flexor.

questions.question: Besides flexing the elbow, the biceps brachii is a powerful:
questions.explanation: Because biceps pulls on the radial tuberosity, it unwinds the radius into supination as well as flexing the elbow.

questions.question: The triceps brachii is supplied by which nerve?
questions.explanation: The radial nerve supplies the posterior compartment, including triceps, and runs in the radial groove of the humerus.

questions.question: Most anterior forearm muscles share a common origin at the:
questions.explanation: Most flexor-pronator muscles arise from the common flexor origin on the medial epicondyle of the humerus.

questions.question: Most anterior forearm muscles are supplied by which nerve?
questions.explanation: The median nerve supplies most anterior forearm muscles; the exceptions are flexor carpi ulnaris and the medial half of FDP.

questions.question: The fibrocartilage articular disc of the distal radioulnar joint separates it from the:
questions.explanation: The articular disc unites the distal radioulnar joint and separates it from the cavity of the wrist joint.

questions.question: Which nerve lies in a groove directly behind the medial epicondyle?
questions.explanation: The ulnar nerve passes behind the medial epicondyle, the 'funny bone', so a blow or fracture there threatens it.

questions.question: In elbow flexion, the two epicondyles and the olecranon form what shape?
questions.explanation: The three points form a triangle in flexion and align horizontally in extension; the triangle is disrupted by dislocation.

questions.question: Posterior dislocation of the elbow drives the forearm bones through which weak structure?
questions.explanation: A fall on the flexed elbow drives the humerus forward through the weak anterior capsule, leaving the ulna and radius behind it.

questions.question: A pulled elbow in a young child involves subluxation of the radial head from the:
questions.explanation: A sudden pull tears the distal attachment of the anular ligament, so the radial head slips partly out of the ring.

questions.question: Which superficial anterior forearm muscle is supplied by the ulnar nerve?
questions.explanation: Flexor carpi ulnaris is the ulnar-supplied exception; with the medial half of FDP it makes up the '1½ muscles' rule.

questions.question: Flexor digitorum superficialis inserts onto which phalanges of the fingers?
questions.explanation: FDS stops short at the middle phalanges (flexing the PIP joints), whereas FDP runs past to the distal phalanges.

questions.question: Flexor digitorum profundus flexes the fingers at which joints?
questions.explanation: FDP inserts on the distal phalanges and flexes the DIP joints; its medial half is supplied by the ulnar nerve.

questions.question: Which small square deep muscle pronates the forearm at its distal end?
questions.explanation: Pronator quadratus spans the distal anterior radius and ulna, pronating the forearm; pronator teres does so proximally.

questions.question: The interosseous membrane transfers load in the forearm mainly from the:
questions.explanation: Force enters at the wrist through the radius and leaves at the elbow through the ulna, so the membrane transfers load radius to ulna.

questions.question: The bicipital aponeurosis forms a protective roof in the cubital fossa over the:
options: A. brachial artery and median nerve
B. radial nerve and cephalic vein
C. ulnar nerve and basilic vein
D. radial artery and ulnar nerve
questions.explanation: The bicipital aponeurosis crosses the cubital fossa as a roof over the brachial artery and median nerve.

questions.question: The long head of triceps brachii originates from which scapular landmark?
questions.explanation: The long head of triceps arises from the infraglenoid tubercle of the scapula and also stabilises the abducted humerus.

bone_physiology_1_mhhs2401.html.title: MHHS2401 W1 PIII · Bone Physiology I
bone_physiology_1_mhhs2401.html.subject: Musculoskeletal System
bone_physiology_1_mhhs2401.html.content: Cells: osteoprogenitor->osteoblast (osteoid=collagen + hydroxyapatite)->osteocyte; osteoclast secretes acid (dissolves hydroxyapatite) + proteases. Osteocytes in lacunae connect via canaliculi/gap junctions. Compact: non-parallel collagen resists torsion; collagen+hydroxyapatite resists compression. Growth at epiphyseal plate until puberty. Remodelling: activation->resorption->reversal->formation. PTH & calcitriol raise blood Ca; calcitonin lowers. PTH continuous=catabolic, intermittent=anabolic (teriparatide). Vitamin D: skin/diet->liver(25-OH)->kidney(1,25 calcitriol). RANKL/OPG master switch. DEXA T-score<=-2.5 = osteoporosis. Osteogenesis imperfecta = collagen I defect.

questions.question: Which bone cell secretes bone matrix and builds new bone?
questions.explanation: Osteoblasts are the builders: they secrete the osteoid and mineral of bone matrix. The suffix -blast means build.

questions.question: Which bone cell resorbs bone using proteases and acid?
questions.explanation: Osteoclasts are the demolition cells: proteases break the collagen and HCl dissolves the hydroxyapatite. The suffix -clast means carve.

questions.question: The organic part of bone matrix (osteoid) is made mainly of:
questions.explanation: Osteoid is the organic component, mainly collagen; hydroxyapatite (calcium and phosphate) is the inorganic mineral component.

questions.question: The skeleton stores roughly what fraction of the body's calcium?
questions.explanation: The skeleton holds about 99 percent of body calcium, so controlling blood calcium means controlling bone.

questions.question: Which imaging test is used to measure bone mineral density?
questions.explanation: Dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DEXA) measures bone mineral density; a T-score of −2.5 or less indicates osteoporosis.

questions.question: Osteocytes are best described as which of the following?
options: A. former osteoblasts trapped in matrix
B. stem cells that become builders
D. cartilage cells of the plate
questions.explanation: Osteocytes are former osteoblasts trapped in the matrix they laid down; they maintain and monitor bone as strain sensors.

questions.question: In compact bone, lamellae are arranged concentrically to form:
questions.explanation: Compact bone lamellae form concentric osteons around a central canal; spongy bone's irregular lamellae form trabeculae.

questions.question: Osteocytes communicate with each other through gap junctions on processes running in:
questions.explanation: Osteocytes sit in lacunae and extend processes through canaliculi, where gap junctions wire neighbouring cells together.

questions.question: Compact bone resists twisting (torsion) chiefly because its collagen fibres are:
options: A. not parallel to each other
questions.explanation: Non-parallel (cross-woven) collagen defeats torsion and gives tensile strength; parallel fibres would unravel under twisting.

questions.question: Long bones lengthen by replacing a cartilage model with bone, a process called:
questions.explanation: Endochondral ossification replaces a cartilage template with bone at the growth plate, driving longitudinal growth until puberty.

questions.question: Longitudinal growth of a long bone occurs at the:
questions.explanation: The epiphyseal (growth) plate between epiphysis and diaphysis is where longitudinal growth happens; it ossifies after puberty.

questions.question: Growth in the diameter of a bone (appositional growth) occurs at the:
questions.explanation: Appositional growth adds bone at the periosteum of the diaphysis (with resorption inside), widening the shaft throughout life.

questions.question: Which hormone lowers blood calcium by inhibiting osteoclasts, favouring bone formation?
questions.explanation: Calcitonin from the thyroid lowers blood calcium by inhibiting osteoclast activity, favouring formation; PTH and calcitriol raise it.

questions.question: Parathyroid hormone raises blood calcium chiefly by:
questions.explanation: Continuous PTH raises RANKL and lowers OPG, driving osteoclastic resorption and raising blood calcium.

questions.question: The final activation of vitamin D3 to calcitriol occurs in the:
questions.explanation: Vitamin D3 is activated skin/diet then liver, but the final step to 1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol (calcitriol) is in the kidney, PTH-induced.

questions.question: A DEXA T-score of which value or lower defines osteoporosis?
questions.explanation: A T-score of −2.5 or less indicates osteoporosis; the T-score compares density with a peak-bone-mass reference of the same sex.

questions.question: Osteomalacia results from a deficiency of which of the following?
questions.explanation: Osteomalacia is defective mineralisation from vitamin D deficiency; matrix is laid down but not mineralised, so bone is soft.

questions.question: Rickets differs from adult osteomalacia mainly because it also involves the:
questions.explanation: Rickets is childhood osteomalacia that also disrupts endochondral ossification at the growth plate, causing bowed legs.

questions.question: Trabeculae in spongy bone are arranged so that they:
options: A. align along lines of stress
C. run parallel to the shaft
questions.explanation: Trabeculae align along stress lines, developing from microfractures of loading, so material sits only where load demands it.

questions.question: Which change in the RANKL to OPG balance drives net bone resorption?
options: A. raised RANKL and lowered OPG
B. lowered RANKL and raised OPG
C. lowered RANKL and lowered OPG
D. raised RANKL and raised OPG
questions.explanation: RANKL activates osteoclasts and OPG is a decoy that blocks it, so raised RANKL with lowered OPG drives resorption.

questions.question: Intermittent low-dose PTH exposure is anabolic for bone, which underlies the therapy:
questions.explanation: Intermittent PTH raises osteoblast differentiation and lowers osteoblast apoptosis, an anabolic effect exploited by teriparatide.

questions.question: Loss of which hormone at menopause unleashes resorption and post-menopausal osteoporosis?
questions.explanation: Estrogens lower RANKL, raise OPG and promote osteoclast apoptosis; losing them at menopause unleashes resorption.

questions.question: Excess glucocorticoids (as in Cushing's syndrome) affect bone by favouring:
questions.explanation: Glucocorticoids raise RANKL and lower OPG like continuous PTH, favouring resorption, so excess cortisol causes osteoporosis.

questions.question: In osteopetrosis, defective osteoclasts produce bone that is:
questions.explanation: Defective osteoclasts cannot resorb, so bone accumulates dense yet weak, is never remodelled, and fills the marrow cavity causing anaemia.

questions.question: Osteogenesis imperfecta, the classic brittle-bone disease, is caused by defective:
questions.explanation: Osteogenesis imperfecta is defective collagen type I, so the organic scaffold is faulty and bones are low-mass and fracture-prone.

questions.question: Paget's disease of bone results from which cellular defect?
questions.explanation: Paget's disease is driven by dysfunctional osteoclasts, producing disorganised, thick but weak bone with deformities and fractures.

questions.question: Excess growth hormone arising after puberty produces which disorder?
questions.explanation: Excess GH after puberty causes acromegaly (more apposition of long bones); before puberty it causes gigantism.

questions.question: The bone remodelling cycle proceeds in which order?
questions.explanation: Remodelling runs activation, then osteoclastic resorption, then reversal, then osteoblastic formation refilling the cavity.

questions.question: Which theory holds that appositional growth is set by genetics rather than mechanical load?
questions.explanation: The sizostat theory says appositional growth is genetically pre-determined; the mechanostat theory ties it to mechanical forces.

pharmacology_intro_medi2004_wk1.html.title: MEDI2004 W1 · Introduction to Pharmacology
pharmacology_intro_medi2004_wk1.html.subject: Pharmacology Fundamentals
pharmacology_intro_medi2004_wk1.html.content: Drug = any substance producing a biological effect when administered (synthetic, natural, or genetically engineered). Endogenous substances aren't drugs unless administered (own insulin = hormone; injected = drug). Drug = active chemical; medicine = drug + excipients in a dose form (medicine contains the drug); drug class = drugs sharing mechanism/target/therapeutic use. Vitamins/herbs act as drugs when they produce effects (label doesn't decide). Pharmacology = study of drugs and their interactions with living systems; branches: pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, pharmacotherapeutics, toxicology, pharmacogenetics, clinical pharmacology. PK = body->drug (ADME; sets dose/timing); PD = drug->body (mechanism/effect; sets effect & side effects). Classes: analgesic (pain), anaesthetic (removes sensation), anxiolytic (anxiety), sedative (sleep), stimulant (CNS activity), antidepressant (SSRIs), antipsychotic, antihypertensive (ACE inhibitors), antineoplastic (cancer), anabolic steroid, hallucinogen, PrEP (HIV prevention). Prefixes: anti- = against, -lytic = relieves/breaks, an-/anaes- = without.

questions.question: In pharmacology, a drug is best defined as any substance that:
options: A. produces a biological effect when administered
B. is manufactured only in a laboratory
C. requires a doctor's prescription to obtain
D. is formulated into a tablet form
questions.explanation: A drug is any substance producing a biological effect when given to a living organism, regardless of source, prescription status or dose form.

questions.question: The body's own insulin is a hormone, but injected insulin is a drug because it is:
options: A. administered from outside the body
B. chemically different from natural insulin
D. present at very low concentrations
questions.explanation: A substance the body makes itself counts as a drug only when it is administered; the same molecule given from outside becomes a drug.

questions.question: Penicillin, obtained from a mould, is an example of a drug derived from:
questions.explanation: Penicillin is a natural chemical produced by a mould — a microorganism. Synthetic drugs are lab-made and biologics come from genetic engineering.

questions.question: What distinguishes a medicine from a drug?
options: A. a medicine is a drug plus excipients
B. a drug is a formulated therapeutic product
C. a medicine has no active chemical
D. a drug always contains several medicines
questions.explanation: A medicine is a drug formulated for therapeutic use — the active drug plus excipients in a dose form. The medicine contains the drug, not the reverse.

questions.question: A drug class groups together drugs that share a:
options: A. mechanism, target or therapeutic use
B. one shared chemical parent structure
C. one common manufacturing process step
D. a single route of administration
questions.explanation: Classes are grouped by shared mechanism, molecular target or therapeutic use — not by chemical family, how they're made, or route.

questions.question: Which question does pharmacokinetics answer?
options: A. what the body does to the drug
B. what the drug does to the body
C. how the drug binds its receptor
D. how the drug produces side effects
questions.explanation: Pharmacokinetics is body→drug (ADME): how the drug is handled. What the drug does to the body — receptor binding and effects — is pharmacodynamics.

questions.question: A change in a drug's ADME handling would most directly alter its:
questions.explanation: PK (ADME) mostly sets how much drug is present and when — the dose and timing. Receptor affinity, mechanism and target are pharmacodynamic properties.

questions.question: Which branch of pharmacology studies the harmful effects of chemicals and drugs?
questions.explanation: Toxicology addresses harmful effects. Pharmacogenetics studies genetic variation in response; pharmacotherapeutics the use of drugs to treat disease.

questions.question: The study of how genetic differences change drug response is called:
questions.explanation: Pharmacogenetics links inherited variation to differences in drug response. Clinical pharmacology is drug use in real patients more broadly.

questions.question: By the pharmacological definition, when is a high-dose vitamin considered a drug?
options: A. when it produces a biological effect
B. when it is labelled a supplement
C. when it is from a natural source
D. when it is taken with food
questions.explanation: The definition turns on effect, not the label: at pharmacological doses a vitamin produces drug-like effects, so it acts as a drug however it is marketed.

questions.question: A drug whose class is 'analgesic' primarily acts to:
questions.explanation: Analgesics relieve pain (e.g. paracetamol, morphine). Reducing anxiety is anxiolytic; lowering blood pressure is antihypertensive.

questions.question: The suffix '-lytic' in 'anxiolytic' indicates a drug that:
options: A. relieves or breaks something down
questions.explanation: '-lytic/-olytic' means breaks or relieves, so an anxiolytic relieves anxiety. 'anti-' means against; 'an-/anaes-' means without.

questions.question: Reading the name alone, an 'antineoplastic' drug acts against:
questions.explanation: 'anti-' means against and 'neoplastic' refers to new growths, so antineoplastics act against tumours (cytotoxic chemotherapy).

questions.question: Drugs in the 'anaesthetic' class are characterised by:
options: C. promoting tissue and muscle growth
questions.explanation: The 'an-/anaes-' root means without: anaesthetics remove sensation or consciousness. Stimulants raise CNS activity; anabolic steroids build tissue.

questions.question: Two patients given an identical dose reach very different blood levels. This is best explained by differing:
options: C. receptor densities in the patients
D. drug mechanisms in the patients
questions.explanation: Different blood levels from the same dose reflect how each body handles the drug — pharmacokinetics. Differences in effect at one level would be pharmacodynamic.

questions.question: The same blood concentration gives a strong effect in one patient and little in another. This reflects differences in:
questions.explanation: When effect differs at an identical concentration, the variation lies in how the drug acts on the body — pharmacodynamics. Absorption and excretion are PK.

questions.question: Caffeine and amphetamine belong to which drug class?
questions.explanation: Stimulants increase CNS activity. Sedatives calm and promote sleep — the opposite direction of effect.

questions.question: An ACE inhibitor used to lower blood pressure belongs to which class?
questions.explanation: 'anti-' + hypertension: antihypertensives lower blood pressure. The other 'anti-' classes target tumours, depression and psychosis.

questions.question: Pharmacology is best described as the study of:
options: A. how drugs interact with living systems
B. how medicines are manufactured in industry
C. how diseases are diagnosed in clinics
D. how medicines are stored and dispensed
questions.explanation: Pharmacology studies drugs and their interactions with living systems — spanning how drugs act and how the body handles them.

questions.question: Which statement correctly describes the relationship between a drug and a medicine?
options: A. a medicine contains a drug
B. a drug contains a medicine
C. they are identical in meaning
D. a drug excludes any excipients
questions.explanation: A medicine is the drug plus excipients in a dose form, so the medicine contains the drug. The terms are not interchangeable.

questions.question: A drug taken as pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) is used to:
questions.explanation: PrEP is pre-exposure prophylaxis — taken before potential exposure to prevent HIV infection, not to treat established disease.

questions.question: Which pair of drug classes have opposite effects on CNS activity?
questions.explanation: Sedatives calm and promote sleep while stimulants increase CNS activity — directly opposing effects. The other pairs don't oppose in that way.

questions.question: The shift from 'magical remedies' to modern pharmacology is best marked by drugs that are:
options: A. tested for proven effect and safety
B. derived only from natural plant sources
C. sold without any formal safety testing
D. based purely on tradition and belief
questions.explanation: Modern pharmacology rests on purified or synthesised drugs tested for evidence of effect and safety — the break from unregulated traditional remedies.

questions.question: Fluoxetine, an SSRI, is an example of which drug class?
questions.explanation: SSRIs such as fluoxetine treat depression and are antidepressants. Antipsychotics treat psychosis; anxiolytics reduce anxiety.

questions.question: Which branch specifically concerns drug use and effects in real patients?
questions.explanation: Clinical pharmacology studies how drugs behave and are used in actual patients. Pharmacotherapeutics is the use of drugs to treat disease more generally.

questions.question: To correct a problem caused purely by a drug's pharmacokinetics, the most logical adjustment is to:
options: A. change the dose or schedule
B. switch to a different receptor
D. select a new molecular target
questions.explanation: PK problems are about how much drug is present and when, so adjusting dose or timing addresses them; changing target or mechanism addresses PD issues.

pharmacokinetics_medi2004.html.title: MEDI2004 W2 · Pharmacokinetics
pharmacokinetics_medi2004.html.subject: Pharmacology Fundamentals
pharmacokinetics_medi2004.html.content: PK = what the body does to a drug (ADME): Absorption, Distribution, Metabolism (cytochrome P450), Excretion. Membrane crossing: passive simple diffusion dominates (no carrier, no energy); active transport moves against gradient using energy; facilitated diffusion is carrier-mediated down-gradient; pinocytosis is fluid endocytosis. Absorption = administration site -> plasma; ~75% of oral drug absorbed in 1-3 h; rate set by lipid solubility/pKa, surface area, gut content, GI transit, blood flow. pKa = pH at 50% ionised; only the uncharged form crosses; weak acid ionises as pH rises, weak base as pH falls; ion trapping accumulates drug where local pH favours ionisation (aspirin + alkaline urine). Henderson-Hasselbalch gives the unionised fraction. Routes: oral/sublingual/rectal/inhalation/injection; sublingual and rectal bypass first-pass. Bioavailability F = fraction reaching systemic circulation intact; IV F=1.0, oral <1 (first-pass + incomplete absorption); oral dose to match IV = IV/F. PK params: AUC (total exposure), Cmax (peak), Tmax (time to peak). Distribution set by perfusion, permeability, binding, fat:water partition. Compartments: plasma, interstitial, intracellular, transcellular + fat. Plasma protein binding: albumin binds acidic drugs, alpha1-acid glycoprotein binds basic; only free drug acts; displacement and low albumin raise free fraction. Vd = amount in body / plasma concentration (apparent, not anatomical); low Vd stays in plasma (warfarin), high Vd = tissue/fat uptake (paracetamol).

questions.question: Pharmacokinetics describes what the body does to a drug. Pharmacodynamics describes:
options: A. what the drug does to the body
B. how the body absorbs and clears it
C. how the drug is chemically made
D. how a dose is set per patient
questions.explanation: Pharmacodynamics is drug→body: receptor binding, effects and dose–response. Absorption and clearance are the pharmacokinetic (body→drug) side.

questions.question: Why is pharmacokinetics logically considered before pharmacodynamics?
options: A. a drug must arrive before acting
B. receptors appear before the drug arrives
C. drug effects occur before any absorption
D. metabolism happens before the drug's administration
questions.explanation: A drug can only act where it reaches and at the concentration it reaches; PK sets that exposure, so it precedes the PD question of what the drug then does.

questions.question: In the ADME scheme, which stage immediately follows absorption?
questions.explanation: ADME runs Absorption → Distribution → Metabolism → Excretion, so distribution spreads drug into tissues before it is metabolised.

questions.question: Biotransformation of most drugs is carried out largely by which enzyme system?
questions.explanation: Metabolism (the M of ADME) is mainly hepatic cytochrome P450 oxidation. ABC transporters move drugs across membranes but don't chemically transform them.

questions.question: Why does passive simple diffusion account for the movement of most drugs?
options: A. it needs no carrier and no energy
B. it moves drug against its gradient
C. it relies on a saturable carrier protein
D. it carries only large, highly charged molecules
questions.explanation: Lipid-soluble, uncharged molecules dissolve straight through the bilayer down their gradient with no carrier and no energy, so diffusion handles most drug movement.

questions.question: Which feature distinguishes active transport from facilitated diffusion?
options: A. it moves solute against a gradient
B. it moves solute down a gradient
C. it uses no membrane carrier protein
D. it operates only in the kidney
questions.explanation: Both use carriers, but active transport spends energy to pump solute against its gradient; facilitated diffusion moves solute down its gradient with no energy.

questions.question: Pinocytosis contributes to drug uptake by:
options: A. engulfing extracellular fluid into vesicles
B. pumping ions across using ATP
C. diffusing lipids through the bilayer
D. carrying glucose down its gradient
questions.explanation: Pinocytosis is fluid endocytosis — the membrane invaginates to internalise extracellular fluid and small suspended particles, unlike carrier or diffusion routes.

questions.question: Absorption is best defined as movement of a drug from:
options: A. the administration site into plasma
B. the plasma into body tissues
C. the liver into the bile
D. the kidney into the urine
questions.explanation: Absorption carries drug from where it's given into the systemic plasma. Plasma-to-tissue movement is distribution; biliary and urinary loss are excretion.

questions.question: Which change would increase the rate of drug absorption from the gut?
options: A. a larger absorptive surface area
B. a lower drug lipid solubility
C. reduced blood flow to gut
D. a more highly ionised drug
questions.explanation: More surface area, higher lipid solubility and good perfusion all speed absorption; ionisation traps drug in the charged form that cannot cross.

questions.question: For a typical oral drug, roughly what fraction is absorbed within 1–3 hours?
questions.explanation: Around 75% of an oral dose is usually absorbed in 1–3 hours, though surface area, transit time, blood flow and drug properties all shift this.

questions.question: The pKa of a drug is the pH at which:
options: A. half the drug is ionised
B. the drug is fully unionised
questions.explanation: At pH = pKa, 50% of the drug is ionised and 50% unionised. It's an intrinsic property of the drug, not a statement about metabolism or absorption.

questions.question: A weak acid crosses a membrane more readily as the local pH:
options: A. falls, favouring the uncharged form
B. rises, favouring the uncharged form
C. falls, favouring the charged form
D. rises, favouring the charged form
questions.explanation: A weak acid keeps its proton when pH is low, so a falling pH holds it uncharged and membrane-permeable; a rising pH ionises it and traps the charged form.

questions.question: For a weak acid between acidic gastric juice and pH-7.4 plasma, drug accumulates in the:
options: A. plasma, where it ionises more
B. gastric juice, where it ionises more
C. plasma, where it stays uncharged
D. gastric juice, where it stays uncharged
questions.explanation: Only the uncharged acid crosses; on the higher-pH plasma side more of it dissociates to the charged form, which can't cross back, so drug builds up in plasma.

questions.question: Alkalinising the urine speeds excretion of aspirin, a weak acid, because it:
options: A. ionises the drug within renal tubules
B. keeps the drug uncharged in tubules
C. increases tubular reabsorption of drug
D. blocks glomerular filtration of drug
questions.explanation: High tubular pH ionises the weak acid, trapping it in the filtrate so it can't be reabsorbed — it's carried out in the urine instead.

questions.question: The Henderson–Hasselbalch equation is used to calculate a drug's:
questions.explanation: From pKa and local pH it gives the fraction present in the uncharged form — the part able to cross membranes. It says nothing about Vd, metabolism or binding.

questions.question: Which route most fully avoids hepatic first-pass metabolism?
options: A. drug given under the tongue
B. drug swallowed as a tablet
C. drug given by nasogastric tube
D. drug swallowed as a solution
questions.explanation: Sublingual drug drains into systemic veins that skip the portal circulation, so it escapes first-pass. All the swallowed/gut routes reach the liver first.

questions.question: First-pass metabolism lowers oral bioavailability because absorbed drug first passes through the:
options: A. portal vein to the liver
B. systemic veins to the heart
D. renal artery to the kidney
questions.explanation: Gut absorption drains into the portal vein, so drug reaches the liver — where gut-wall and hepatic enzymes destroy much of it — before the systemic circulation.

questions.question: Bioavailability (F) is the fraction of a dose that:
options: B. is metabolised on first pass
D. is filtered by the glomerulus
questions.explanation: F is the proportion of the given dose arriving intact in the systemic blood. IV dosing is F = 1.0 by definition; first-pass and incomplete absorption drop oral F.

questions.question: By definition, the bioavailability of an intravenous dose is:
questions.explanation: IV drug enters the systemic circulation directly, so the whole dose is available: F = 1.0, with no absorption step and no first pass.

questions.question: A drug's oral bioavailability is 40%. What oral dose matches the exposure of a 20 mg IV dose?
questions.explanation: Only fraction F of an oral dose reaches the blood, so oral dose = IV ÷ F = 20 mg ÷ 0.4 = 50 mg. Multiplying by F instead gives the 8 mg error.

questions.question: On a concentration–time curve, the area under the curve (AUC) represents:
options: C. the time to reach peak
questions.explanation: AUC integrates concentration over time, giving total exposure. The peak height is Cmax and the time to that peak is Tmax.

questions.question: Tmax on a plasma concentration–time curve is the:
options: A. time to reach peak concentration
B. peak concentration that is reached
C. total exposure over all time
D. time for concentration to halve
questions.explanation: Tmax is when the peak (Cmax) occurs. Cmax is the peak value, AUC is total exposure, and the halving time is the half-life.

questions.question: Distribution refers to a drug's movement:
options: B. from the gut into plasma
C. out through bile and urine
questions.explanation: Distribution spreads drug between plasma and tissue compartments. Gut-to-plasma is absorption, biliary/urinary loss is excretion, P450 changes are metabolism.

questions.question: Which factor most directly limits how fast a drug enters a poorly perfused tissue?
options: A. blood flow to that tissue
questions.explanation: Distribution depends on delivery, so perfusion sets how fast drug reaches a tissue; poorly perfused tissues equilibrate slowly regardless of dose or route.

questions.question: Lipophilic drugs tend to accumulate in which compartment?
questions.explanation: The non-polar fat compartment takes up lipid-soluble drug as a reservoir; the aqueous compartments hold water-soluble drug.

questions.question: Which form of a drug is able to leave the plasma and enter tissues?
questions.explanation: Only free drug crosses capillary walls into tissue; protein-bound drug is too large to leave the plasma until it dissociates.

questions.question: In plasma, albumin binds mainly which class of drugs?
questions.explanation: Albumin carries mostly acidic drugs, while α₁-acid glycoprotein carries mostly basic drugs. Both hold drug in an inactive, bound reservoir.

questions.question: Which statement about plasma protein binding is correct?
options: A. only unbound drug produces effect
B. only bound drug produces effect
C. bound and free are equally active
questions.explanation: Only the free fraction can leave plasma to act; the bound fraction is a reversible, inactive reservoir in equilibrium with free drug.

questions.question: Adding a second highly protein-bound drug can cause toxicity by:
options: A. raising the first drug's free fraction
B. lowering the first drug's free fraction
C. speeding renal filtration of both
D. blocking absorption of both drugs
questions.explanation: The two drugs compete for albumin, so one displaces the other and suddenly raises its free, active concentration — the classic warfarin-bleeding interaction.

questions.question: In a patient with low plasma albumin, the free fraction of a highly bound drug will:
questions.explanation: Fewer binding sites means less drug held in the bound reservoir, so the free, active fraction increases — raising the risk of effect or toxicity.

questions.question: The apparent volume of distribution (Vd) is best described as:
options: A. an apparent, not anatomical, volume
B. the true volume of plasma
C. the volume of total body fat
D. the volume filtered per minute
questions.explanation: Vd is a proportionality constant linking dose to plasma concentration; it can exceed body water and maps to no real anatomical space.

questions.question: A 500 mg dose gives a plasma concentration of 10 mg/L. The apparent Vd is:
questions.explanation: Vd = amount in body ÷ plasma concentration = 500 mg ÷ 10 mg/L = 50 L. Dividing the other way gives the 0.02 L error.

questions.question: A drug with a very small Vd, near the plasma volume, is most likely:
options: A. highly bound to plasma proteins
B. highly concentrated in body fat
C. widely bound within deep tissues
D. rapidly cleared by the kidney
questions.explanation: Heavy plasma-protein binding keeps drug in the blood, so it appears to occupy little more than the plasma volume — warfarin is the classic small-Vd example.

questions.question: Which finding best explains a drug whose Vd greatly exceeds total body water?
options: A. extensive uptake into tissues and fat
B. tight confinement to the plasma pool
C. very rapid urinary drug excretion
D. complete binding to plasma albumin
questions.explanation: When a lipophilic drug leaves plasma for tissues and fat, little remains in blood, so the apparent volume can exceed the body's actual water volume.

respiratory_anatomy_pt2_mhhs2402.html.title: MHHS2402 W2 · Respiratory Anatomy II
respiratory_anatomy_pt2_mhhs2402.html.subject: Cardiovascular, Renal & Respiratory Systems
respiratory_anatomy_pt2_mhhs2402.html.content: Neck posterior triangle: CN XI, brachial plexus, subclavian vessels. Carotid sheath: vagus (X), internal jugular vein, common carotid. Larynx cartilages: thyroid, cricoid (only complete ring), arytenoid, corniculate, epiglottis; true cord=vocal fold. Posterior cricoarytenoid = only abductor; recurrent laryngeal supplies all intrinsic except cricothyroid. Ribs: true 1-7, false 8-10, floating 11-12. Diaphragm hiatuses: caval T8, oesophageal T10, aortic T12; phrenic C3-5 -> referred shoulder pain. Intercostal bundle VAN in costal groove; chest drain above the lower rib. Parietal pleura=somatic (pain), visceral=autonomic. Right lung 3 lobes (oblique+horizontal), left 2 lobes+cardiac notch. Type I pneumocyte=gas exchange, Type II=surfactant.

questions.question: Which laryngeal cartilage is the only COMPLETE ring?
questions.explanation: The cricoid is the only complete cartilage ring; the thyroid is a shield open at the back.

questions.question: The 'true' vocal cords are also known as the:
questions.explanation: The true cords are the vocal folds (phonation); the false cords are the vestibular folds.

questions.question: Which nerve supplies the diaphragm?
questions.explanation: The phrenic nerve (C3–C5) gives motor and sensory supply to the diaphragm.

questions.question: How many lobes does the LEFT lung have?
questions.explanation: The left lung has 2 lobes plus a cardiac notch; the right has 3.

questions.question: How many lobes does the RIGHT lung have?
questions.explanation: The right lung has 3 lobes (oblique + horizontal fissures); the left has 2.

questions.question: Which alveolar cell produces surfactant?
questions.explanation: Type II pneumocytes make surfactant; Type I pneumocytes are the thin gas-exchange cells.

questions.question: Gas exchange across the alveolar wall occurs mainly through which cell?
questions.explanation: Thin Type I pneumocytes form most of the alveolar surface for gas exchange.

questions.question: The main muscle of quiet inspiration is the:
questions.explanation: The diaphragm increases the vertical dimension of the thorax during quiet inspiration.

questions.question: Which pleura directly covers the lung surface?
questions.explanation: Visceral pleura covers the lung; parietal pleura lines the thoracic wall.

questions.question: Which muscle divides the neck into anterior and posterior triangles?
questions.explanation: Sternocleidomastoid divides the neck; trapezius forms the posterior boundary of the posterior triangle.

questions.question: Which intrinsic laryngeal muscle is the ONLY abductor of the vocal cords?
questions.explanation: The posterior cricoarytenoid is the sole abductor (opens the cords); the others adduct or tense them.

questions.question: Most intrinsic laryngeal muscles are supplied by which nerve?
questions.explanation: The recurrent laryngeal nerve (from the vagus) supplies all intrinsic muscles except cricothyroid.

questions.question: The suprahyoid muscles act to:
options: A. elevate the hyoid and larynx
B. depress the hyoid and larynx
questions.explanation: Suprahyoids (digastric, mylohyoid) elevate the hyoid and larynx; infrahyoids depress them.

questions.question: Which pleura is pain-sensitive, and why?
questions.explanation: Parietal pleura has somatic innervation (intercostal and phrenic) and is pain-sensitive; visceral pleura is not.

questions.question: True ribs (1–7) attach to the sternum by:
options: B. the costal cartilage of rib 7
questions.explanation: True ribs (1–7) each have their own costal cartilage to the sternum; false ribs share or float.

questions.question: The central non-muscular part of the diaphragm is the:
questions.explanation: Muscle fibres converge on the central tendon; the crura anchor the diaphragm to the lumbar spine.

questions.question: The oesophageal hiatus of the diaphragm is at which vertebral level?
questions.explanation: The oesophageal hiatus is at T10 (with the vagus); caval hiatus T8, aortic hiatus T12.

questions.question: In the costal groove, the intercostal neurovascular bundle runs in what order (top to bottom)?
questions.explanation: From superior to inferior in the costal groove it is Vein, Artery, Nerve (VAN).

questions.question: The cardiac notch is a feature of which lung?
questions.explanation: The cardiac notch and lingula are on the left lung, making room for the heart.

questions.question: Phonation (voice production) occurs at which laryngeal division?
questions.explanation: The glottis — the vocal folds and rima glottidis — is the phonation region of the larynx.

questions.question: The caval opening (IVC) passes through the diaphragm at which level?
questions.explanation: The caval hiatus is at T8, through the central tendon, with the right phrenic nerve.

questions.question: The aortic hiatus of the diaphragm lies at which vertebral level?
questions.explanation: The aortic hiatus is at T12, behind the diaphragm, transmitting the aorta, thoracic duct and azygos vein.

questions.question: The internal laryngeal nerve provides which function?
options: A. sensation above the vocal cords
B. sensation below the vocal cords
C. motor to the cricothyroid muscle
D. motor to all intrinsic muscles
questions.explanation: The internal laryngeal nerve (from the superior laryngeal) is sensory above the vocal cords.

questions.question: The external laryngeal nerve supplies which single muscle?
questions.explanation: The external laryngeal nerve is motor to cricothyroid, which tenses the vocal cords.

questions.question: How do the bronchial arteries differ from the pulmonary circulation?
options: A. they nourish lung tissue from the aorta
B. they carry the blood for gas exchange
C. they drain the lungs into the heart
D. they supply only the pleura
questions.explanation: Bronchial arteries (from the thoracic aorta) nourish the lung tissue; the pulmonary arteries carry blood for gas exchange.

questions.question: Why is the RIGHT main bronchus the more common site of foreign-body aspiration?
options: A. wider, shorter and more vertical
B. narrower, longer and more horizontal
C. the same shape as the left
D. blocked by the aortic arch
questions.explanation: The right main bronchus is wider, shorter and more vertical, so inhaled objects tend to lodge there.

questions.question: The conducting zone differs from the respiratory zone in that it:
options: A. has no alveoli and no gas exchange
B. holds most of the body's alveoli
C. is the main site of gas exchange
D. contains no airways at all
questions.explanation: The conducting zone (trachea to terminal bronchioles) moves air but has no alveoli, so no gas exchange.

questions.question: The right oblique fissure of the lung roughly follows which rib?
questions.explanation: The oblique fissure runs from about T4 along the 6th rib to the 6th costal cartilage.

questions.question: Phrenic nerve palsy typically causes:
options: C. complete loss of all breathing
D. spasm of the vocal cords
questions.explanation: Losing phrenic supply paralyses a hemidiaphragm, which then sits raised and moves paradoxically.

questions.question: In the pulmonary plexus, sympathetic activity to the airway causes:
questions.explanation: Sympathetic activity dilates the bronchi (bronchodilation); parasympathetic activity constricts them.

cell_organisation_study_guide.html.title: MEDI2200 W1 · Cell Organisation
cell_organisation_study_guide.html.subject: Cell Biology
cell_organisation_study_guide.html.content: Cell theory: all living things built from cells. Shared by all cells: boundary membrane, DNA (DNA->RNA->protein), ATP, ribosomes, common ancestor, dynamic. Prokaryotes (no nucleus/membrane organelles, DNA in nucleoid, binary fission, peptidoglycan wall) vs eukaryotes (nucleus + organelles, mitosis/meiosis). Domains: Bacteria + Archaea (prokaryotic), Eucarya (eukaryotic). Membrane = phospholipid bilayer (amphipathic: hydrophilic heads out, hydrophobic tails in), fluid mosaic, proteins (receptors/channels/carriers/adhesion), cholesterol. Cytoplasm = all inside membrane except nucleus. Cytoskeleton: microfilaments (actin, shape/contraction), intermediate filaments (strength), microtubules (tracks + spindle). Nucleus: double membrane (outer continuous with ER), nuclear pores, lamina, chromatin (heterochromatin packed/silent, euchromatin loose/active), nucleolus makes ribosomes. Rough ER (ribosomes, proteins) vs smooth ER (lipids/steroids, detox, Ca storage). Golgi: modify/sort/ship, cis (receive from ER) -> trans (ship). Lysosome (acidic pH ~4.5-5 hydrolytic enzymes, digests engulfed material + autophagy); peroxisome (oxidation, catalase, H2O2, fatty acids). Mitochondrion: double membrane, inner folded into cristae (surface area), matrix (respiration enzymes + own DNA), makes ATP by respiration. Centrosome = MTOC + pair of centrioles, builds mitotic spindle.

questions.question: The cell theory states that all living things are:
questions.explanation: Cell theory holds that cells are the basic units of all living things — every organism is built from one or more cells.

questions.question: Which feature is shared by every cell, prokaryote or eukaryote?
options: D. a rigid peptidoglycan cell wall
questions.explanation: All cells have ribosomes, a boundary membrane, DNA-based information and ATP. A nucleus and mitochondria are eukaryote-only; peptidoglycan walls are bacterial.

questions.question: The universal flow of genetic information in cells is:
options: A. DNA to RNA to protein
B. protein to RNA to DNA
C. RNA to DNA to protein
D. DNA to protein to RNA
questions.explanation: Information flows DNA → RNA → protein: DNA is transcribed to RNA, which is translated into protein.

questions.question: Prokaryotic cells are defined by their lack of:
questions.explanation: Prokaryotes ('before nucleus') have no nucleus and no membrane-bound organelles — their DNA sits loose in the cytoplasm as a nucleoid.

questions.question: Which domain of life is eukaryotic?
questions.explanation: Of the three domains, only Eucarya is eukaryotic. Bacteria and Archaea are both prokaryotic; viruses aren't a cellular domain.

questions.question: Prokaryotes typically reproduce by:
questions.explanation: Prokaryotes divide by binary fission — a fast, simple split. Mitosis and meiosis are eukaryotic division mechanisms.

questions.question: A phospholipid bilayer self-assembles because each phospholipid has:
options: A. a hydrophilic head and hydrophobic tails
B. two hydrophilic heads and no tails
D. a rigid crystalline lipid structure
questions.explanation: Each phospholipid is amphipathic — a hydrophilic head and hydrophobic tails — so in water the tails hide inward and heads face out, forming a self-sealing bilayer.

questions.question: The 'fluid mosaic' description of the membrane means that:
options: A. lipids and proteins can drift sideways
B. the membrane is rigid and quite fixed
C. only proteins can move within it
D. it contains no embedded proteins
questions.explanation: Membrane lipids and embedded proteins are free to move laterally, giving a fluid, mosaic-like sheet rather than a rigid wall.

questions.question: Transmembrane channel and carrier proteins in the cell membrane mainly:
options: A. let specific molecules cross it
C. store the cell's genetic code
D. generate the cell's ATP supply
questions.explanation: Channels and carriers admit specific molecules; receptors relay signals and adhesion proteins bind cells. Protein synthesis, DNA storage and ATP are other structures' jobs.

questions.question: Which cytoskeletal filament forms the spindle that separates chromosomes?
questions.explanation: Microtubules (the thickest filaments) act as tracks for motor proteins and build the mitotic spindle. Actin microfilaments drive shape/contraction; intermediate filaments give strength.

questions.question: Actin microfilaments are chiefly responsible for:
options: D. storing the cell's genetic code
questions.explanation: The thinnest filaments, actin microfilaments, drive cell shape and muscle contraction. Microtubules build the spindle; intermediate filaments give strength.

questions.question: The outer membrane of the nuclear envelope is continuous with the:
questions.explanation: The nuclear envelope is a double membrane whose outer layer is continuous with the ER — reflecting their shared membrane network.

questions.question: The nucleolus is the site where the cell assembles its:
questions.explanation: The dense nucleolus assembles ribosomes. Remember: nucleolus makes ribosomes (both carry the 'o').

questions.question: Compared with euchromatin, heterochromatin is:
options: A. tightly packed and transcriptionally silent
B. loosely packed and actively transcribed
C. found only outside the cell nucleus
D. made entirely of ribosomal RNA
questions.explanation: Heterochromatin is condensed and silent; euchromatin is loose and actively transcribed. Packing state controls gene accessibility.

questions.question: The rough endoplasmic reticulum, studded with ribosomes, mainly:
options: C. generates ATP for the cell
questions.explanation: Rough ER (Rough = Ribosomes = pRoteins) makes and folds proteins for membranes, secretion or lysosomes. Smooth ER makes lipids and steroids.

questions.question: Which function is carried out by the smooth endoplasmic reticulum?
questions.explanation: Smooth ER has no ribosomes; it makes lipids and steroids, detoxifies, and stores calcium. Protein folding is the rough ER's role.

questions.question: In the Golgi apparatus, vesicles arriving from the ER fuse at the:
questions.explanation: The Golgi has a cis (receiving) face toward the ER and a trans (shipping) face; products move cis → trans, being modified along the way.

questions.question: The main role of the Golgi apparatus is to:
options: A. modify, sort and ship products
questions.explanation: The Golgi is the post office: it receives ER products, modifies and labels them (e.g. adds sugars), then sorts and ships them onward.

questions.question: Lysosomal digestive enzymes work only at acidic pH, which serves as:
options: A. a safety catch if they leak out
B. a way to speed up ATP synthesis
C. a signal to build more ribosomes
D. a trigger for the cell to divide
questions.explanation: Because the enzymes need pH ~4.5–5, any that leak into the neutral cytosol do little harm — a built-in safety catch protecting the cell.

questions.question: A lysosome's main function is to:
options: A. digest engulfed material and organelles
C. assemble the ribosomal subunits fully
D. package proteins ready for export
questions.explanation: The lysosome is a membrane sac of hydrolytic enzymes that breaks down engulfed material and worn-out organelles (autophagy).

questions.question: Autophagy refers to the cell:
options: A. digesting its own damaged organelles
C. secreting material out of itself
questions.explanation: Autophagy ('self-eating') sends damaged organelles in an autophagosome to fuse with a lysosome for digestion. Engulfing external particles is phagocytosis.

questions.question: Peroxisomes, which contain catalase, specialise in:
questions.explanation: Peroxisomes run oxidation reactions, make and then destroy hydrogen peroxide via catalase, and break down fatty acids.

questions.question: The mitochondrion's main job is to:
options: A. generate ATP by cellular respiration
B. synthesise and fold new proteins
D. store the cell's genetic material
questions.explanation: Mitochondria generate most of the cell's ATP by cellular respiration using oxygen — the powerhouse of the cell.

questions.question: The inner mitochondrial membrane is folded into cristae in order to:
options: A. increase surface area for ATP synthesis
B. store the cell's genetic material
C. seal the organelle from the cytosol
questions.explanation: ATP is made on the inner membrane, so folding it into cristae packs a huge surface area into a small organelle — more membrane, more ATP.

questions.question: Which two organelles both have a double membrane?
questions.explanation: Both the mitochondrion and the nucleus are bounded by a double membrane. The Golgi, lysosome and ER each have a single membrane.

questions.question: The centrosome (with its pair of centrioles) functions as the:
questions.explanation: The centrosome is the microtubule-organising centre; before division it duplicates and builds the mitotic spindle that separates chromosomes.

questions.question: All traffic between the nucleus and cytoplasm passes through the:
questions.explanation: Nuclear pores bridge both layers of the nuclear envelope and gate all molecular traffic in and out of the nucleus.

questions.question: The cytoplasm is best described as everything inside the membrane:
questions.explanation: Cytoplasm is all membrane-enclosed contents except the nucleus — the organelles plus the jelly-like cytosol.

questions.question: The rigid cell wall of a bacterium is made mainly of:
questions.explanation: Bacterial walls are built of peptidoglycan, giving shape and protection. Cellulose walls are found in plants, not bacteria.

questions.question: Cells look different outside but similar inside mainly because they:
options: A. descend from a common ancestor
B. all perform the exact same job
C. were built at the same time
D. cannot change their shape at all
questions.explanation: Shared descent from one ancestral cell means all cells inherited the same core toolkit — membrane, DNA, ribosomes, ATP — while shape diverged to suit each job.

respiratory_anatomy_pt1.html.title: MHHS2402 W1 · Respiratory Anatomy I
respiratory_anatomy_pt1.html.subject: Cardiovascular, Renal & Respiratory Systems
respiratory_anatomy_pt1.html.content: Skull: 22 bones (8 cranial + 14 facial); key respiratory bones = ethmoid & sphenoid. Ethmoid: cribriform plate (roof), perpendicular plate (septum), conchae (lateral wall). Nasal septum = perpendicular plate of ethmoid + vomer + septal cartilage. Cranial fossae: anterior (frontal/ethmoid/sphenoid), middle (sphenoid/temporal), posterior (temporal/occipital). Foramen=through, fossa=sit in, sinus=air cavity. CN I olfactory through cribriform plate; CN V trigeminal (face sensation + chewing) V1 superior orbital fissure, V2 foramen rotundum, V3 foramen ovale (all sphenoid); CN IX & X through jugular foramen (posterior fossa). Olfactory nerve != bulb != tract.
