questions.question: Which two skull bones are the key 'respiratory' bones of the nasal airway?
questions.explanation: The ethmoid (roof, walls, upper septum) and the vomer (lower septum) build the bony nasal airway.

questions.question: The lower bony nasal septum is formed by which bone?
questions.explanation: The bony septum is the perpendicular plate of the ethmoid above plus the vomer below.

questions.question: Which cranial fossa is the most anterior?
questions.explanation: The anterior cranial fossa is most forward; its floor includes the cribriform plate.

questions.question: The olfactory nerve (CN I) reaches the brain by passing through the:
questions.explanation: Olfactory (CN I) axons pass through the cribriform plate of the ethmoid to the olfactory bulb.

questions.question: The chief role of the trigeminal nerve (CN V) is:
questions.explanation: CN V (trigeminal) is the main sensory nerve of the face, with motor fibres to the chewing muscles.

questions.question: In bone terminology, a 'foramen' is:
options: A. a hole or opening in bone
B. a shallow depression in the bone
C. an air-filled cavity within bone
D. a rounded projection on bone
questions.explanation: A foramen is a hole or opening in bone through which nerves or vessels pass; a fossa is a depression, a sinus an air space.

questions.question: The glossopharyngeal (IX) and vagus (X) nerves leave the skull through the:
questions.explanation: CN IX, X and XI exit via the jugular foramen; CN I uses the cribriform plate.

questions.question: Which cranial nerve carries the sense of smell?
questions.explanation: The olfactory nerve (CN I) carries smell from the olfactory epithelium through the cribriform plate.

questions.question: The ethmoid contributes ALL of the following to the nasal cavity EXCEPT the:
questions.explanation: The ethmoid gives the cribriform plate, perpendicular plate, crista galli and conchae; the vomer is a separate bone.

questions.question: The cribriform plate forms part of the floor of which fossa?
questions.explanation: The cribriform plate floors part of the anterior cranial fossa and roofs the nasal cavity.

questions.question: The three divisions of the trigeminal nerve all exit through foramina in which bone?
questions.explanation: All three trigeminal divisions leave through the sphenoid — V1 superior orbital fissure, V2 foramen rotundum, V3 foramen ovale.

questions.question: Which trigeminal division exits through the foramen rotundum?
questions.explanation: V2 (maxillary) exits via the foramen rotundum; V1 via the superior orbital fissure, V3 via the foramen ovale.

questions.question: The superior and middle nasal conchae are projections of which bone?
questions.explanation: The superior and middle conchae are ethmoid; the inferior concha is a separate bone.

questions.question: The respiratory mucosa lining the nasal cavity chiefly serves to:
options: A. warm, humidify and filter air
B. detect the smell of the air
C. produce new red blood cells
D. drain the tears into the nose
questions.explanation: Respiratory mucosa warms, humidifies and filters inspired air before it reaches the lungs.

questions.question: Olfactory receptor neurons are located in the:
questions.explanation: The olfactory epithelium in the roof of the nasal cavity holds the smell receptor neurons.

questions.question: The crista galli, an attachment for the falx cerebri, is a projection of the:
questions.explanation: The crista galli projects up from the ethmoid's cribriform plate and anchors the falx cerebri.

questions.question: The perpendicular plate of the ethmoid forms which part of the septum?
questions.explanation: The perpendicular plate of the ethmoid forms the upper bony septum; the vomer forms the lower part.

questions.question: The ophthalmic division (V1) of the trigeminal exits the skull through the:
questions.explanation: V1 (ophthalmic) leaves via the superior orbital fissure; V2 the foramen rotundum, V3 the foramen ovale.

questions.question: The mandibular division (V3) of the trigeminal exits through the:
questions.explanation: V3 (mandibular) exits via the foramen ovale and is the only trigeminal division carrying motor fibres.

questions.question: Besides IX and X, which other cranial nerve passes through the jugular foramen?
questions.explanation: The jugular foramen transmits CN IX, X and XI — glossopharyngeal, vagus and accessory.

questions.question: After crossing the cribriform plate, olfactory axons synapse in the:
questions.explanation: After crossing the cribriform plate, olfactory nerve fibres synapse in the olfactory bulb.

questions.question: The middle cranial fossa is largely formed by which bone and houses which lobes?
questions.explanation: The sphenoid, with the temporal bone, forms the middle cranial fossa, which cradles the temporal lobes.

questions.question: The nasal conchae improve air conditioning mainly by:
options: A. adding surface area and turbulence
B. cooling and drying the air
questions.explanation: The scroll-like conchae increase mucosal surface area and create turbulence, improving warming, humidifying and filtering.

questions.question: Which single bone provides the cribriform plate, crista galli, perpendicular plate and conchae?
questions.explanation: The cribriform plate, crista galli, perpendicular plate and superior/middle conchae are all parts of the ethmoid.

posterior_forearm_wrist_mhhs2401_wk3.htm.title: MHHS2401 W3 PI · Posterior Forearm & Wrist
posterior_forearm_wrist_mhhs2401_wk3.htm.subject: Musculoskeletal System
posterior_forearm_wrist_mhhs2401_wk3.htm.content: L4: posterior forearm extensors, hand bones, wrist joint, fractures and healing.

questions.question: The muscles of the posterior forearm are all supplied by which nerve?
questions.explanation: The posterior compartment is supplied by the radial nerve or its deep branch, so one lesion can cause wrist-drop.

questions.question: How many carpal bones are there in the wrist?
questions.explanation: There are eight carpal bones arranged in two rows of four; beyond them lie five metacarpals and fourteen phalanges.

questions.question: The radiocarpal (wrist) joint is which type of synovial joint?
questions.explanation: The wrist is a synovial condyloid (ellipsoid) joint, allowing movement in two planes plus circumduction.

questions.question: Which muscle is the principal extensor of the medial four fingers?
questions.explanation: Extensor digitorum sends four tendons to digits 2 to 5 and is the main opener of the fingers.

questions.question: Which carpal bone forms the floor of the anatomical snuffbox?
questions.explanation: The scaphoid forms the snuffbox floor, so snuffbox tenderness suggests a scaphoid fracture until proven otherwise.

questions.question: Although it lies in the extensor compartment, brachioradialis actually acts to:
questions.explanation: Brachioradialis passes anterior to the elbow axis, so it flexes the elbow despite living among the extensors.

questions.question: Most superficial posterior forearm muscles share a common origin on the:
questions.explanation: The common extensor origin is on the lateral epicondyle; brachioradialis is the exception, arising from the supracondylar ridge.

questions.question: Extensor carpi radialis longus and brevis extend the wrist and also produce:
questions.explanation: The radial wrist extensors deviate the wrist radially; extensor carpi ulnaris deviates it toward the ulnar side.

questions.question: The central band of the extensor expansion inserts on the:
questions.explanation: The central band inserts on the middle phalanx to extend the PIP joint, while the two lateral bands reach the distal phalanx.

questions.question: Tennis elbow is a tendinopathy at which bony landmark?
questions.explanation: Tennis elbow is lateral epicondylitis, microtrauma of the common extensor tendon, worsened by resisted wrist extension.

questions.question: The deep branch of the radial nerve passes between the two heads of which muscle?
questions.explanation: The deep radial nerve pierces the supinator, dividing it into two heads, and continues as the posterior interosseous nerve.

questions.question: The deep thumb and index muscles are all supplied by which nerve?
questions.explanation: The posterior interosseous nerve, the continuation of the deep radial nerve, supplies the supinator and the outcropping thumb and index muscles.

questions.question: Which of these bones belongs to the proximal carpal row?
questions.explanation: The proximal row is scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum and pisiform; the trapezium, trapezoid, capitate and hamate form the distal row.

questions.question: Which two carpal bones mainly articulate with the distal radius at the wrist?
questions.explanation: The scaphoid and lunate form the carpal side of the radiocarpal joint, with the triquetrum joining in ulnar deviation.

questions.question: The ulna is kept out of the wrist joint by the:
questions.explanation: A triangular fibrocartilage articular disc caps the ulnar head and separates the ulna from the carpal bones.

questions.question: How many phalanges does the thumb have?
questions.explanation: The thumb has two phalanges (proximal and distal), whereas each finger has three.

questions.question: The extensor retinaculum at the wrist mainly serves to:
questions.explanation: The extensor retinaculum straps the tendons against the wrist so they do not bowstring on extension, and divides them into six compartments.

questions.question: Radial deviation of the wrist is limited to about 15 degrees by the:
questions.explanation: The radial styloid projects further distally than the ulnar styloid and jams against the carpus, capping radial deviation near 15 degrees.

questions.question: A scaphoid waist fracture risks avascular necrosis because its blood supply runs:
options: A. retrograde from distal to proximal
B. straight up from proximal to distal
C. only through the articular disc
D. from the ulnar artery alone
questions.explanation: The scaphoid's blood supply enters distally and runs retrograde, so a waist fracture can cut off the proximal fragment.

questions.question: The medial border of the anatomical snuffbox is formed by the tendon of:
questions.explanation: Extensor pollicis longus forms the medial snuffbox border; extensor pollicis brevis and abductor pollicis longus form the lateral border.

questions.question: Powerful supination against resistance with the elbow flexed is driven chiefly by the:
questions.explanation: Biceps is the powerful supinator when the elbow is flexed; the supinator muscle dominates slow, unresisted turning with the elbow extended.

questions.question: Compression of the posterior interosseous nerve in the supinator typically causes:
options: A. finger drop without sensory loss
B. numbness over the whole hand
C. complete loss of wrist extension
questions.explanation: The nerve is purely motor there, so entrapment gives finger drop with no sensory loss, and wrist extension is preserved via ECRL.

questions.question: The extensor pollicis longus tendon changes direction by hooking around which landmark?
questions.explanation: Extensor pollicis longus uses Lister's tubercle on the dorsal radius as a pulley to redirect its pull to the thumb tip.

questions.question: The pisiform bone is best classified as a:
options: B. bone of the distal row
questions.explanation: The pisiform is a sesamoid bone within the flexor carpi ulnaris tendon, sitting on the palmar side of the proximal carpal row.

questions.question: A fall on the outstretched hand transmits force up the radius, classically fracturing the:
questions.explanation: Because the hand hangs off the radius, force from a fall runs up it and fractures its distal end, a Colles' fracture.

questions.question: The palmar radiocarpal ligaments are thicker than the dorsal ones because we habitually load the wrist in:
questions.explanation: We take load on an extended wrist when pushing or breaking a fall, which tensions and thickens the palmar ligaments.

questions.question: A boxer's fracture typically breaks the shaft or neck of which bone?
questions.explanation: A boxer's fracture typically breaks the fifth metacarpal from a punch delivered with a closed fist.

questions.question: Which deep muscle abducts and extends the thumb at the carpometacarpal joint?
questions.explanation: Abductor pollicis longus, the most lateral outcrop muscle, abducts and extends the thumb at the CMC joint.

drug_metabolism_excretion_medi2004_wk3.h.title: MEDI2004 W3 · Drug Elimination
drug_metabolism_excretion_medi2004_wk3.h.subject: Pharmacology Fundamentals
drug_metabolism_excretion_medi2004_wk3.h.content: Elimination = irreversible removal via metabolism (liver) + excretion (kidney). Strategy: make lipid-soluble drugs water-soluble so kidney can excrete them. Metabolism = enzymatic chemical change of xenobiotics. Metabolites can be less/more/inactive; prodrug (codeine->morphine via CYP2D6) inactive until metabolised. Phase 1 (functionalisation) = oxidation/reduction/hydrolysis, adds polar group, catabolic, can be more toxic (paracetamol->NAPQI, cleared by glutathione; overdose treated with N-acetylcysteine). CYP450 in smooth ER of hepatocytes; big five (1A2, 2C9, 2C19, 2D6, 3A4) do >50%; 3A4 busiest, grapefruit inhibits it. Phase 2 = conjugation (transferase, glucuronic acid/sulfate/glutathione), anabolic, usually inactive + very water-soluble. Stereoselectivity: warfarin S-form ~3-5x more potent, metabolised by CYP2C9. Factors: genetic polymorphism (acetylators), induction (slow, level falls, failure) vs inhibition (fast, level rises, toxicity), saturation, disease. Codeine + CYP2D6 inhibitor (fluoxetine) = no analgesia. Alcohol: ADH->acetaldehyde->acetate (ALDH; disulfiram blocks), CYP2E1, zero-order. Excretion: renal main; 25-30% excreted unchanged (renal impairment->toxicity); other routes hepatobiliary (MW>350, conjugates), pulmonary, sweat/saliva/tears, breast milk. Renal 3 processes: glomerular filtration (not protein-bound), active tubular secretion (OAT acidic, OCT basic), passive reabsorption (lipid-soluble). Enterohepatic circulation (bile->gut->reabsorption; gut bacteria cleave glucuronides; prolongs half-life; probenecid blocks OAT->penicillin high). PK params: F, Vd=amount/Cp (apparent), CL (volume cleared/time, sets maintenance dose = CL x target), t1/2 (time to halve; =0.693*Vd/CL; ~6 t1/2 to clear; kel=0.693/t1/2), Css (rate in=rate out, 3-5 t1/2; oral Css=F*Dose/(CL*T)). First-order (constant fraction, most drugs) vs zero-order (constant amount, saturation, alcohol/phenytoin). Two-compartment model: central (plasma) + peripheral (tissue); distribution then elimination.

questions.question: Drug elimination is the irreversible removal of a drug by:
questions.explanation: Elimination irreversibly removes drug two ways — metabolism (chemically changing it) and excretion (physically removing it). Absorption and distribution get it in and around.

questions.question: The body's core strategy for eliminating most drugs is to make them:
options: A. more water-soluble for renal excretion
B. more lipid-soluble for renal excretion
C. more tightly protein-bound in plasma
D. more volatile for lung excretion
questions.explanation: Lipid-soluble drugs are reabsorbed in the tubule and never leave, so metabolism converts them to water-soluble products the kidney can excrete.

questions.question: Which two organs are most important for drug elimination?
questions.explanation: The liver is the main site of metabolism and the kidney the main site of excretion — the two organs that dominate elimination.

questions.question: Biotransformation of a drug refers to the:
options: A. enzymatic chemical change of drug
B. physical filtration of the drug
C. reversible binding of the drug
D. passive reabsorption of the drug
questions.explanation: Metabolism (biotransformation) is the enzymatic chemical modification of a drug, mostly in the liver — it changes the molecule rather than just moving or removing it.

questions.question: Codeine is described as a prodrug because it is:
options: A. inactive until metabolised to morphine
B. active until metabolised to morphine
C. excreted unchanged by the kidney
D. bound irreversibly to plasma protein
questions.explanation: A prodrug is given inactive and switched on by metabolism; CYP2D6 converts codeine to active morphine — so metabolism can create activity, not only remove it.

questions.question: Which statement about drug metabolites is correct?
options: A. they may be more active than parent
B. they are always less active than parent
C. they are always completely inactive
D. they are always more toxic than parent
questions.explanation: Metabolism can yield less-active, more-active or inactive products — equating it with inactivation is a trap, since codeine becomes the more active morphine.

questions.question: Phase 1 metabolism typically involves which type of reaction?
options: C. conjugation with a sulfate group
D. active transport into the bile
questions.explanation: Phase 1 (functionalisation) uses oxidation, reduction or hydrolysis to add a polar handle. Conjugation reactions belong to Phase 2.

questions.question: A key caution about Phase 1 metabolism is that its products:
options: A. can be more toxic than parent
B. are always safer than the parent
C. are always ready for excretion
D. can never be further metabolised
questions.explanation: Phase 1 can create reactive, more toxic metabolites — paracetamol's NAPQI is the classic example, normally mopped up by Phase 2 glutathione conjugation.

questions.question: In paracetamol overdose, liver injury occurs when the cofactor that clears NAPQI is:
options: B. glucuronic acid, which is overproduced
D. acetate, which becomes fully saturated
questions.explanation: NAPQI is normally conjugated with glutathione; in overdose glutathione runs out, NAPQI accumulates and injures the liver — treated by replenishing it with N-acetylcysteine.

questions.question: The cytochrome P450 enzymes are mainly located in the:
options: A. smooth endoplasmic reticulum of hepatocytes
B. mitochondrial matrix of the hepatocytes
C. lysosomes of the kidney tubule cells
D. plasma membrane of the red cells
questions.explanation: CYP enzymes are embedded in the smooth ER of liver cells, where lipid-soluble drugs reach them after crossing the plasma membrane.

questions.question: Roughly what share of small-molecule drug metabolism is handled by just five CYP enzymes?
questions.explanation: Five CYPs — 1A2, 2C9, 2C19, 2D6 and 3A4 — carry out over 50% of small-molecule drug metabolism, which is why so many interactions funnel through them.

questions.question: Why do a handful of CYP enzymes cause most drug interactions?
options: A. much metabolism funnels through them
B. they are found only in the plasma
C. they cannot be induced or inhibited
D. each of them handles just one drug
questions.explanation: Because so much metabolism passes through a few CYPs with overlapping substrates, inducing or inhibiting one shifts the levels of many drugs at once.

questions.question: Phase 2 conjugation reactions generally produce metabolites that are:
questions.explanation: Phase 2 attaches a large endogenous molecule (e.g. glucuronic acid), usually inactivating the drug and making it very water-soluble for excretion.

questions.question: Warfarin illustrates stereoselectivity because its two enantiomers differ in:
options: A. potency and which CYP metabolises them
B. molecular formula and their total charge
C. the route by which they are given
D. the colour and shape of the tablet
questions.explanation: The R and S forms share a formula but S-warfarin is far more potent and is metabolised by CYP2C9, so a 2C9 inhibitor selectively raises the potent isomer.

questions.question: Inherited variation described as 'slow vs fast acetylators' is an example of:
options: B. enzyme induction by another drug
C. saturation of a metabolic enzyme
questions.explanation: Acetylator status is an inherited (polymorphic) difference in a metabolising enzyme that shifts drug levels between individuals.

questions.question: Compared with enzyme inhibition, enzyme induction changes a substrate's level:
options: A. downward and slowly over days
B. upward and rapidly within hours
C. downward and rapidly within hours
D. upward and slowly over days
questions.explanation: An inducer makes the cell synthesise more enzyme over days–weeks, so the substrate falls slowly (treatment failure); an inhibitor blocks enzyme at once, so levels rise fast.

questions.question: Grapefruit juice raises the plasma level of many drugs because it:
questions.explanation: Grapefruit juice inhibits CYP3A4 — the busiest CYP — so 3A4 substrates such as statins and diazepam are metabolised less and accumulate.

questions.question: Giving a CYP2D6 inhibitor with codeine reduces pain relief because it:
options: A. prevents codeine's activation to morphine
B. speeds codeine's activation to morphine
C. blocks morphine binding at receptors
D. increases renal excretion of codeine
questions.explanation: Codeine needs CYP2D6 to become active morphine; inhibiting 2D6 blocks that conversion, so little morphine forms and analgesia fails.

questions.question: The main enzyme converting ethanol to acetaldehyde is:
questions.explanation: Alcohol dehydrogenase turns ethanol into acetaldehyde; aldehyde dehydrogenase then clears acetaldehyde to acetate — the step disulfiram blocks.

questions.question: About 25–30% of drugs are excreted mainly unchanged, which matters because:
options: A. renal impairment causes them to accumulate
B. hepatic impairment causes them to accumulate
C. they cannot be filtered at the glomerulus
D. they are always highly bound to protein
questions.explanation: Drugs excreted mainly as active, unchanged molecules depend on the kidney, so renal impairment lets them build up to toxic levels.

questions.question: Which excretion route mainly handles larger molecules and drug conjugates?
questions.explanation: The hepatobiliary route secretes larger molecules (MW > 350) and conjugates into bile. Volatiles leave via the lungs; small polar drugs go renally.

questions.question: A highly protein-bound drug is filtered slowly at the glomerulus because:
options: A. bound drug is too large to filter
B. bound drug is too small to filter
C. binding makes the drug lipid-soluble
D. binding pumps the drug back actively
questions.explanation: Only free drug crosses the glomerular filter; protein-bound drug is too big to be filtered, so heavy binding slows renal removal.

questions.question: Active tubular secretion of acidic drugs is carried out by:
questions.explanation: OATs secrete acidic (anionic) drugs and OCTs secrete basic (cationic) drugs into the tubule; both are carrier-mediated active steps.

questions.question: Lipid-soluble drugs are poorly excreted by the kidney because they are:
options: A. reabsorbed from the tubule with water
B. secreted into the tubule by carriers
C. unable to be filtered at all
D. destroyed within the tubular lumen
questions.explanation: A filtered lipid-soluble drug diffuses back out of the tubule with reabsorbed water, so it never truly leaves — the reason metabolism must make drugs water-soluble first.

questions.question: The enterohepatic circulation tends to:
options: A. prolong a drug's stay in the body
B. shorten a drug's stay in the body
C. prevent any renal excretion of drug
D. abolish the biliary secretion of drug
questions.explanation: Recycling drug from bile to gut and back via reabsorption keeps it in the body longer, effectively lengthening the half-life.

questions.question: Gut bacteria contribute to enterohepatic recycling by:
options: A. cleaving glucuronides to free the drug
B. conjugating the drug with glucuronide
C. filtering the drug in the kidney
D. binding the drug tightly to albumin
questions.explanation: Bacterial enzymes split glucuronide conjugates in the gut, freeing the parent drug so it can be reabsorbed into the portal blood.

questions.question: Probenecid raises and sustains penicillin levels by:
options: A. blocking its active tubular secretion
D. increasing its plasma protein binding
questions.explanation: Probenecid competes for the OAT that secretes penicillin into the tubule, slowing its excretion and keeping levels high for longer.

questions.question: A 500 mg IV dose gives a plasma concentration of 25 mg/L. The apparent Vd is:
questions.explanation: Vd = dose ÷ plasma concentration = 500 mg ÷ 25 mg/L = 20 L — larger than plasma, so the drug distributes into tissues.

questions.question: Which parameter most directly determines the maintenance dose rate?
questions.explanation: To hold a steady level you replace exactly what is removed, so maintenance-dose rate = clearance × target concentration. Half-life is a derived number.

questions.question: Elimination half-life is:
options: A. proportional to Vd, inverse to clearance
B. inverse to Vd, proportional to clearance
C. independent of Vd and of clearance
D. proportional to both Vd and clearance
questions.explanation: t½ = 0.693 × Vd ÷ CL, so it rises with volume of distribution and falls as clearance increases.

questions.question: A drug has a half-life of 4 hours. Its elimination rate constant (kel) is about:
questions.explanation: kel = 0.693 ÷ t½ = 0.693 ÷ 4 h ≈ 0.17 h⁻¹ — about 17% of the remaining drug leaves each hour.

questions.question: With regular dosing, steady state is reached after approximately:
questions.explanation: Repeated dosing accumulates drug until input equals elimination — reached after 3–5 half-lives, independent of dose size. Near-complete elimination takes about six.

questions.question: With F = 0.7, 200 mg every 8 h and clearance 6 L/h, the average steady-state level is about:
Which feature defines zero-order (saturation) elimination?
options: A. a constant amount removed per time
B. a constant fraction removed per time
C. clearance that stays perfectly constant
D. a half-life that never once changes
questions.explanation: In zero-order elimination the enzymes are saturated, so a fixed amount is removed per unit time and clearance falls as concentration rises — as with alcohol and phenytoin.

questions.question: Most drugs follow first-order elimination, in which:
options: A. a constant fraction leaves per time
B. a constant amount leaves per time
C. clearance falls as levels rise
D. the half-life keeps on increasing
questions.explanation: First-order kinetics removes a constant fraction per unit time because enzymes have spare capacity, giving a constant clearance and a constant half-life.

questions.question: Phenytoin needs careful dosing near the top of its range because it shows:
options: A. zero-order kinetics, so levels jump sharply
B. first-order kinetics, so levels stay stable
C. no metabolism, so it leaves fully unchanged
D. rapid clearance, so it is quickly removed
questions.explanation: Phenytoin saturates its enzymes at therapeutic doses (zero-order), so clearance falls as level rises and a small dose increase can cause a large, toxic jump.

questions.question: In the two-compartment model, the early steep fall in plasma concentration after an IV dose reflects:
options: B. true elimination from the body
C. absorption from the gut lumen
questions.explanation: The fast initial decline is redistribution from the central (plasma) compartment into slower peripheral tissues; the later shallow fall is true elimination.

shoulder_region_mhhs2401_wk1.html.title: MHHS2401 W1 PII · Shoulder Region
shoulder_region_mhhs2401_wk1.html.subject: Musculoskeletal System
shoulder_region_mhhs2401_wk1.html.content: L2 Anatomy of the shoulder region: bones, joints, muscles and rotator cuff.

questions.question: The pectoral girdle is an incomplete bony ring made of which two bones?
questions.explanation: The pectoral girdle is the clavicle plus the scapula; its only bony link to the axial skeleton is the sternoclavicular joint.

questions.question: Which muscle of the rotator cuff (SITS) inserts on the lesser tubercle?
questions.explanation: Subscapularis is the only anterior cuff muscle; it inserts on the lesser tubercle, while S, I and T reach the greater tubercle.

questions.question: Which joint is the most mobile joint in the body?
questions.explanation: The glenohumeral ball-and-socket joint is the most mobile in the body, trading bony stability for range of motion.

questions.question: Which bone is described as the most commonly fractured long bone?
questions.explanation: The clavicle is the most commonly fractured long bone; force along the strut fails at the middle/lateral-third junction.

questions.question: Which nerve is most at risk with a surgical-neck fracture of the humerus?
questions.explanation: The axillary nerve winds around the surgical neck, so a fracture there can paralyse deltoid and numb the 'regimental badge' area.

questions.question: The long head of biceps brachii originates from which scapular landmark?
questions.explanation: The supraglenoid tubercle (above the glenoid) gives origin to the long head of biceps; the infraglenoid tubercle gives the long head of triceps.

questions.question: The long head of triceps brachii originates from which scapular landmark?
questions.explanation: The infraglenoid tubercle (below the glenoid) gives origin to the long head of triceps; biceps takes the supraglenoid tubercle.

questions.question: Serratus anterior receives its sole motor supply from which nerve?
questions.explanation: The long thoracic nerve is the sole supply to serratus anterior; running superficially, it is vulnerable to injury.

questions.question: A winged scapula results from paralysis of which muscle?
questions.explanation: Losing serratus anterior stops the scapula being held to the ribs, so it lifts off as a winged scapula and overhead abduction fails.

questions.question: The two bands of the coracoclavicular ligament are named the:
questions.explanation: The coracoclavicular ligament has a lateral trapezoid band and a medial conoid band, anchoring to the clavicle's matching marks.

questions.question: True stability of the acromioclavicular joint comes chiefly from which ligament?
questions.explanation: The extrinsic coracoclavicular ligament slings the scapula from the clavicle and bears the limb's weight, providing real AC stability.

questions.question: The deltoid muscle is supplied by which nerve?
questions.explanation: Deltoid is supplied by the axillary nerve; its damage in surgical-neck fracture or dislocation abolishes abduction.

questions.question: Latissimus dorsi inserts into which part of the intertubercular groove?
questions.explanation: In the 'lady between two majors', latissimus dorsi (the lady) inserts on the floor, with pec major laterally and teres major medially.

questions.question: Pectoralis major inserts onto which part of the intertubercular groove?
options: C. the floor of the groove
questions.explanation: Pectoralis major inserts on the lateral lip of the bicipital groove; teres major takes the medial lip and latissimus the floor.

questions.question: The trapezius receives its motor supply from which nerve?
questions.explanation: Trapezius is supplied by the spinal accessory nerve (CN XI) for motor function, with C3/C4 carrying sensation.

questions.question: Scapulohumeral rhythm during abduction follows roughly which glenohumeral-to-scapular ratio?
questions.explanation: Overall abduction is roughly 2:1 — about 120 degrees glenohumeral plus 60 degrees scapular rotation for around 180 degrees total.

questions.question: Which muscle initiates the first 0-15 degrees of arm abduction?
questions.explanation: Supraspinatus initiates the first 15 degrees of abduction and pulls the head into the glenoid, after which deltoid takes over.

questions.question: The sternoclavicular joint is formed by the clavicle, the manubrium and the:
questions.explanation: The SC joint unites the sternal clavicle, the clavicular notch of the manubrium and part of the first costal cartilage.

questions.question: Which three rotator-cuff muscles insert on the greater tubercle?
questions.explanation: Supraspinatus, infraspinatus and teres minor all reach the greater tubercle; only subscapularis inserts on the lesser tubercle.

questions.question: Teres major inserts into which part of the intertubercular groove?
options: C. the floor of the groove
questions.explanation: Teres major takes the medial lip of the bicipital groove, flanking latissimus (floor) opposite pec major (lateral lip).

questions.question: A clavicle fracture most often occurs at which point along the bone?
questions.explanation: Force concentrates where the forward convex medial curve meets the concave lateral curve — the middle/lateral-third junction fails.

questions.question: The humeral head most commonly dislocates in which direction?
questions.explanation: The capsule is weakest antero-inferiorly and the arch blocks superior escape, so dislocation is usually antero-inferior in abduction and external rotation.

questions.question: Supraspinatus and infraspinatus are both supplied by which nerve?
questions.explanation: The suprascapular nerve supplies supraspinatus and infraspinatus; subscapularis takes the subscapular nerves and teres minor the axillary.

questions.question: Teres minor, a rotator-cuff muscle, is supplied by which nerve?
questions.explanation: Teres minor is supplied by the axillary nerve, unlike the other cuff muscles which take the suprascapular or subscapular nerves.

questions.question: Which structure is chiefly pinched in subacromial impingement under the coraco-acromial arch?
options: C. the long head of triceps
questions.explanation: The supraspinatus tendon and subacromial bursa run through the tight space under the arch, so supraspinatus impinges and tears first.

questions.question: The fibrocartilage glenoid labrum contributes to the joint chiefly by:
questions.explanation: The labrum is a fibrocartilage rim that deepens the shallow glenoid about 50 percent; tearing it (Bankart lesion) eases dislocation.

questions.question: The transverse humeral ligament functions to:
options: A. hold the biceps tendon in place
B. deepen the glenoid cavity rim
D. bind the clavicle to rib one
questions.explanation: The transverse humeral ligament bridges the tubercles and roofs the bicipital groove, keeping the long head of biceps tendon in place.

questions.question: A painful arc from subacromial impingement classically occurs over which range of abduction?
questions.explanation: Impingement gives a painful arc around 60-120 degrees of abduction, with weak initiation and a positive 'empty can' test.

questions.question: The sternoclavicular joint is structurally a saddle joint that functions as a:
questions.explanation: The SC joint is a synovial saddle joint that functions as a ball-and-socket, serving as the pivot for all girdle movement.

bone_physiology_2_mhhs2401.html.title: MHHS2401 W3 PII · Bone Physiology II
bone_physiology_2_mhhs2401.html.subject: Musculoskeletal System
bone_physiology_2_mhhs2401.html.content: Bone fracture healing cascade, callus formation, remodelling, malunion and nonunion.

questions.question: Which structure forms in the very first stage of fracture healing?
questions.explanation: Stage one is the fracture haematoma: blood from torn vessels clots at the break within the first day.

questions.question: Bone is unusual among tissues because it repairs a fracture with:
options: A. new bone rather than scar
B. scar tissue rather than bone
questions.explanation: Bone regenerates with bone, not scar, so a healed fracture can regain the full strength of the original.

questions.question: Which cells lay down the cartilage of the soft (fibrocartilaginous) callus?
questions.explanation: Chondrocytes lay down the cartilage bridge of the soft callus, which then serves as a template for bone.

questions.question: The bony (hard) callus is laid down by which cells?
questions.explanation: Osteoblasts lay down the bone matrix of the hard callus, first as woven bone and later as lamellar bone.

questions.question: A fracture that has not healed after about how long is called a nonunion?
questions.explanation: Nonunion is defined as a fracture that fails to heal by 9 months, from lost stability or blood supply.

questions.question: What is the correct order of the four stages of fracture healing?
options: A. haematoma, soft callus, bony callus, remodelling
B. soft callus, haematoma, remodelling, bony callus
C. haematoma, bony callus, soft callus, remodelling
D. remodelling, haematoma, soft callus, bony callus
questions.explanation: Healing runs haematoma, then fibrocartilaginous (soft) callus, then bony (hard) callus, then remodelling.

questions.question: The callus route of fracture repair is known as:
questions.explanation: Callus formation is secondary healing, which needs a little movement; absolutely rigid fixation gives callus-free primary healing.

questions.question: Primary (direct) fracture healing with no visible callus occurs when the fragments are:
questions.explanation: If a surgeon holds fragments absolutely rigid, bone heals directly across the gap with no callus, called primary healing.

questions.question: Low oxygen in the fracture clot triggers new blood vessel growth by releasing:
questions.explanation: Hypoxia in the clot drives release of VEGF, which grows new blood vessels into the fracture during angiogenesis.

questions.question: Which cells are recruited into the fracture to differentiate into chondrocytes and osteoblasts?
questions.explanation: Growth factors summon mesenchymal stem cells into the fracture, where they differentiate into chondrocytes and osteoblasts.

questions.question: Within the clot, which scaffold do repair cells crawl along to reach the gap?
questions.explanation: The clot's fibrin meshwork is the scaffold that surface cells crawl along to reach and bridge the fracture gap.

questions.question: The soft-callus cartilage is converted to bone by which process?
questions.explanation: The cartilage template undergoes endochondral ossification, the same mechanism that grew long bones at the growth plate.

questions.question: Woven bone laid down in the callus is best described as:
options: A. fast to form but weak
B. slow to form but strong
questions.explanation: Woven bone has irregular collagen, so it forms rapidly but is weak; it is later replaced by stronger lamellar bone.

questions.question: Compared with woven bone, lamellar bone in the healed callus is:
questions.explanation: Lamellar bone has regular, ordered collagen laid in laminae, making it load-bearing; it slowly replaces the woven bone.

questions.question: Which pair of cells reshapes the bulky bony callus into proper bone?
questions.explanation: Remodelling uses osteoclasts resorbing and osteoblasts depositing to sculpt the over-built callus into compact and spongy bone.

questions.question: Malunion of a fracture means the bone has healed:
questions.explanation: Malunion is a fracture that heals but misaligned, with a changed angle or length; nonunion is failure to heal at all.

questions.question: Which two requirements, when lost, lead to nonunion of a fracture?
questions.explanation: Nonunion follows loss of stability or blood supply, the two things a healing fracture most needs.

questions.question: Why is restoring blood supply the make-or-break step in fracture healing?
options: A. bone cannot form without oxygen
B. cartilage cannot form at all
C. clots need oxygen to develop
questions.explanation: Cartilage tolerates low oxygen but bone does not, so without angiogenesis the repair stalls at cartilage, risking nonunion.

questions.question: During remodelling a healed fracture re-grows along its stress lines, an idea captured by:
questions.explanation: Wolff's law states bone is laid where loaded and removed where not, so remodelling rebuilds along mechanical stress lines.

questions.question: Platelets in the fracture clot are activated by thrombin and then:
questions.explanation: Thrombin-activated platelets release growth factors that start the repair cascade and help recruit stem cells.

questions.question: The standard treatment of a malunion is:
questions.explanation: Malunion is treated by osteotomy to realign, followed by fixation such as open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF).

questions.question: Which agent can be used to internally stimulate a nonunion but rarely causes heterotopic ossification?
questions.explanation: Bone morphogenic protein (BMP) can rescue a nonunion by internal stimulation but rarely causes bone to form where it should not.

questions.question: Smoking, diabetes and peripheral vascular disease impair healing mainly by reducing:
questions.explanation: Smoking, diabetes and peripheral vascular disease all impair blood supply and angiogenesis, starving the cascade of oxygen.

questions.question: Children's fractures are often managed more conservatively because children:
questions.explanation: Children remodel so vigorously that even a slightly angled union can straighten over time, so conservative management often suffices.

questions.question: Which structure is a key blood source that surgeons try to protect during fracture surgery?
questions.explanation: The periosteum is a key blood source whose intactness predicts healing, so it is protected during surgery wherever possible.

muscle_physiology_1_mhhs2401.html.title: MHHS2401 W3 PIII · Muscle Physiology I
muscle_physiology_1_mhhs2401.html.subject: Musculoskeletal System
muscle_physiology_1_mhhs2401.html.content: Skeletal muscle structure, neuromuscular junction, sliding filament contraction and relaxation.

questions.question: Skeletal muscle is best described as:
questions.explanation: Skeletal muscle is striated, multinucleate and under voluntary control, unlike involuntary cardiac and smooth muscle.

questions.question: The contractile unit of a myofibril, running from Z disc to Z disc, is the:
questions.explanation: The sarcomere is the contractile unit, running Z disc to Z disc; sarcomeres sit in series along each myofibril.

questions.question: Which neurotransmitter carries the signal across the neuromuscular junction?
questions.explanation: Somatic motor neurons release acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction, and its effect on skeletal muscle is always excitatory.

questions.question: Which structure inside the muscle fibre stores calcium?
questions.explanation: The sarcoplasmic reticulum is modified endoplasmic reticulum wrapping each myofibril; it is the fibre's calcium store.

questions.question: The thick filament of the sarcomere is made of which protein?
questions.explanation: Myosin forms the thick filament and performs the power stroke; actin forms the thin filament it pulls on.

questions.question: Which connective-tissue sheath wraps an individual muscle fibre?
questions.explanation: Endomysium wraps each fibre, perimysium wraps each fascicle, and epimysium wraps the whole muscle; all merge into the tendon.

questions.question: Which sheath surrounds a fascicle, a bundle of muscle fibres?
questions.explanation: Perimysium wraps each fascicle and carries the larger nerves and vessels; endomysium wraps single fibres.

questions.question: The transverse (T) tubules of a muscle fibre function to:
options: A. carry the action potential inward
questions.explanation: T-tubules are infoldings of the sarcolemma that carry the action potential deep into the fibre so it contracts as one.

questions.question: The I band of the sarcomere contains:
questions.explanation: The I band is the light band of actin only, either side of the Z disc; the H zone is myosin only.

questions.question: The Z disc of the sarcomere serves to anchor which filament?
questions.explanation: The Z disc anchors actin and marks the sarcomere edge; the M line at the middle anchors myosin.

questions.question: At rest, the myosin-binding sites on actin are physically blocked by:
questions.explanation: Tropomyosin lies over actin's binding sites as a safety catch; troponin pulls it aside when calcium binds.

questions.question: The nicotinic ACh receptor at the motor end plate is a:
questions.explanation: The nicotinic ACh receptor is a ligand-gated ion channel: it opens when ACh binds, not in response to voltage.

questions.question: The nAChR passes both sodium and potassium, but the end plate depolarises because:
options: A. sodium influx exceeds potassium efflux
B. potassium efflux exceeds sodium influx
C. only sodium can cross it
D. only potassium can cross it
questions.explanation: The channel is non-specific, but sodium influx exceeds potassium efflux, so the net inward current depolarises the end plate.

questions.question: Botulinum toxin causes flaccid paralysis by:
questions.explanation: Botulinum toxin inhibits ACh release from the axon terminal, so there is no depolarisation and the muscle goes flaccid.

questions.question: Tetanus toxin produces spastic paralysis because it:
options: B. blocks ACh release from axons
D. pumps calcium into the SR
questions.explanation: Tetanus toxin inhibits inhibitory interneurons in the CNS, causing disinhibition so motor neurons fire unchecked and muscles go rigid.

questions.question: Myasthenia gravis is caused by autoimmune destruction of the:
questions.explanation: In myasthenia gravis, antibodies destroy the nicotinic ACh receptors, so the muscle responds less to ACh and contraction weakens.

questions.question: During contraction, the A band of the sarcomere:
questions.explanation: The A band is unchanged because myosin length is fixed; the I band and H zone narrow as filaments slide together.

questions.question: In excitation-contraction coupling, calcium is released from the SR into the:
questions.explanation: When the RyR opens, calcium floods out of the SR store into the sarcoplasm, the trigger for the cross-bridge cycle.

questions.question: Which feature is unique to cardiac muscle among the three muscle types?
questions.explanation: Cardiac muscle is striated, branched and involuntary and is joined by intercalated discs found only in the heart.

questions.question: In the T-tubule, the voltage sensor that mechanically opens the SR calcium channel is the:
questions.explanation: The DHP receptor in the T-tubule senses voltage and physically tugs open the ryanodine receptor on the SR to release calcium.

questions.question: In the cross-bridge cycle, the power stroke that pulls actin is triggered by release of:
questions.explanation: After myosin binds actin, release of inorganic phosphate (Pi) triggers the power stroke that pivots myosin and pulls actin.

questions.question: When calcium binds troponin, the immediate effect on the thin filament is to:
options: A. pull tropomyosin off the sites
B. split ATP on the myosin head
D. pump calcium back into the SR
questions.explanation: Calcium binding troponin changes its shape and pulls tropomyosin aside, exposing actin's myosin-binding sites.

questions.question: What breaks the myosin-actin cross-bridge to allow relaxation?
questions.explanation: A fresh ATP binding to myosin detaches it from actin; without ATP the muscle stays locked, as in rigor mortis.

questions.question: Calcium is returned to the SR during relaxation by which mechanism?
questions.explanation: The SR calcium ATPase (SERCA) actively pumps calcium back into the store against its gradient, using ATP.

questions.question: Rigor mortis occurs after death because there is no ATP to:
options: C. release calcium from the SR
questions.explanation: At death the SR leaks calcium so cross-bridges keep forming, but no ATP is made to detach myosin, so muscle locks stiff.

questions.question: Curariform muscle relaxants used in surgery cause paralysis by:
questions.explanation: Curariform relaxants bind and inhibit the nAChR so the muscle cannot be depolarised, giving controlled surgical paralysis.

questions.question: Myasthenia gravis is treated with neostigmine, which works by:
options: D. pumping calcium into the SR
questions.explanation: Neostigmine is an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor; by slowing ACh breakdown it leaves more ACh to find the surviving receptors.

questions.question: Arrival of the action potential at the axon terminal triggers ACh release by opening:
questions.explanation: The action potential opens voltage-gated calcium channels in the terminal, and the calcium influx triggers ACh vesicle release.

ventilation_gas_exchange_mhhs2402_wk3.ht.title: MHHS2402 W3 · Ventilation & Gas Exchange
ventilation_gas_exchange_mhhs2402_wk3.ht.subject: Cardiovascular, Renal & Respiratory Systems
ventilation_gas_exchange_mhhs2402_wk3.ht.content: Respiratory functions, fluid-movement laws, lung mechanics, volumes and capacities, gas diffusion and V/Q.

questions.question: Boyle's law states that, for a fixed gas mass, pressure and volume are:
questions.explanation: Boyle's law says pressure is inversely proportional to volume; expanding the lungs drops the pressure so air flows in.

questions.question: Surfactant in the alveoli acts to:
questions.explanation: Surfactant reduces alveolar surface tension, lowering the pressure needed to keep alveoli open and preventing collapse.

questions.question: The main muscle of inspiration is the:
questions.explanation: The diaphragm is the main inspiratory muscle; it contracts and flattens to enlarge the thorax and draw air in.

questions.question: The volume of air moved in one normal quiet breath is the:
questions.explanation: Tidal volume is the air of one normal breath, about 0.5 litres in an adult.

questions.question: Oxygen and carbon dioxide cross the alveolar membrane by:
questions.explanation: Gas exchange is pure diffusion down partial-pressure gradients; there is no active transport across the membrane.

questions.question: Which of these is one of the five functions of the respiratory system?
questions.explanation: The five functions are conduction, conditioning, gas exchange, blood pH regulation and vocalisation.

questions.question: The epiglottis protects the airway during swallowing by:
questions.explanation: The epiglottis is an elastic-cartilage flap that closes over the larynx during swallowing to keep food out of the trachea.

questions.question: As it conditions inspired air, the respiratory mucosa warms it to about:
questions.explanation: The mucosa warms air to about 37 degrees, humidifies it to 100 percent and filters particles before the alveoli.

questions.question: By Laplace's law, the pressure needed to hold an alveolus open rises as its radius:
questions.explanation: Laplace's law, P equals 2T over r, means a smaller radius needs a higher pressure to stay open, so small alveoli tend to collapse.

questions.question: A rise in blood carbon dioxide shifts blood pH in which direction?
questions.explanation: More CO2 forms more carbonic acid and releases more H+, lowering pH, so the blood becomes more acidic.

questions.question: During inspiration, enlarging the thorax lowers alveolar pressure so that it becomes:
questions.explanation: By Boyle's law, increasing lung volume drops alveolar pressure below atmospheric, so air flows into the lungs.

questions.question: By Poiseuille's law, airway resistance depends most strongly on the airway's:
questions.explanation: Resistance varies with radius to the fourth power, so small changes in radius cause large changes in flow.

questions.question: At rest, the pressure in the pleural space is:
questions.explanation: Intrapleural pressure is negative and becomes more negative in inspiration, keeping the elastic lung against the chest wall.

questions.question: Quiet (unforced) exhalation is achieved mainly by:
questions.explanation: Quiet exhalation is passive, relying on elastic recoil of the lung; forced exhalation adds the internal intercostals and abdominals.

questions.question: The residual volume is the air that:
options: B. enters in one normal breath
C. is exhaled beyond a tidal breath
D. is inhaled beyond a tidal breath
questions.explanation: Residual volume is the air left after maximal exhalation; it cannot be exhaled and so cannot be measured by simple spirometry.

questions.question: Minute ventilation is calculated as tidal volume multiplied by:
questions.explanation: Minute ventilation equals tidal volume times respiratory rate, for example 0.5 litres times 12 breaths gives 6 litres per minute.

questions.question: Dalton's law states that the total pressure of a gas mixture equals the:
options: A. sum of the partial pressures
questions.explanation: By Dalton's law, total pressure is the sum of each component's partial pressure, letting us calculate the pO2 of air.

questions.question: The ventilation-perfusion ratio compares alveolar ventilation with:
questions.explanation: The V/Q ratio is alveolar ventilation divided by perfusion, measuring how well air and blood are matched at the alveoli.

questions.question: Surfactant is produced by which alveolar cells?
questions.explanation: Type II alveolar cells make surfactant, which is produced late in fetal life, so premature infants can develop respiratory distress.

questions.question: If an airway's radius is halved, its resistance increases by roughly what factor?
questions.explanation: Resistance varies with radius to the fourth power, so halving the radius raises resistance 2 to the fourth, or 16-fold.

questions.question: Total airway resistance is lowest at the alveoli because they have the greatest:
questions.explanation: Repeated branching gives the alveoli an enormous combined cross-sectional area, so resistance is lowest and velocity slows for diffusion.

questions.question: A pneumothorax causes the lung to collapse because it abolishes the:
options: B. elastic recoil of the lung
questions.explanation: Air entering the pleural space equalises the pressure, abolishing the negative intrapleural pressure that held the lung expanded.

questions.question: Which lung capacity equals tidal volume plus inspiratory and expiratory reserve volumes?
questions.explanation: Vital capacity is TV plus IRV plus ERV; total lung capacity adds the residual volume on top.

questions.question: Functional residual capacity cannot be measured by simple spirometry because it includes the:
questions.explanation: FRC contains the residual volume, which cannot be exhaled and so never crosses the spirometer, needing indirect methods.

questions.question: In healthy lungs, the dominant factor setting the rate of gas diffusion is the:
questions.explanation: In health the partial-pressure difference dominates diffusion; in disease the area or membrane distance terms become limiting.

questions.question: Emphysema impairs gas diffusion mainly by reducing the:
questions.explanation: Emphysema destroys alveolar walls, cutting the surface area available for diffusion; fibrosis and oedema instead thicken the membrane.

questions.question: Humidifying inspired air lowers its oxygen partial pressure because water vapour:
questions.explanation: By Dalton's law, water vapour contributes its own partial pressure, so it claims part of the total, lowering pO2 from about 160 to 155 mmHg.

questions.question: In the oxygen cascade, the lowest partial pressure of oxygen is found at the:
questions.explanation: pO2 falls step by step from the atmosphere down to the mitochondria, the sink where oxygen is finally consumed.

questions.question: The normal whole-lung ventilation-perfusion ratio is approximately:
questions.explanation: The normal average is about 0.8, matching roughly 4 litres per minute of ventilation against 5 litres of cardiac output.

questions.question: A ventilation-perfusion ratio of zero describes a region that is:
questions.explanation: A V/Q of zero is a shunt: blood perfuses the region but no air reaches it, so the blood passes without being oxygenated.

questions.question: A high V/Q from blocked perfusion, as in a pulmonary embolism, creates:
questions.explanation: Blocked perfusion leaves ventilated but unperfused alveoli, or dead space; a pulmonary embolism is the classic cause.

questions.question: External respiration differs from cellular respiration in that external respiration is the:
options: A. movement of gases into blood
B. use of oxygen to make ATP
C. production of carbon dioxide in cells
D. breakdown of glucose for energy
questions.explanation: External respiration is the bulk and diffusive movement of gases between atmosphere, lung, blood and cells; cellular respiration uses O2 to make ATP.

respiratory_regulation_mhhs2402_wk4.html.title: MHHS2402 W4 · Respiratory Regulation Inputs
respiratory_regulation_mhhs2402_wk4.html.subject: Cardiovascular, Renal & Respiratory Systems
respiratory_regulation_mhhs2402_wk4.html.content: Respiratory regulation = a homeostatic negative-feedback loop: change (stimulus) -> detector (sensor) -> processing centre -> effector (action on minute ventilation). Homeostasis is dynamic balance, not rest. You don't breathe because you 'think' you should; a detected physical/chemical change must occur. Negative feedback opposes the change (stabilises); positive feedback amplifies it (e.g. a viral post). Three regulated arterial parameters: O2, CO2, pH (pH tracks CO2). Gas moves high->low partial pressure. Carbonic anhydrase: CO2+H2O <-> H2CO3 <-> H+ + HCO3-; rising CO2 lowers pH. CO2 carried dissolved, as bicarbonate, and as carbaminohaemoglobin; O2 carried Hb-bound and dissolved. Normal arterial: paO2 80-100 mmHg, SaO2 95-99%, paCO2 35-45 mmHg, pH 7.35-7.45, HCO3- 22-26 mEq/L; pH<7.35 acidosis, >7.45 alkalosis (respiratory or metabolic). Peripheral chemoreceptors: carotid + aortic bodies, fed ~20x their weight in blood/min so sample arterial blood; sense O2, CO2, H+; the main O2 sensor. O2 response flat until PO2 below normal then steep (hypoxic drive); CO2 response steep/linear; low PO2 and low pH raise CO2 sensitivity; peripheral respond to CO2 ~7x stronger and 5x faster than central. Central chemoreceptors sense CSF H+; H+ can't cross the blood-brain barrier but CO2 can (forms H+ in CSF) -> sensitive to blood CO2, not blood H+ or O2. Reflexes: Hering-Breuer (bronchial stretch receptors via vagus cease inspiration, only at hyperinflation >~3x TV); apnoea (central loss of pacing / physical soft-palate / reflex via J receptors); J (juxtacapillary) receptors in alveolar wall -> apnoea (congestion, pneumonia, histamine, serotonin). Five receptors raise ventilation: irritant (also bronchospasm), proprioceptors (immediate feed-forward in exercise), metaboreceptors (local muscle metabolites CO2/H+/lactate), thermoreceptors, pain. Cough (larynx/trachea/bronchi, vagal, glottis closed, intrapleural >100 mmHg, air out up to 160 km/h), sneeze (nasal), deglutition apnoea. Hyperventilation = excess CO2 loss (hypocapnia), not just fast breathing. Respiratory centre: minute ventilation = rate x tidal volume. DRG generates pacemaker + inspiratory ramp and receives glossopharyngeal input; VRG silent at rest, drives forced breathing; pontine pneumotaxic centre limits inspiration and raises rate; apneustic centre deepens inspiration. Transection: sever pons -> lose smooth rhythm but still breathe; sever medulla -> no breathing (medulla = obligatory generator). Inputs: higher brain, peripheral chemoreceptors (glossopharyngeal), central chemoreceptors, sensory reflexes. Outputs: phrenic nerve (diaphragm), intercostal nerves (intercostals). Communicate any change as: change -> detected how -> processed how -> output where -> action.

questions.question: Breathing is regulated mainly by which type of control?
questions.explanation: Breathing runs on negative feedback, which opposes any deviation and stabilises minute ventilation around a set point.

questions.question: Which three blood variables does the respiratory system regulate?
options: A. oxygen, carbon dioxide and pH
questions.explanation: The three regulated variables are oxygen, carbon dioxide and pH, and pH largely tracks carbon dioxide.

questions.question: The peripheral chemoreceptors are located in the carotid bodies and the:
questions.explanation: Peripheral chemoreceptors sit in the carotid bodies at the carotid bifurcation and the aortic bodies on the aortic arch.

questions.question: The respiratory centre is located in the brainstem, chiefly the:
questions.explanation: The respiratory centre lies in the brainstem, with the obligatory rhythm generator in the medulla and fine-tuning from the pons.

questions.question: Whatever the input, the respiratory centre can only change:
questions.explanation: The centre's only output is a change in minute ventilation, which is respiratory rate multiplied by tidal volume.

questions.question: Homeostasis is best described as:
options: A. dynamic balance around an optimum
B. the body being fully at rest
questions.explanation: Homeostasis is dynamic balance, holding a variable near its optimum through constant adjustment, not a state of rest.

questions.question: A homeostatic control loop needs a change, a sensor, an effector and a:
questions.explanation: The four parts are change, detect (sensor), process (centre) and action (effector); the centre interprets the signal and decides.

questions.question: A rise in blood carbon dioxide affects blood pH by:
questions.explanation: Rising CO2 generates more hydrogen ions through the carbonic anhydrase reaction, so blood pH falls.

questions.question: The normal arterial pH range is approximately:
questions.explanation: Normal arterial pH is 7.35 to 7.45; below is acidosis and above is alkalosis.

questions.question: Most oxygen is carried in the blood in which form?
questions.explanation: Most oxygen is carried bound to haemoglobin, with only a small amount dissolved in plasma.

questions.question: Signals from the carotid body travel to the medulla along which nerve?
questions.explanation: The carotid body sends its afferents in the glossopharyngeal nerve; the aortic body uses the vagus nerve.

questions.question: Ventilation begins to rise steeply only once arterial oxygen falls:
questions.explanation: The ventilatory response to oxygen is nearly flat across the normal range and climbs steeply only when PO2 drops below normal.

questions.question: The body's main sensor of arterial oxygen is the:
questions.explanation: Only the peripheral chemoreceptors sense oxygen; the central chemoreceptors are not sensitive to oxygen.

questions.question: The Hering-Breuer reflex uses stretch receptors to:
questions.explanation: Bronchial stretch receptors signal via the vagus to cease inspiration, but only during hyperinflation, as a safety cut-out.

questions.question: The juxtacapillary (J) receptors in the alveolar wall produce which effect?
questions.explanation: J receptors respond to pulmonary congestion and chemicals like histamine and produce apnoea and rapid shallow breathing.

questions.question: The cough reflex from irritation of the lower airway is carried by which nerve?
questions.explanation: The cough reflex from larynx, trachea and bronchi is carried by the vagus; a forceful expiration against a closed glottis expels the irritant.

questions.question: The respiratory centre drives the diaphragm through which nerve?
questions.explanation: The phrenic nerve, from spinal roots C3 to C5, carries the centre's command to the diaphragm.

questions.question: The central chemoreceptors directly detect which substance?
questions.explanation: The central chemoreceptors detect hydrogen ions in the cerebrospinal fluid, generated when CO2 crosses into it.

questions.question: Central chemoreceptors respond to blood CO2 but not blood H+ because the barrier lets through:
questions.explanation: The lipid blood-brain barrier passes small uncharged CO2 but blocks charged H+, so CO2 enters the CSF and is converted to H+ there.

questions.question: Compared with the central chemoreceptors, the peripheral ones respond to CO2 that is:
questions.explanation: The peripheral chemoreceptors respond to CO2 about seven times more strongly and five times faster, acting as the rapid alarm.

questions.question: In chronic CO2 retainers with COPD, breathing comes to rely more on the:
questions.explanation: Chronic CO2 retention dulls the central CO2 drive as CSF buffers, so breathing leans more on the peripheral hypoxic drive.

questions.question: The Hering-Breuer reflex fires only during hyperinflation because its threshold is set at about:
questions.explanation: The stretch receptors fire only above roughly three times normal tidal volume, keeping the reflex a backstop against over-inflation.

questions.question: During the onset of exercise, proprioceptors raise ventilation in a way best described as:
questions.explanation: Movement stimulates proprioceptors immediately, raising ventilation before blood oxygen falls, a feed-forward response that anticipates demand.

questions.question: Metaboreceptors differ from chemoreceptors because they sense:
questions.explanation: Metaboreceptors in skeletal muscle sense the local chemical environment such as CO2, H+ and lactate, not circulating arterial gases.

questions.question: True hyperventilation is defined by an excessive loss of:
questions.explanation: Hyperventilation means blowing off too much CO2, causing hypocapnia, which is why over-breathing causes tingling and light-headedness.

questions.question: The dorsal respiratory group of the medulla is chiefly responsible for:
questions.explanation: The dorsal respiratory group generates the pacemaker and the inspiratory ramp and is the input site for peripheral chemoreceptor signals.

questions.question: The ventral respiratory group is recruited mainly during:
questions.explanation: The ventral respiratory group is inactive in quiet breathing and is recruited for forced inspiration and expiration when demand rises.

questions.question: The pneumotaxic centre of the pons acts to:
questions.explanation: The pneumotaxic centre arrests the inspiratory phase and increases respiratory rate; the apneustic centre instead deepens inspiration.

questions.question: Transecting the brainstem below the medulla abolishes breathing, showing the medulla holds the:
questions.explanation: Cutting below the medulla stops breathing, so the medulla holds the obligatory rhythm generator; cutting the pons only makes the rhythm ragged.

questions.question: An opioid overdose stops breathing by depressing the:
questions.explanation: Opioids directly depress the medullary respiratory centre, slowing then stopping breathing; naloxone reverses this effect.

questions.question: The correct way to explain any change in breathing is the chain change, detected, processed, output and:
questions.explanation: The chain runs change, detected how, processed how, output where and action, where the action is always a change in minute ventilation.

questions.question: Carbon dioxide is often called the master respiratory variable because it also determines blood:
questions.explanation: Each dissolved CO2 molecule generates a hydrogen ion, so blood CO2 and pH are two readings of the same thing, making CO2 the master variable.

muscle_physiology_2_mhhs2401.html.title: MHHS2401 W4 · Muscle Physiology II — Tension & Performance
muscle_physiology_2_mhhs2401.html.subject: Musculoskeletal System
muscle_physiology_2_mhhs2401.html.content: Muscle Physiology II (Dr Linda Ban): energy, tension and fibre types. ATP is spent by myosin ATPase (contraction/cross-bridges), Ca-ATPase (relaxation, returns Ca to SR) and Na-K-ATPase (rest, restores ion gradients). Three energy systems: (1) phosphagen/PCr — creatine kinase shuttles phosphate; at rest stores it on creatine as phosphocreatine, during activity regenerates ATP fast (1 ATP/PCr, ~15 s, no O2, rate 4 mol/min, fastest); (2) anaerobic glycolysis — cytoplasm, glucose/glycogen, 2 ATP + pyruvate (rate 2.5), pyruvate becomes lactic acid without O2; (3) aerobic/oxidative phosphorylation — mitochondria, glucose + fatty acids, ~32 ATP + heat (rate 1, slowest, most efficient), O2 from myoglobin + haemoglobin. Speed-vs-yield trade-off, handed off sprint->jog->marathon. Fatigue = muscle can no longer generate/sustain power; depletion (glycogen/O2) and accumulation (lactate, low pH impairing CK/ATPases and Ca-troponin) theories, associative not causal. Recovery repays oxygen debt: alactacid (aerobic ATP restores PCr, reloads myoglobin) and lactacid (regenerates NAD+, lactate->pyruvate->glucose->glycogen). Tension = force/load a fibre resists; 4 S's: stretch, stimulation, size, stores. Length-tension: max tension at optimal resting sarcomere length ~2.0-2.3um (best filament overlap/cross-bridges); too short or too long lowers tension. Structural proteins: nebulin aligns/stabilises actin (Z disc along actin); titin stabilises myosin + elasticity + longitudinal force transfer (Z disc to M line); dystrophin anchors sarcomere to sarcolemma via beta-actin, lateral force transfer. Duchenne muscular dystrophy: no functional dystrophin (X-linked recessive, ~1 in 5000 male births) -> destabilised sarcolemma, fragile fibres rupture, inflammation/scarring, weakness, Duchenne gait, reduced cardiorespiratory function. Motor unit = one motor neuron + all fibres it innervates; grade tension by recruiting more/larger units and firing faster. Twitch = one excitation-contraction-relaxation; treppe (staircase) = rising early-twitch tension (delayed Ca re-uptake); wave summation = tension adds when the fibre can't fully relax; tetanus = fused twitches (unfused with slight relaxation, then complete smooth maximum); fatigue drops tension despite stimuli. Underlying cause: cytoplasmic Ca stays elevated so cross-bridges keep cycling. Muscle tone = resting tension from low-frequency twitches (posture); hypotonia/flaccidity (lower MND/ALS, myasthenia gravis, DMD), hypertonia/spasticity (upper MND, tetanus), prolonged hypertonia -> contracture. Motor neuron disease: degeneration of neurons controlling muscle; ALS affects upper + lower; atrophy, weakness. Isometric = constant length (hold), some cross-bridges, elastic proteins stretch to compensate; isotonic = constant tension (move) — concentric shortens, eccentric lengthens. Fibre types: Type I slow oxidative (red, high myoglobin/mitochondria/capillaries, fatigue-resistant, recruited first, endurance/posture); Type IIa fast oxidative-glycolytic (red-pink, intermediate); Type IIb fast glycolytic (white, few mitochondria, high glycogen, fatigable, recruited last, powerful bursts). Colour/capillaries/fatigue follow the fuel. Proportion mainly genetic (nature = sport suitability); training shifts it up to ~10% and increases diameter; diet (carbs) boosts glycogen. Exercise -> hypertrophy = more myofibrils per fibre (not more fibres) + more PCr/glycogen/triglyceride/mitochondrial enzymes. Progressive-overload strength training raises muscle strength (fewer back injuries), bone strength (less osteoporosis) and BMR (less weight gain); optimal ~6 near-maximal contractions x 3 sets, 3 days/week.

questions.question: Which energy system yields the most ATP per glucose molecule?
questions.explanation: Aerobic respiration makes about 32 ATP per glucose in the mitochondria, far more than glycolysis or the phosphagen system.

questions.question: Which fibre type is slow, red and best suited to endurance?
questions.explanation: Type I slow oxidative fibres are red, rich in mitochondria and myoglobin, and fatigue-resistant, ideal for endurance and posture.

questions.question: An isometric contraction is one in which the muscle:
questions.explanation: Isometric means same length: the muscle holds an object without moving, whereas isotonic contractions keep tension constant while moving.

questions.question: A motor unit consists of one motor neuron and:
questions.explanation: A motor unit is a single motor neuron plus all the muscle fibres its axon branches innervate; they contract together.

questions.question: Duchenne muscular dystrophy is caused by the absence of which protein?
questions.explanation: DMD results from a deleted dystrophin gene, so the fibre lacks the lateral anchor and the sarcolemma becomes fragile.

questions.question: The phosphagen system regenerates ATP rapidly using which stored molecule?
questions.explanation: Creatine kinase strips phosphate from phosphocreatine to regenerate ATP almost instantly, bridging the first seconds of effort.

questions.question: Anaerobic glycolysis produces how many ATP per glucose, plus pyruvate?
questions.explanation: Anaerobic glycolysis yields 2 ATP plus pyruvate in the cytoplasm; without oxygen the excess pyruvate becomes lactic acid.

questions.question: Which ATPase spends ATP to pump calcium back into the sarcoplasmic reticulum?
questions.explanation: The calcium ATPase pumps calcium back into the SR to end contraction, showing relaxation itself costs ATP.

questions.question: Which energy system dominates a maximal effort lasting only a few seconds?
questions.explanation: The phosphagen system delivers ATP fastest but for only about 15 seconds, so it dominates brief maximal efforts like a sprint.

questions.question: Sarcomere length affects tension because it determines the amount of:
questions.explanation: Filament overlap sets how many cross-bridges can form, so tension peaks at the optimal resting length of about 2.0 to 2.3 micrometres.

questions.question: Maximum tension is generated when a sarcomere is at which length?
questions.explanation: At the optimal resting length, thin and thick filament overlap allows the most cross-bridges and therefore the greatest tension.

questions.question: Which structural protein acts as a molecular spring from the Z disc to the M-line?
questions.explanation: Titin runs from Z disc to M-line, stabilising myosin and providing elasticity that recentres the sarcomere.

questions.question: Which structural protein aligns and stabilises the thin actin filament?
questions.explanation: Nebulin spans the Z disc along actin, aligning and stabilising the thin filament; titin does this job for myosin.

questions.question: Wave summation increases tension because the fibre is stimulated again before it can:
questions.explanation: When stimuli arrive before full relaxation, cytoplasmic calcium stacks up and successive twitches partially add, raising tension.

questions.question: Complete tetanus is best described as:
questions.explanation: In complete tetanus, twitches fully fuse into a smooth steady maximum because calcium never falls between rapid stimuli.

questions.question: Lowering a weight slowly under control is which kind of contraction?
questions.explanation: An eccentric isotonic contraction lengthens the muscle under control at constant tension, as when lowering a load.

questions.question: Muscle tone is best defined as:
questions.explanation: Muscle tone is resting muscle tension from low-frequency twitches, keeping you upright and balanced.

questions.question: Type IIb fast glycolytic fibres are characterised by:
options: A. high glycogen and few mitochondria
B. high myoglobin and many mitochondria
C. slow speed and red colour
questions.explanation: Type IIb fibres run on anaerobic glycolysis, so they hoard glycogen but have few mitochondria and capillaries, are pale and fatigue fast.

questions.question: The alactacid part of recovery uses aerobic ATP mainly to:
options: B. convert lactate back to glucose
questions.explanation: The alactacid component restores phosphocreatine and refills muscle oxygen stores in myoglobin; the lactacid component clears lactate.

questions.question: Accumulation theories of muscle fatigue attribute it to a build-up of lactate and a fall in:
questions.explanation: Accumulation theories say rising lactate lowers pH, impairing enzymes like the ATPases and calcium binding to troponin.

questions.question: The oxygen for aerobic respiration in muscle is stored locally by which molecule?
questions.explanation: Myoglobin stores oxygen within the muscle, while haemoglobin delivers oxygen from the blood; both feed aerobic respiration.

questions.question: Duchenne muscular dystrophy follows which pattern of inheritance?
questions.explanation: DMD is X-linked recessive, affecting roughly 1 in 5000 male births, and also weakens the diaphragm and heart.

questions.question: Dystrophin transfers force laterally by linking internal actin out to which matrix protein?
questions.explanation: Dystrophin links the internal actin cytoskeleton through membrane proteins out to laminin in the extracellular matrix.

questions.question: During an isometric contraction, overall muscle length stays constant because:
options: A. elastic elements stretch to compensate
B. no cross-bridges form at all
questions.explanation: Sarcomeres do shorten as cross-bridges cycle, but elastic elements such as titin stretch by the same amount, so total length is unchanged.

questions.question: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, the commonest motor neuron disease, affects:
options: A. both upper and lower neurons
B. only the lower motor neurons
C. only the upper motor neurons
questions.explanation: ALS degenerates both upper and lower motor neurons, causing atrophy, weakness and impaired respiration and speech.

questions.question: Muscle hypertrophy from training reflects an increase in:
options: D. the number of sarcomeres only
questions.explanation: Hypertrophy means more myofibrils within each fibre, not more fibres, along with more phosphocreatine, glycogen and mitochondria.

questions.question: In what order are the fibre types typically recruited as force demand rises?
options: A. type I, then IIa, then IIb
B. type IIb, then IIa, then I
C. type IIa, then I, then IIb
D. type IIb, then I, then IIa
questions.explanation: Fatigue-resistant type I fibres are recruited first, then type IIa, and finally the powerful fatigable type IIb fibres.

questions.question: About how much can training shift a person's relative proportion of fibre types?
questions.explanation: Fibre proportion is mostly genetic, but training can shift it by roughly 10 percent and also increase fibre diameter.

pharmacodynamics_medi2004_wk4.html.title: MEDI2004 W4 · Pharmacodynamics — Drug Action
pharmacodynamics_medi2004_wk4.html.subject: Pharmacology Fundamentals
pharmacodynamics_medi2004_wk4.html.content: PD = what the drug does to the body (mechanism of action). Four targets (RITE): Receptors, Ion channels, Transporters, Enzymes. Modes: receptor agonist/antagonist; channel blocker/modulator; enzyme inhibitor/false substrate; transporter inhibitor. Acceptors bind drug without a response (affect distribution). Specificity = one target/site/effect (ideal, reciprocal, never complete); selectivity = preference for a target in certain cells/tissues (propranolol = non-selective beta-blocker, blocks b1+b2; cardioselective spares lungs). Affinity = tendency/strength of reversible binding, set by structure; KD = conc at 50% occupancy; lower KD = higher affinity. Occupation (affinity) != activation (efficacy). Agonist occupies + activates; antagonist occupies with zero efficacy. Efficacy = capacity to activate (Emax, curve height); potency = affinity + efficacy (EC50, curve position; lower EC50 = more potent = leftward). CRC: full agonist reaches Emax, partial plateaus lower, antagonist flat. Opioids: enkephalin most potent + full, morphine less potent + full, buprenorphine partial (~55%, limits respiratory depression). Inverse agonist = negative efficacy, stabilises inactive receptor below constitutive baseline. Competitive antagonist = same site, reversible, right-shift, Emax unchanged (surmountable; naloxone).
