Irreversible antagonist = covalent, right-shift + reduced Emax (insurmountable; aspirin/COX). Receptor reserve = spare receptors. Allosteric modulator binds a non-orthosteric site, positive/negative (benzodiazepines = positive allosteric modulators of GABA-A).

questions.question: Pharmacodynamics is the study of:
options: A. what a drug does to the body
B. what the body does to a drug
C. how a drug is absorbed and cleared
D. how a drug is discovered and made
questions.explanation: Pharmacodynamics is drug→body — the mechanism of action by which a drug produces its effect. Body→drug (ADME) is pharmacokinetics.

questions.question: The four main protein targets for drugs are receptors, ion channels, transporters and:
questions.explanation: The four targets (RITE) are Receptors, Ion channels, Transporters and Enzymes — nearly every drug binds one of these.

questions.question: A plasma protein that binds a drug without producing a direct response is called:
questions.explanation: Acceptors bind drug but generate no direct response; they affect distribution (e.g. albumin), unlike receptors which transduce a signal.

questions.question: An antagonist acting at a receptor produces its effect by:
options: A. occupying it without triggering a response
B. occupying it and triggering a response
C. permanently destroying the receptor protein
D. increasing the receptor's natural activity
questions.explanation: An antagonist has affinity but no efficacy — it occupies the receptor and blocks endogenous mediators without activating it.

questions.question: The ideal property of a drug interacting with only one target, site and effect is called:
questions.explanation: Specificity is the ideal of a single target, site and effect. It is reciprocal and never complete — real drugs instead show selectivity.

questions.question: Propranolol is called a non-selective beta-blocker because it:
options: A. blocks both β1 and β2 receptors
B. blocks only β1 cardiac receptors
C. binds no beta receptors at all
D. activates β2 receptors in airways
questions.explanation: Propranolol blocks both β1 and β2 receptors, so it also affects the airways — cardioselective β1 blockers were designed to spare the lungs.

questions.question: Affinity describes a drug's:
options: A. tendency to bind its receptor
B. capacity to activate a receptor
questions.explanation: Affinity is the strength of the reversible drug–receptor binding, set by chemical structure. The capacity to activate once bound is efficacy.

questions.question: The dissociation constant KD is the drug concentration that:
options: A. occupies half of the receptors
B. activates half of the receptors
questions.explanation: KD is the concentration occupying 50% of receptors — a binding measure. It concerns occupancy, not the response produced.

questions.question: A drug with a lower KD than another has:
options: A. a higher affinity for the receptor
B. a lower affinity for the receptor
C. a greater maximal response ceiling
D. a slower rate of receptor binding
questions.explanation: A lower KD means half-occupancy is reached at a lower concentration — less drug needed, so affinity is higher.

questions.question: Which pair correctly matches the property to the step it governs?
options: A. affinity to occupation, efficacy to activation
B. efficacy to occupation, affinity to activation
C. potency to occupation, affinity to activation
D. affinity to occupation, potency to activation
questions.explanation: Occupation (binding) is governed by affinity; activation (flipping the receptor to its active form) is governed by efficacy. Only agonists achieve activation.

questions.question: An agonist differs from an antagonist in that it:
options: A. both occupies and activates the receptor
B. only occupies but never activates it
C. binds a completely different target
D. is destroyed on binding the receptor
questions.explanation: An agonist occupies and activates the receptor to produce a response; an antagonist occupies it with zero efficacy, producing none.

questions.question: On a concentration–response curve, Emax (the curve's height) is a measure of:
questions.explanation: Emax is the maximal response a drug can produce — the vertical measure of efficacy. The horizontal EC50 measures potency.

questions.question: The EC50 on a concentration–response curve measures a drug's:
questions.explanation: EC50 is the concentration giving 50% of the maximal response — the curve's horizontal position, measuring potency. A lower EC50 means more potent.

questions.question: A drug that binds tightly but caps at 55% of the maximal response is best described as:
options: A. potent but low in efficacy
B. efficacious but low in potency
C. both highly potent and efficacious
questions.explanation: Tight binding (leftward curve) makes it potent, but a low plateau means low efficacy — potency and efficacy are independent axes.

questions.question: A partial agonist differs from a full agonist in that it:
options: A. plateaus below the maximal response
B. reaches the full maximal response
D. lowers response below the baseline
questions.explanation: A partial agonist activates the receptor but caps below Emax even at full occupancy — lower efficacy than a full agonist.

questions.question: On the opioid curves enkephalin sits furthest left, then morphine, then buprenorphine. This shows:
options: A. enkephalin is the most potent
B. buprenorphine is the most potent
C. morphine has the highest efficacy
D. enkephalin has the lowest efficacy
questions.explanation: The leftmost curve has the lowest EC50, so enkephalin is the most potent. Curve position is potency; the plateau height shows efficacy.

questions.question: Buprenorphine's ceiling on Emax is clinically useful because it:
options: A. limits respiratory depression at high doses
B. worsens respiratory depression at high doses
C. removes any effect on opioid receptors
D. makes it far more potent than morphine
questions.explanation: As a partial agonist it can't drive the receptor past ~55%, so its built-in ceiling limits respiratory depression — useful in dependence treatment.

questions.question: An inverse agonist differs from a competitive antagonist in that it:
options: A. pushes response below the resting baseline
B. holds response exactly at resting baseline
C. drives response up to the full maximum
D. has no affinity for the receptor at all
questions.explanation: An inverse agonist has negative efficacy, stabilising the inactive receptor and lowering response below the constitutive baseline; an antagonist merely holds baseline.

questions.question: Constitutive receptor activity refers to a receptor that is:
options: A. active without any ligand bound
B. active only when an agonist binds
D. unable to change its conformation
questions.explanation: Some receptors idle between inactive and active forms with no ligand present — constitutive activity — which is what an inverse agonist turns down.

questions.question: A competitive antagonist shifts the agonist concentration–response curve:
options: A. to the right with Emax unchanged
B. to the left with Emax unchanged
C. to the right with Emax reduced
questions.explanation: A reversible competitive block at the same site shifts the curve rightward but preserves Emax — extra agonist can overcome it (surmountable).

questions.question: A competitive antagonist's block is described as 'surmountable' because:
options: A. enough extra agonist restores full response
B. no amount of agonist restores response
C. it covalently removes the receptors
D. it binds a separate allosteric site
questions.explanation: Because the block is reversible and at the same site, flooding with agonist out-competes it and restores the full maximum — hence surmountable.

questions.question: Compared with a competitive antagonist, an irreversible antagonist additionally:
options: A. lowers the maximal response Emax
B. shifts the curve to the left
D. restores response with more agonist
questions.explanation: An irreversible (covalent) block permanently removes receptors, so beyond the right-shift the Emax falls and extra agonist can't restore it (insurmountable).

questions.question: Aspirin is the classic irreversible antagonist because it:
options: A. covalently acetylates the COX enzyme
B. reversibly competes at the COX enzyme
C. binds an allosteric site on COX
D. is out-competed by more substrate
questions.explanation: Aspirin covalently acetylates COX, an irreversible block lasting the platelet's lifetime — why low-dose aspirin thins blood for days.

questions.question: Receptor reserve ('spare receptors') means a tissue can reach its maximal response:
options: B. only by occupying every receptor
C. only with an irreversible agonist
D. without any receptors being occupied
questions.explanation: With spare receptors, full response is reached before all are occupied, so early irreversible block just shifts the curve before Emax finally falls.

questions.question: An allosteric modulator differs from a competitive antagonist because it binds:
options: A. a site other than the agonist site
B. exactly the same site as the agonist
C. the enzyme that metabolises the drug
D. the plasma protein carrying the drug
questions.explanation: An allosteric modulator binds a separate (allosteric) site, not the orthosteric agonist site, and turns the agonist's effect up or down like a dimmer.

questions.question: Benzodiazepines act on the GABA-A receptor as:
options: A. positive allosteric modulators of GABA
B. direct full agonists at the pore
D. irreversible blockers of the channel
questions.explanation: Benzodiazepines don't open the channel themselves; they bind an allosteric site and make GABA better at opening it — positive allosteric modulation.

questions.question: Naloxone reverses an opioid overdose by acting as:
options: A. a competitive antagonist at opioid receptors
B. a partial agonist at the opioid receptors
C. an allosteric modulator of the receptor
D. an inhibitor of the opioid's metabolism
questions.explanation: Naloxone reversibly out-competes the opioid at the μ-receptor — a competitive antagonist — restoring normal function during overdose.

questions.question: An antagonist can have excellent affinity yet produce no response because it has:
questions.explanation: Affinity only governs binding; without efficacy the occupied receptor never activates, so a high-affinity antagonist still produces no response.

questions.question: Saying one drug is 'more potent' than another means its curve sits:
questions.explanation: More potent means less drug is needed, so the curve sits further left (lower EC50). It says nothing about the maximum effect achievable.

questions.question: A drug that acts as a 'false substrate' at an enzyme is:
options: A. processed into an abnormal metabolite
B. blocking the enzyme's active site
C. binding a separate allosteric site
D. carried across a membrane transporter
questions.explanation: A false substrate is accepted by the enzyme and processed into an abnormal product, unlike an inhibitor which simply blocks the normal reaction.

questions.question: Which statement correctly pairs the curve axis with its meaning?
options: A. horizontal is potency, vertical is efficacy
B. horizontal is efficacy, vertical is potency
C. horizontal is affinity, vertical is potency
D. horizontal is potency, vertical is affinity
questions.explanation: EC50 (left–right) is potency; Emax (up–down) is efficacy. Left means potent, tall means effective — keep the two axes distinct.

hand_anatomy_mhhs2401_wk4.html.title: MHHS2401 W4 · Anatomy of the Hand
hand_anatomy_mhhs2401_wk4.html.subject: Musculoskeletal System
hand_anatomy_mhhs2401_wk4.html.content: Anatomy of the hand (Dr Strkalj). Skeleton: 8 carpals, 5 metacarpals (I-V from thumb), 14 phalanges (thumb has proximal + distal only, no middle). Carpals proximal row radial->ulnar: scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, pisiform; distal row: trapezium, trapezoid, capitate, hamate ('Some Lovers Try Positions That They Can't Handle'). Carpals not visible at birth; capitate ossifies first (1-3 months) then anticlockwise. Carpal bones form a bony arch closed by the flexor retinaculum = carpal tunnel; contents = 9 tendons + median nerve (4 flexor digitorum superficialis, 4 flexor digitorum profundus, 1 flexor pollicis longus tendon + median nerve). Ulnar nerve and extensor tendons lie OUTSIDE the tunnel. Carpal tunnel syndrome = median nerve compression. Scaphoid is the most fractured carpal (risk of avascular necrosis). Joints: wrist (radiocarpal) = condyloid synovial (distal radius + articular disc / proximal carpal row EXCEPT pisiform); movements flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, circumduction. Intercarpal = plane (gliding); midcarpal (between rows) aids extension/abduction. Carpometacarpal (CMC) joints of medial 4 = plane; thumb CMC = SADDLE synovial joint (trapezium + base of 1st metacarpal) giving opposition. Metacarpophalangeal (MCP) of medial 4 = condyloid (flex/ext/abd/add) with collateral ligaments, palmar ligament, deep transverse metacarpal ligaments (tie metacarpal heads 2-5). Interphalangeal (IP) = hinge (flexion/extension). Rheumatoid arthritis = chronic autoimmune disease of synovial joints (~1 in 50 Australians, women>men), small joints of hand/feet, MCP ulnar deviation + erosion. Muscles: extrinsic (forearm bellies, long tendons) - anterior superficial (pronator teres, FCR, palmaris longus, FCU), intermediate (FDS), deep (FDP, FPL, pronator quadratus); posterior superficial (ECRL, ECRB, ED, EDM, ECU), deep (supinator, APL, EPB, EPL, EI). Intrinsic: thenar (abductor pollicis brevis, flexor pollicis brevis, opponens pollicis), hypothenar (abductor/flexor/opponens digiti minimi), adductor pollicis, 4 lumbricals, 4 dorsal + 3 palmar interossei, palmaris brevis. Innervation: ULNAR nerve supplies all intrinsics EXCEPT thenar muscles and lateral 2 lumbricals (median). Median = 'MEat LOAF' (Lumbricals 1&2, Opponens pollicis, Abductor pollicis brevis, Flexor pollicis brevis). Dorsal interossei ABduct = DAB (from adjacent metacarpal shafts, insert extensor hood + base proximal phalanx of index/middle/ring); palmar interossei ADduct = PAD. First dorsal interosseous is pierced by the radial artery. Lumbricals arise from FDP tendons, insert extensor hoods, flex MCP + extend IP. Ulnar nerve lesion = claw hand (worst ring/little fingers); median lesion = thenar wasting/ape hand. Fascia (5): palmar aponeurosis (deep fascia continuous with palmaris longus tendon, 4 bands -> fibrous digital sheaths, aids grip + protects neurovascular), flexor retinaculum (roof of carpal tunnel, limits flexor tendon bowstringing), fibrous digital sheaths (enclose flexor tendons + synovial sheaths, limit movement/friction), extensor retinaculum (holds extensor tendons, 6 osteofibrous tunnels, synovial sheaths), extensor hoods (expansions of extensor digitorum + extensor pollicis longus; lumbricals/interossei insert). Tenosynovitis = inflammation of tendon + synovial sheath. Mallet/baseball finger = avulsion of terminal extensor slip.

questions.question: How many bones are there in the hand altogether?
questions.explanation: The hand has 27 bones: 8 carpals, 5 metacarpals and 14 phalanges.

questions.question: Which nerve passes through the carpal tunnel?
questions.explanation: The median nerve is the only nerve in the carpal tunnel and is the structure compressed in carpal tunnel syndrome.

questions.question: The carpometacarpal joint of the thumb is which type of synovial joint?
questions.explanation: The thumb CMC is a saddle joint between the trapezium and the first metacarpal, giving the thumb its wide range and opposition.

questions.question: The interphalangeal joints of the fingers are which type of joint?
questions.explanation: Interphalangeal joints are hinge joints, so they allow only flexion and extension.

questions.question: Muscles located entirely within the hand are described as:
questions.explanation: Intrinsic muscles lie wholly within the hand and provide fine control; extrinsic muscles have forearm bellies and long tendons.

questions.question: Besides the median nerve, how many tendons pass through the carpal tunnel?
questions.explanation: Nine tendons pass through: four of flexor digitorum superficialis, four of flexor digitorum profundus, and one of flexor pollicis longus.

questions.question: The roof of the carpal tunnel is formed by the:
questions.explanation: The flexor retinaculum closes over the anteriorly concave carpal arch to form the roof of the tunnel.

questions.question: Carpal tunnel syndrome spares sensation in which digit?
questions.explanation: The little finger is in ulnar territory, outside the tunnel, so it is spared; the median nerve serves the thumb to half the ring finger.

questions.question: The radiocarpal joint articulates the distal radius and disc with the proximal carpal row, except the:
questions.explanation: The scaphoid, lunate and triquetrum meet the radius and disc, but the pisiform is excluded from the radiocarpal joint.

questions.question: The saddle shape of the thumb CMC joint uniquely allows the thumb to:
questions.explanation: The two perpendicular axes of the saddle joint let the thumb rotate to oppose the fingers, making the hand a precision tool.

questions.question: The metacarpophalangeal joints of the medial four fingers are which type?
questions.explanation: The MCP joints are condyloid, allowing flexion, extension, abduction and adduction of the fingers.

questions.question: The deep transverse metacarpal ligaments function to:
options: A. tie the metacarpal heads together
C. deepen the thumb saddle joint
questions.explanation: The deep transverse metacarpal ligaments tie the heads of metacarpals 2 to 5 together so the fingers move as a unit.

questions.question: The thenar muscles of the thumb are supplied by which nerve?
questions.explanation: The thenar muscles are supplied by the median nerve; most other intrinsic hand muscles take the ulnar nerve.

questions.question: The dorsal interossei of the hand act to:
questions.explanation: Dorsal interossei abduct the fingers (DAB), spreading them from the midline; palmar interossei adduct them (PAD).

questions.question: The palmar interossei of the hand act to:
questions.explanation: Palmar interossei adduct the fingers (PAD), drawing them toward the midline; dorsal interossei abduct them.

questions.question: The palmar aponeurosis blends proximally with the tendon of which muscle?
questions.explanation: The apex of the palmar aponeurosis blends with the palmaris longus tendon and splits distally into four digital bands.

questions.question: Rheumatoid arthritis of the hand classically drives the fingers into:
questions.explanation: As the MCP joints and ligaments erode, the fingers drift into ulnar deviation, a read-out of failing collateral ligaments.

questions.question: Which carpal bone ossifies first, at around one to three months of age?
questions.explanation: The capitate ossifies first at one to three months, and the other carpals follow in an anticlockwise order.

questions.question: The lumbricals are unusual because they arise from and insert into:
questions.explanation: Each lumbrical arises from an FDP tendon and inserts into an extensor hood, letting it flex the MCP while extending the IP joints.

questions.question: Which nerve supplies most of the intrinsic muscles of the hand?
questions.explanation: The ulnar nerve supplies most intrinsics; the exceptions are the thenar muscles and the two lateral lumbricals, which are median.

questions.question: An ulnar nerve lesion produces a claw hand that is worst in which digits?
options: A. the little and ring fingers
B. the thumb and index finger
C. the index and middle fingers
questions.explanation: The ulnar claw is worst in the little and ring fingers, whose lumbricals are ulnar, so their MCP joints hyperextend and IP joints claw.

questions.question: Wasting of the thenar muscles after a median nerve lesion produces the:
questions.explanation: Losing the median-supplied thenar muscles flattens the thumb into the plane of the palm, the ape hand, unable to oppose.

questions.question: Contracting the lumbricals and interossei produces which combined movement?
options: A. flex MCP and extend IP
B. extend MCP and flex IP
C. flex both MCP and IP
D. extend both MCP and IP
questions.explanation: Through the extensor hoods, the intrinsics flex the MCP joints while extending the IP joints, the intrinsic-plus position.

questions.question: Forcibly flexing an extended fingertip can avulse the extensor slip, causing:
questions.explanation: Avulsion of the terminal extensor slip leaves a drooping DIP joint that cannot straighten, known as mallet finger.

questions.question: The radial artery enters the palm by passing between the two heads of which muscle?
questions.explanation: The radial artery dives between the heads of the first dorsal interosseous, the large muscle in the thumb web, to reach the palm.

questions.question: The ulnar nerve reaches the hand through which passage, not the carpal tunnel?
questions.explanation: The ulnar nerve travels through Guyon's canal, outside the carpal tunnel, so it is spared in carpal tunnel syndrome.

questions.question: The extensor retinaculum divides the dorsal wrist tendons into how many compartments?
questions.explanation: Septa from the extensor retinaculum to the radius and ulna create six osteofibrous compartments, each with synovial-sheathed tendons.

questions.question: Infection in a fibrous digital sheath can spread proximally because the sheaths connect to the:
questions.explanation: Because the digital sheaths connect to the common flexor sheath, a fingertip infection can track up into the palm and wrist.

cell_division_medi2200_wk3.html.title: MEDI2200 W3 · Cell Division — DNA Organisation & Mitosis
cell_division_medi2200_wk3.html.subject: Human Cell & Molecular Biology
cell_division_medi2200_wk3.html.content: Cell division (Week 3). Eukaryotes hold DNA in a nucleus; prokaryotes have a free nucleoid. ~2 m of DNA is packed: DNA -> wound on histones as nucleosomes -> chromatin fibre -> further looping/supercoiling -> condensed chromosome. Packing also controls gene expression (accessibility). Euchromatin = loose, light, gene-rich, active; heterochromatin = tight, dark, silent (constitutive at centromeres/telomeres; facultative e.g. X-inactivation). Epigenetic control without changing sequence: HATs (acetylation) open chromatin -> active transcription; HDACs, KMTs, DNMTs (deacetylation/methylation) close it -> repressed. Chromosome: replication makes 2 identical sister chromatids joined at the centromere (spindle-attachment point) until anaphase; short arm p ('petit'), long arm q ('queue'); telomere caps each end. Centromere-position classes: metacentric (central), submetacentric (off-centre), acrocentric (near end), telocentric (at end; not in humans). Telomeres are repetitive caps that prevent end fusion, nuclease digestion and false double-strand-break signalling; end-replication problem shortens them each division -> replicative senescence (Hayflick limit); telomerase re-adds repeats (stem/germ cells, and reactivated in most cancers -> unlimited division). Human genome = 46 chromosomes = 23 pairs; homologous pairs (one per parent); 22 autosome pairs + 1 sex pair (XX/XY). Karyotype/karyogram arranges chromosomes by size to check number/structure. Locus = chromosome + arm(p/q) + region + band + sub-band, e.g. 3p22.1; bands numbered outward from the centromere. Somatic cells divide by mitosis (growth/maintenance/repair; identical diploid daughters = genomic stability); germ cells by meiosis (haploid gametes; genetic variation); prokaryotes by binary fission (replicate, segregate, split). Cell cycle = interphase (G1 growth, S DNA replication making sister chromatids, G2 prep) + M phase (mitosis + cytokinesis); G0 = resting. Mitosis PMAT: prophase (condense, spindle forms, nuclear envelope breaks) -> metaphase (align on metaphase plate) -> anaphase (sister chromatids to opposite poles) -> telophase (nuclei re-form, decondense) -> cytokinesis (2 identical diploid daughters). Progression driven by cyclins + CDKs; checkpoints: G1/S restriction (size/nutrients/DNA damage), G2/M (DNA fully/correctly replicated), spindle/M (all chromosomes attached). Checkpoint failure (e.g. p53 loss) -> division with damaged DNA -> cancer.

questions.question: The defining structural difference between a eukaryotic and a prokaryotic cell is that the eukaryote:
options: A. keeps its DNA inside a nucleus
B. lacks any internal membrane compartments
C. stores its DNA as a free nucleoid
D. carries a single circular chromosome only
questions.explanation: A membrane-bound nucleus houses eukaryotic DNA; a free nucleoid and a lone circular chromosome are prokaryotic traits.

questions.question: Ordered from least to most condensed, DNA is packaged as:
options: A. DNA → nucleosomes → chromatin fibre → chromosome
B. nucleosomes → DNA → chromosome → chromatin fibre
C. chromatin fibre → DNA → nucleosomes → chromosome
D. chromosome → chromatin fibre → nucleosomes → DNA
questions.explanation: DNA winds onto histones as nucleosomes, which coil into the chromatin fibre and condense into the chromosome.

questions.question: A single nucleosome is best described as:
options: A. DNA wound around a histone protein core
B. two histones bridged by a DNA loop
C. a coil of pure histone with no DNA
D. supercoiled DNA with no bound protein
questions.explanation: The nucleosome — DNA wrapped on a histone core — is chromatin's repeating unit and always contains both DNA and histones.

questions.question: Beyond compacting ~2 m of DNA, chromatin condensation also determines:
options: A. which genes are accessible for transcription
B. how much total DNA the cell holds
C. the number of chromosomes present
D. the speed of DNA polymerase itself
questions.explanation: Packing tightness sets DNA accessibility, so condensation doubles as a transcriptional switch; it alters neither DNA quantity nor chromosome count.

questions.question: Euchromatin is chromatin that is:
options: A. loosely packed and actively transcribed
B. tightly packed and transcriptionally silent
C. permanently condensed at every centromere
D. found only inside dividing gametes
questions.explanation: Euchromatin is open, gene-rich and active; the tightly packed, silent form is heterochromatin.

questions.question: Which enzyme loosens chromatin to promote transcription?
questions.explanation: Acetyltransferases add acetyl groups that loosen histone grip and open chromatin; deacetylases and methyltransferases tighten and close it.

questions.question: A gene can be silenced without altering its DNA sequence when:
options: A. its chromatin is methylated and deacetylated
B. a point mutation disrupts its promoter
C. the whole gene is deleted from the chromosome
D. a frameshift scrambles its coding region
questions.explanation: Methylation and deacetylation lock a gene into heterochromatin epigenetically; mutation, deletion and frameshift all change the sequence itself.

questions.question: The inactivated X chromosome in females is an example of:
questions.explanation: X-inactivation condenses one X only in some contexts, making it facultative; centromeric and telomeric silencing is constitutive.

questions.question: Sister chromatids are:
options: A. identical DNA copies joined at the centromere
B. a maternal and paternal chromosome pair
C. two unrelated chromosomes of different size
D. the two arms of a single chromosome
questions.explanation: Replication produces two identical copies held at the centromere until anaphase; the maternal/paternal pair are homologues, not sisters.

questions.question: The centromere is critical for division because it:
options: A. anchors the spindle that separates chromatids
B. caps and protects the chromosome ends
C. carries most of the cell's active genes
D. replicates the DNA during S phase
questions.explanation: The centromere is the kinetochore/spindle-attachment point for accurate segregation; end protection is the telomere's role.

questions.question: On a chromosome, the p arm is the:
questions.explanation: p ('petit') denotes the short arm; q ('queue') is the long arm.

questions.question: A chromosome with a slightly off-centre centromere and unequal arms is:
questions.explanation: Off-centre with unequal arms is submetacentric; metacentric is central, acrocentric sits near an end, telocentric right at the end.

questions.question: Which centromere position does NOT occur in human chromosomes?
questions.explanation: Humans lack telocentric chromosomes, whose centromere sits at the very tip; these are common in mice.

questions.question: Which is a protective function of telomeres?
options: A. stopping chromosome ends from fusing
B. attaching chromosomes to the spindle
C. replicating DNA at each cell division
questions.explanation: Telomere caps prevent end-to-end fusion, nuclease digestion and false damage signals; spindle attachment is the centromere's job.

questions.question: Telomeres shorten at every division because:
options: A. polymerase cannot finish a linear chromosome's end
B. nucleases deliberately trim both of the chromosome ends
C. the centromere consumes telomeric repeats
D. histones strip repeats during condensation
questions.explanation: The end-replication problem leaves the very tip uncopied, costing telomere each division; telomerase, not nucleases, offsets this.

questions.question: When a normal cell's telomeres grow critically short, it:
options: A. enters senescence and stops dividing
B. immediately becomes a cancer cell
C. doubles its rate of division
D. reverses its telomere shortening alone
questions.explanation: Critically short telomeres trigger replicative senescence — the Hayflick limit; re-lengthening would need telomerase reactivation.

questions.question: Most cancers achieve limitless division largely because they:
options: A. reactivate telomerase to rebuild telomeres
B. permanently silence every checkpoint gene
C. stop replicating their DNA altogether
D. lose all their centromeres at once
questions.explanation: Reactivated telomerase resets the shortening clock, granting unlimited divisions; checkpoint loss contributes but is a separate lesion.

questions.question: The human genome comprises:
questions.explanation: Humans carry 46 chromosomes arranged as 23 homologous pairs.

questions.question: Among the 23 human chromosome pairs:
options: A. 22 are autosomes and one the sex pair
B. 23 are autosomes with no sex pair
C. 21 are autosomes and two are sex pairs
D. all 23 pairs are sex chromosomes
questions.explanation: There are 22 autosome pairs plus one sex pair, XX or XY.

questions.question: Homologous chromosomes are:
options: A. a matched pair carrying the same genes
B. the two identical copies from replication
C. two chromosomes of completely different genes
D. the short and long arms of one chromosome
questions.explanation: Homologues are the maternal and paternal partners carrying the same genes; the identical replication copies are sister chromatids.

questions.question: The locus 3p22.1 specifies chromosome 3,:
options: A. short arm, region 2, band 2, sub-band 1
B. long arm, region 2, band 2, sub-band 1
C. short arm, region 1, band 2, sub-band 2
D. long arm, region 1, band 2, sub-band 2
questions.explanation: p marks the short arm; the digits read as region 2, band 2, sub-band 1.

questions.question: Chromosome bands are numbered:
options: A. outward from the centromere toward the telomere
B. inward from the telomere toward the centromere
C. randomly by staining intensity alone
D. from the p tip to the q tip
questions.explanation: Numbering starts at the centromere and rises outward along each arm toward the telomere.

questions.question: Somatic cells undergo mitosis to produce:
options: A. genetically identical diploid daughter cells
C. four cells from one division
D. cells with half the chromosome number
questions.explanation: Mitosis yields identical diploid daughters for growth, maintenance and repair; the other options describe meiosis.

questions.question: Compared with mitosis, meiosis uniquely:
options: A. produces haploid, genetically varied gametes
B. produces identical diploid daughter cells
C. copies DNA twice per single division
D. skips the S phase entirely
questions.explanation: Meiosis generates haploid, varied gametes; identical diploid output is the hallmark of mitosis.

questions.question: Prokaryotic binary fission proceeds by:
options: A. replicating, segregating, then splitting the cell
B. building a spindle to align chromosomes
C. pairing homologues before two divisions
D. forming four haploid daughter cells
questions.explanation: Binary fission replicates the single chromosome, segregates the copies and splits — no spindle; the others describe mitosis and meiosis.

questions.question: DNA is replicated during which part of interphase?
questions.explanation: Synthesis (S) phase copies the DNA into sister chromatids; G1 and G2 are growth and preparation, G0 is resting.

questions.question: The defining event of anaphase is:
options: A. sister chromatids moving to opposite poles
B. chromosomes aligning on the metaphase plate
C. the nuclear envelope breaking apart
D. the cytoplasm dividing into two cells
questions.explanation: Anaphase is chromatid separation to opposite poles; alignment is metaphase, envelope breakdown prophase, cytoplasmic split cytokinesis.

questions.question: The mitotic phases occur in the order:
questions.explanation: PMAT orders the phases: prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase.

questions.question: The spindle-assembly (M) checkpoint delays anaphase until:
options: A. every chromosome is attached to the spindle
B. all the DNA has been fully replicated
C. the cell has reached sufficient size
D. nutrients and growth signals are adequate
questions.explanation: The M checkpoint blocks anaphase until every kinetochore is correctly attached; replication completeness is the G2/M check, size and nutrients the G1/S check.

questions.question: Cell-cycle dysregulation drives cancer when:
options: A. checkpoints fail, letting cells divide with damage
B. checkpoints halt division before any DNA damage
C. telomeres lengthen normally each cycle
D. cyclins are destroyed at every phase
questions.explanation: Lost checkpoint control — as with p53 mutation — lets damaged genomes replicate and proliferate; functioning checkpoints instead arrest such cells.

questions.question: Progression through the cell cycle is driven mainly by:
options: A. cyclins activating their partner CDKs
B. telomerase extending the chromosome ends
D. nucleases trimming the spindle fibres
questions.explanation: Rising cyclins bind and activate cyclin-dependent kinases that push the cycle forward; the other enzymes act elsewhere.

questions.question: A non-dividing cell that has exited the cycle rests in:
questions.explanation: Quiescent cells sit in G0, outside the active cycle; S, G2 and M are all part of ongoing division.

questions.question: A karyogram is used chiefly to:
options: A. check chromosome number and structure
B. measure a cell's telomerase activity
C. sequence every gene on a chromosome
D. time the length of S phase
questions.explanation: A karyogram arranges chromosomes by size to screen number and gross structure; it does not sequence genes or measure enzyme activity.

meiosis_medi2200_wk4.html.title: MEDI2200 W4 · Meiosis — Cell Division & Genetic Variation
meiosis_medi2200_wk4.html.subject: Human Cell & Molecular Biology
meiosis_medi2200_wk4.html.content: Meiosis (Week 4). Meiosis makes haploid (n) gametes from diploid (2n) germ cells (ovaries/testes) so fertilisation (n + n -> 2n zygote) keeps the chromosome number constant; it also mixes the genome for variation. Gametogenesis: spermatogenesis (sperm), oogenesis (ova). Meiosis vs mitosis: both have one DNA replication (S phase); mitosis = 1 division -> 2 identical diploid somatic cells; meiosis = 2 divisions (no replication between) -> up to 4 varied haploid cells; homologues pair only in meiosis. Stages: interphase replicates DNA (each chromosome = 2 sister chromatids). Meiosis I (PMAT I) is reductional: homologous chromosomes pair then SEPARATE (sister chromatids stay together) -> 2 haploid cells whose chromosomes still have 2 chromatids. Meiosis II (PMAT II) is like mitosis: sister chromatids separate -> 4 haploid cells with single/unreplicated chromosomes. Anaphase I = homologues apart; anaphase II = sister chromatids apart. Three sources of genetic variation: (1) crossing over in prophase I - homologues pair (synapsis, bivalent/tetrad, synaptonemal complex) and non-sister chromatids exchange DNA at chiasmata; prophase I substages leptotene (condense) -> zygotene (synapsis) -> pachytene (crossing over) -> diplotene (chiasmata visible) -> diakinesis; without chiasmata segregation can be erroneous. (2) Independent assortment at metaphase I - homologue pairs orient randomly (2^23 combinations). (3) Random assortment at metaphase II of the now non-identical sister chromatids. Non-disjunction = failure of chromosomes to separate: homologues fail in meiosis I, sister chromatids fail in meiosis II -> gametes with an extra/missing chromosome -> aneuploidy. Trisomy 21 = Down syndrome (47,+21); monosomy X = Turner syndrome (45,X); 47,XXY = Klinefelter. Trisomy-21 risk rises with maternal age (long-arrested oocyte meiosis I). Chiasmata tether homologues for correct segregation, so failed crossover is one cause of non-disjunction.

questions.question: Gametes must be haploid so that fertilisation:
options: A. restores the normal diploid number
B. doubles the diploid number each generation
C. keeps every offspring genetically identical
D. removes one chromosome from the zygote
questions.explanation: Two haploid gametes fuse to a diploid zygote, holding chromosome number constant; diploid gametes would double it each generation.

questions.question: In terms of ploidy, fertilisation is:
questions.explanation: Two haploid (n) gametes fuse to form one diploid (2n) zygote.

questions.question: Meiosis takes place only in:
options: A. germ cells of the ovaries and testes
B. somatic cells throughout the body
C. red blood cells within the bone marrow
D. skin cells during wound repair
questions.explanation: Meiosis is confined to germ cells during gametogenesis; somatic cells everywhere else divide by mitosis.

questions.question: Compared with mitosis, meiosis produces:
options: A. four haploid cells from two divisions
B. two diploid cells from one division
C. two haploid cells from one division
D. four diploid cells from two divisions
questions.explanation: Two meiotic divisions give up to four haploid cells; mitosis's single division gives two diploid cells.

questions.question: Across the whole of meiosis, DNA is replicated:
options: B. once between meiosis I and II
D. never, since cells start diploid
questions.explanation: A single S-phase precedes meiosis I with none between the two divisions — two divisions on one replication.

questions.question: Which event happens in meiosis but never in mitosis?
options: C. the nuclear envelope breaking down
D. the spindle attaching to chromosomes
questions.explanation: Homologue pairing (synapsis) in prophase I is unique to meiosis; the other events occur in both processes.

questions.question: Meiosis I separates:
questions.explanation: Meiosis I is reductional — homologues part while sister chromatids stay joined until meiosis II.

questions.question: Meiosis II separates:
questions.explanation: Meiosis II resembles mitosis — sister chromatids separate, giving four haploid cells with single chromosomes.

questions.question: Which statement about meiotic anaphase is correct?
options: A. anaphase I parts homologues; anaphase II parts sisters
B. anaphase I parts sisters; anaphase II parts homologues
C. both anaphases separate only the sister chromatids
D. both anaphases separate only the homologous pairs
questions.explanation: Anaphase I pulls homologues apart with sisters still joined; anaphase II then pulls the sister chromatids apart.

questions.question: The cells produced at the end of meiosis I are:
options: A. haploid, with chromosomes of two chromatids
B. diploid, with chromosomes of two chromatids
questions.explanation: Meiosis I halves the chromosome number but each chromosome still carries two sister chromatids until meiosis II.

questions.question: Meiosis II is said to resemble mitosis because it:
options: A. separates the sister chromatids of each chromosome
B. pairs homologues before they separate
C. replicates the DNA one more time first
D. doubles the chromosome number again
questions.explanation: Like mitosis, meiosis II separates sister chromatids — but from a haploid cell with no preceding replication.

questions.question: Crossing over takes place during:
questions.explanation: Homologues pair and exchange segments during prophase I.

questions.question: Crossing over exchanges DNA between:
options: A. non-sister chromatids of paired homologues
B. the two sister chromatids of one chromosome
D. the two arms of a single chromatid
questions.explanation: Recombination swaps segments between non-sister chromatids of the paired homologues, mixing maternal and paternal alleles.

questions.question: During which substage of prophase I does crossing over occur?
questions.explanation: Homologues condense (leptotene), pair (zygotene), cross over (pachytene), then show chiasmata (diplotene).

questions.question: Chiasmata are:
options: A. the visible crossover points between homologues
B. the spindle fibres that pull chromatids
C. the centromeres joining sister chromatids
D. the caps protecting each chromosome end
questions.explanation: Chiasmata are the crossover points seen once the synaptonemal complex dissolves; they tether homologues for correct segregation.

questions.question: Independent assortment of homologous pairs occurs at:
questions.explanation: At metaphase I the homologue pairs line up in random orientation, so each gamete inherits a random mix.

questions.question: Random assortment in meiosis II adds variation because the sister chromatids are now:
options: A. no longer identical, owing to crossing over
B. identical copies of one another still
C. fused permanently at the centromere
D. reduced to a single DNA strand each
questions.explanation: Crossing over in prophase I made the sisters non-identical, so their random orientation in meiosis II reshuffles alleles again.

questions.question: Synapsis refers to:
options: A. the pairing of homologous chromosomes
B. the splitting of sister chromatids
C. the breakdown of the nuclear envelope
D. the copying of DNA in S phase
questions.explanation: Synapsis is the close pairing of homologues into a bivalent in prophase I, enabling crossing over.

questions.question: For 23 chromosome pairs, independent assortment alone yields how many gamete combinations?
questions.explanation: Each of the 23 pairs orients two independent ways, giving 2^23 (~8 million) combinations before crossing over adds more.

questions.question: Non-disjunction is:
options: A. failure of chromosomes to separate properly
B. exchange of DNA between homologues
C. random alignment on the metaphase plate
D. normal halving of the chromosome number
questions.explanation: Non-disjunction is failed separation — of homologues in meiosis I or sister chromatids in meiosis II.

questions.question: Non-disjunction during meiosis I specifically means that:
options: A. homologous chromosomes fail to separate
B. sister chromatids fail to separate
C. the DNA fails to replicate at all
D. the spindle fails to form entirely
questions.explanation: In meiosis I the failure is of homologues to separate; a meiosis-II failure instead involves the sister chromatids.

questions.question: Non-disjunction produces gametes that:
options: A. have an extra or missing chromosome
B. carry exactly the normal chromosome set
C. contain double the usual DNA amount
D. lack any centromeres at all
questions.explanation: A gamete gains or loses a chromosome, so the resulting individual is aneuploid — a wrong chromosome number.

questions.question: Three copies of chromosome 21 cause:
questions.explanation: Trisomy 21 (47,+21) is Down syndrome — the commonest autosomal aneuploidy.

questions.question: The karyotype of Turner syndrome is:
questions.explanation: Turner syndrome is a single X — 45,X, i.e. 45 chromosomes instead of 46.

questions.question: Klinefelter syndrome has the karyotype:
questions.explanation: Klinefelter syndrome is an extra X in a male — 47,XXY.

questions.question: Failure to form chiasmata can cause non-disjunction because chiasmata normally:
options: A. hold homologues aligned for correct segregation
B. copy the DNA before the first division
C. dissolve the nuclear envelope at prophase
D. attach the spindle to each telomere
questions.explanation: Chiasmata physically tether paired homologues in correct orientation until anaphase I; without them a pair may missegregate.

questions.question: Trisomy 21 risk rises with maternal age chiefly because of:
options: A. errors in the long-arrested oocyte's meiosis I
B. faster oocyte division in older women
C. extra rounds of DNA replication with age
D. loss of all telomeres from the oocyte
questions.explanation: Oocytes stay arrested in meiosis I for years; the longer arrest raises the chance of meiosis-I non-disjunction with age.

questions.question: A gamete is:
options: D. a resting germ-line stem cell
questions.explanation: Gametes are the haploid products of meiosis — sperm or ova — that fuse at fertilisation.

questions.question: The formation of sperm cells is specifically called:
questions.explanation: Spermatogenesis makes sperm; oogenesis makes ova — both are forms of gametogenesis by meiosis.

questions.question: The four-chromatid structure formed when homologues pair in prophase I is a:
questions.explanation: Two paired homologues, each of two chromatids, form a four-strand bivalent (tetrad) where crossing over occurs.

soci1010_wk1_everyday_life.html.title: SOCI1010 W1 · What is Everyday Life? — Intro to Sociology
soci1010_wk1_everyday_life.html.subject: Sociology
soci1010_wk1_everyday_life.html.content: SOCI1010 Introduction to Sociology: Understanding Everyday Life — Week 1 'Making something out of nothing?' (A/Prof Selvaraj Velayutham). SOURCE 1 LECTURE: Sociology = the study of society and how society shapes our lives, and a tool for understanding the world. C. Wright Mills (1959) — the SOCIOLOGICAL IMAGINATION: a quality of mind, the vivid awareness of the relationship between personal experience and the wider society; neither an individual's life nor a society's history can be understood without understanding both; 'thinking yourself away from the familiar routines of everyday life'. The MONOBLOC chair (ubiquitous cheap stackable plastic chair, petroleum-derived, ignored, despised by designers, yet world's most popular furniture) = making something out of nothing: the mundane object is significant. Ben Highmore (2011): in ordinary life there is never 'nothing' going on, just nothing 'much'. Everyday life = taken-for-granted, mundane, routine daily life; the sociology of everyday life interrogates daily practices, activities and interactions. TOOTHBRUSHING unpacked: routine (mundane/taken-for-granted); RITUALISTIC (repetition & habituation, personal techniques — brush, bristle, paste, floss); EMBODIED PRACTICE (socialisation/training in the correct way, internalised); SOCIAL NORM (can't imagine anyone not doing it; tied to age, class, gender, race); personal hygiene & idealised beauty (the 'perfect smile' originates in Hollywood); PUBLIC HEALTH (WHO 2022: oral disease affects ~3.5 billion; cavities prevented by constant low fluoride; periodontal disease in 15-20% of 35-44s; ~30% of 65-74s have no natural teeth; worse among the poor; risk factors diet/tobacco/alcohol/poor hygiene/social determinants); STRUCTURAL INEQUALITY ('the unseen dentist' — dentists cluster in middle-class areas, haves vs have-nots); GLOBAL CAPITALISM (toothpaste brands owned by a few multinationals — Colgate-Palmolive, P&G [Crest, Oral B], GlaxoSmithKline [Macleans, Aquafresh, Sensodyne], Unilever, Johnson & Johnson [Listerine]; 'unlimited choice' is an illusion). SOCIOLOGY & COMEDY: Peter Berger (1970) — the social scientist who misses the comic dimension misses essential features of social reality; Zijderveld (1997) — the sociologist is like the fool holding up a mirror. Sociology is LIKE comedy (puts everyday manners/customs under the microscope, questions authority) but DIFFERS (more systematic/objective methods, specialised concepts). Seinfeld = 'the show about nothing'; characters constantly monitor the rules of interaction = REFLEXIVITY (what are the rules? how to interpret them? do they make sense/why exist? consequences of breaking them?). SOURCE 2 READING — Susie Scott, Making Sense of Everyday Life (2009), Ch.1 'What is Everyday Life?': everyday life IS the wider picture — micro-level small-scale practices relate to and are shaped by macro-level patterns; social order/disorder/change reflect individual-society, agency-structure. Moran (2005) four 'quotidian spaces': workspaces, urban/mobile spaces, living spaces, non-places (transit spaces between contexts — buses, service stations). Silva & Bennett (2004): home/family/community, sexuality/'race'/age, technology. Three defining FEATURES: (1) mundane/familiar/unremarkable ('daily lives of ordinary people', Bennett & Watson 2002); (2) routine/repetitive/rhythmic — habitual (Felski 1999), reproduces social life; (3) private/personal — Mills: relate 'private troubles' to 'public issues'. Everyday phenomena 'obvious to the point of elusiveness' (Martin 2003), the 'connective tissue' (Bennett 2004), yet infused with power/politics/history (Martin). DEVELOPMENT: an 'absent presence' — implicit in studies of poverty (Rowntree 1901), kinship (Willmott & Young 1960), deviance (Becker 1963); now studied in its own right like the sociology of the body (Turner 1996). Bennett & Watson's three reasons: (1) ordinary lives become worthy of public representation (photojournalism, diaries, reality TV); (2) Foucauldian 'disciplinary society' of control/surveillance; (3) social movements (feminism, black civil rights, Gay Pride). Prominent theorists: Lukács (pre-reflective acceptance stops authentic living), Lefebvre (capitalist workplace alienation, false consciousness, la vie quotidienne), de Certeau (people 'do'/practise everyday life; resistance via minor rule-breaking = 'making do'). Douglas (1981): study common-sense meanings. Berger & Luckmann (1967): we construct our own social reality through everyday encounters; no single objective reality — central to interpretivist sociology (Symbolic Interactionism, phenomenology, ethnomethodology). Cultural Studies: places/images/artefacts read as 'texts' transmitting ideologies. HOW TO STUDY: (1) make the familiar strange — view objectively, bracket assumptions/value judgements, morally neutral; 'anthropologist on Mars' (Sacks 1996), detective story (Highmore 2002); (2) search for underlying rules/routines/regularities, link micro to macro; (3) challenge taken-for-granted assumptions (Garfinkel 1967) by studying norm-breaking; Durkheim (1893): deviance is FUNCTIONAL — unites 'us' vs 'them', reinforces shared values, makes the group cohesive; some rules only visible when broken (faux pas). Three THEMES per topic: rituals & routines; social order; challenges (norm-breaking, 'exceptions that prove the rule'). SOURCE 3 — Jorge Gracia, 'The Secret of Seinfeld's Humor: The Significance of the Insignificant' (Seinfeld and Philosophy, 2000): THESIS — we laugh at something because in it we see the SIGNIFICANCE OF THE INSIGNIFICANT, and we cry at something because through it we grasp the INSIGNIFICANCE OF THE SIGNIFICANT. Not a universal/scientific law — a matter of emotion/feeling, not intellect. Comedy is about the ordinary/everyday: it makes our unnoticed idiosyncrasies, manners, customs come alive, revealing the follies, absurdities and idiosyncrasies of cultures. Seinfeld's success = capturing the significance of the insignificant ('a show about nothing'); characters never think their doings significant. Tragedy is the opposite: momentous subject matter (love, death, betrayal, vice, virtue, pain, injustice, cruelty, revenge), characters 'larger than life' (heroes, villains, victims, ogres); no tragedy is written about the sale of a van, mail delivery or non-fat yogurt. Tragedy underscores significance then reveals the insignificance of what we hold dear (a shattering realisation); comedy teaches without pain. Comedy dates more easily than tragedy because it turns on culture-specific everyday customs, whereas tragedy taps the more universal core of human nature.

questions.question: In the lecture, sociology is defined as:
options: A. the study of how society shapes our lives
B. the study of individual psychology and choice
C. the study of ancient human biology
D. the study of economic markets on their own
questions.explanation: Sociology examines society and how it shapes our lives — and serves as a tool for understanding the world.

questions.question: C. Wright Mills (1959) gave the name 'sociological imagination' to:
options: A. a quality of mind linking personal life to society
B. a talent for inventing fictional social worlds
C. a statistical method for surveying populations
D. a bias that hides society behind the lone individual
questions.explanation: Mills called it a quality of mind: vivid awareness of the relationship between personal experience and the wider society.

questions.question: Which statement best captures Mills's sociological imagination?
options: A. neither a life nor a history makes sense alone
B. individual choices explain all of history
C. society can be fully grasped without any real individuals
D. personal biography is irrelevant to sociology
questions.explanation: The individual and society are mutually intelligible — you cannot grasp one without the other.

questions.question: For Mills, to 'relate private troubles to public issues' means to:
options: A. find the social patterns within individual lives
B. blame individuals for their own hardships
C. treat every problem as purely personal
D. ignore the structures around a person
questions.explanation: Thinking sociologically links private troubles to public issues — seeing the social structure behind individual experience.

questions.question: For Mills, blaming an unemployed person for 'laziness':
options: A. mistakes a public issue for a private trouble
B. mistakes a private trouble for a public issue
C. correctly locates the cause in the person
D. shows a fully developed sociological imagination
questions.explanation: Unemployment is shaped by social forces such as the job market and offshoring; blaming the individual misreads a public issue.

questions.question: Why does the lecture open with the mass-produced monobloc plastic chair?
options: A. to show a mundane object is sociologically significant
B. to argue design history is the core of sociology
C. to prove cheap objects have no social meaning
D. to celebrate the genius of industrial designers
questions.explanation: The monobloc — cheap, mass-produced, ignored — is 'making something out of nothing', showing the mundane is worth study.

questions.question: Ben Highmore's point about answering 'nothing much' to 'what have you been up to?' is that:
options: A. ordinary life is never 'nothing', only 'nothing much'
B. most people genuinely do nothing much at all
C. small talk should always be avoided
D. ordinary life is too trivial to study
questions.explanation: Highmore (2011) insists the 'nothing much' of ordinary life is full of social activity worth examining.

questions.question: 'Everyday life' is best defined as:
options: A. the taken-for-granted, routine parts of daily life
B. the rare, dramatic events of a lifetime
C. the formal rituals of the state and church
D. the private thoughts we never act upon
questions.explanation: Everyday life refers to the common-sensical, mundane, routine activities we all take for granted.

questions.question: The lecture calls tooth-brushing 'ritualistic' because it is:
options: A. based on repetition and habituation
B. performed only on special occasions
C. required by an explicit written law
D. done differently every single time
questions.explanation: As a ritual, brushing rests on repetition and habituation; each person develops their own methods over time.

questions.question: Learning the 'proper way' to brush until it feels natural is described as:
options: A. an embodied practice acquired through socialisation
B. an instinct we are simply born with
C. a purely biological reflex action
D. a one-off choice made in adulthood
questions.explanation: Embodied practice means socialisation and training in the correct technique, which becomes familiar and internalised.

questions.question: That we 'can't imagine anyone NOT brushing their teeth' expresses:
options: A. a social norm, a shared expectation
B. a formal law with legal penalties
D. a biological need for survival
questions.explanation: The sense that everyone does it marks brushing as a social norm — a shared expectation about behaviour.

questions.question: Saying brushing norms are 'tied to age, class, gender and race' makes the point that:
options: A. personal habits are socially structured, not just individual
B. hygiene is identical across every single social group
C. class has no bearing on daily routines
D. private habits are beyond sociology's reach
questions.explanation: A private-seeming act is patterned by social position — the recurring theme that the personal is social.

questions.question: The lecture traces the modern demand for a 'perfect smile' to:
options: A. Hollywood and idealised standards of beauty
D. the invention of the toothbrush itself
questions.explanation: The 'perfect smile' originates in Hollywood, where perfectly white teeth became an idealised beauty requirement.

questions.question: The 'unseen dentist' — dentists clustering in middle-class areas — illustrates:
options: A. structural inequality between haves and have-nots
B. a free market working perfectly for everyone
C. individual laziness among rural patients
D. the irrelevance of geography to health
questions.explanation: Unequal access to dental care exposes structural inequality and power differences between rich and poor.

questions.question: Most toothpaste brands being owned by a few multinationals makes the point that:
options: A. everyday consumption sits inside global capitalism
B. consumers enjoy truly unlimited free choice
C. small local firms dominate the market
D. branding has no effect on what we buy
questions.explanation: A handful of corporations control production and supply, so the apparent variety of choice is largely an illusion.

questions.question: Medicine's monopoly of expert knowledge over the human body is called:
questions.explanation: The 'unseen dentist' example introduces medicalisation — medicine holding a monopoly of knowledge over the body.

questions.question: Peter Berger argued a social scientist blind to the comic dimension will:
options: A. miss essential features of social reality
B. produce more objective, rigorous work
C. avoid all bias in their findings
D. understand society far more deeply
questions.explanation: Berger (1970) held that the comic dimension reveals essential features of social reality that are otherwise missed.

questions.question: Zijderveld compared the scrutinising sociologist to which figure?
options: A. the fool holding up a mirror to society
B. the king who issues the laws to society
C. the priest blessing the community
D. the soldier defending the nation
questions.explanation: Zijderveld (1997) likened the sociologist to the traditional fool who holds up a mirror to show people themselves.

questions.question: In what way is sociology LIKE comedy, according to the lecture?
options: A. both hold everyday customs up to scrutiny
B. both aim mainly to entertain an audience
C. both avoid questioning any authority
D. both rely on invented, fictional data
questions.explanation: Like comedy, sociology holds everyday arrangements up to scrutiny and asks whether they make sense, often questioning authority.

questions.question: How does the lecture say sociology DIFFERS from comedy?
options: A. its methods are systematic and objective
B. it never examines everyday manners
C. it always avoids specialised concepts
D. it aims only to make people laugh
questions.explanation: Unlike comedy, sociology employs more systematic, objective methods and a specialised set of concepts and language.

questions.question: When Seinfeld's characters constantly reflect on how to act, they show what sociologists call:
questions.explanation: Reflexivity is the ongoing monitoring of the rules of interaction — asking what the rules are and how to read them.

questions.question: Scott answers the charge that everyday life is 'trivial' by arguing that:
options: A. everyday life is the wider picture in miniature
B. big events have nothing to do with small acts
C. only large institutions deserve real study
D. daily routines truly are of no importance
questions.explanation: Scott's core claim: micro-level small-scale practices relate to and are shaped by macro-level patterns.

questions.question: Social order, disorder and change, Scott says, reflect the relationship between:
options: A. individual and society, agency and structure
B. profit and loss in the marketplace
C. nature and the physical environment
D. past and future technological change
questions.explanation: Everyday life expresses the relationship between individual and society, agency and structure, process and regularity.

questions.question: In sociology, 'structure' refers to:
options: A. the social rules we largely conform to
B. the physical buildings that a society constructs
C. an individual's freedom to rebel
D. the biology of the human body
questions.explanation: Structure is the social rules — from parents and teachers to the law — that most of us conform to most of the time.

questions.question: 'Agency' refers to:
options: A. the capacity to express individuality and challenge norms
B. the fixed rules society imposes on everyone else
C. a government office that enforces law
D. the inability to act against structure
questions.explanation: Agency is the individual's capacity to express individuality, think differently and challenge restrictive norms.

questions.question: Someone who refuses to conform to social structure is typically labelled:
questions.explanation: Those who do not conform to social rules are often seen as deviant.

questions.question: Durkheim argued that deviance is:
options: B. purely destructive of every society
C. entirely a matter of individual choice
D. completely absent from healthy groups
questions.explanation: For Durkheim (1893) deviance is functional: labelling a rule-breaker as deviant reinforces the group's shared values.

questions.question: In Moran's four types of 'quotidian space', a 'non-place' is:
options: A. a transit space such as a bus or station
B. a private family home that is full of memories
C. a workplace where people earn a wage
D. a sacred site of religious worship
questions.explanation: Moran (2005) lists workspaces, urban/mobile spaces, living spaces and non-places — the last being transit spaces.

questions.question: Scott says everyday life is mundane, private and also:
questions.explanation: The three defining features are mundane and unremarkable, private and personal, and routine, repetitive and rhythmic.

questions.question: The claim that everyday life is 'habitual in nature' is attributed to:
questions.explanation: Felski (1999) characterised everyday life as habitual, which is what makes it feel so familiar.

questions.question: Martin (2003) describes everyday phenomena as 'obvious to the point of...':
questions.explanation: Martin's phrase is 'obvious to the point of elusiveness' — the everyday is so pervasive it slips from view.

questions.question: Everyday phenomena are called the 'connective tissue' holding everything together by:
questions.explanation: Bennett (2004) called the everyday the 'connective tissue' forming the background against which experience stands out.

questions.question: Martin (2003) insists the everyday is NOT trivial because it is:
options: A. infused with power, politics and history
B. merely a set of harmless routines
C. separate from all social structures
D. beyond the reach of any analysis
questions.explanation: Martin reminds us the everyday world is infused with power, politics and historical significance.

questions.question: Before it was studied in its own right, Scott says everyday life had an:
options: B. exclusive focus of every scholar
C. official ban from academic work
D. clearly named field of its own
questions.explanation: Everyday life had an 'absent presence' — implicitly addressed within earlier studies of poverty, kinship and deviance.

questions.question: Scott names which trio as the most prominent early theorists of everyday life?
options: A. Lukács, Lefebvre and de Certeau
questions.explanation: The most prominent theorists in this mode were Georg Lukács, Henri Lefebvre and Michel de Certeau.

questions.question: Lukács warned that being too immersed in daily routine produces:
options: C. a creative resistance to authority
D. a total escape from all structure
questions.explanation: Lukács's 'pre-reflective acceptance' stops people realising their potential or living authentically.

questions.question: Applying Marx, Lefebvre argued dreary, repetitive capitalist workplaces kept people in:
options: A. false consciousness, alienated from their conditions
B. full awareness of their exploitation
C. permanent open rebellion against bosses
D. complete control of the means of production
questions.explanation: Lefebvre held that the factory's repetitive cycles alienated workers and sustained false consciousness.

questions.question: de Certeau argued people subvert authority by breaking minor everyday rules — a tactic he called:
questions.explanation: de Certeau (1984) stressed how people 'do' everyday life creatively and defiantly, resisting through minor rule-breaking.

questions.question: Berger and Luckmann (1967) famously argued that:
options: A. we construct social reality through everyday encounters
B. one fixed objective reality exists for all
C. society is determined only by biology
D. individuals have no role in shaping reality
questions.explanation: For Berger and Luckmann there is no single objective reality but many local, subjective realities built with others.

questions.question: The view that there is no single objective reality, only local realities seen from the insider's view, is central to:
questions.explanation: This tenet informs interpretivist sociology — symbolic interactionists, phenomenologists and ethnomethodologists.

questions.question: Cultural Studies theorists treat the places and artefacts of everyday life as:
options: A. 'texts' to be read for their ideologies
B. neutral objects that carry no real meaning
C. purely economic units of value
D. facts to be counted statistically
questions.explanation: Cultural Studies reads everyday places and artefacts as 'texts' conveying particular ideologies (Moran 2005).

questions.question: Garfinkel's contribution to studying everyday life is the technique of:
options: A. challenging assumptions by studying broken rules
B. surveying huge populations by questionnaire
C. measuring behaviour in a laboratory
D. reading historical archives for patterns
questions.explanation: Garfinkel (1967) urged us to challenge taken-for-granted assumptions; norm-breaking makes implicit rules visible.

questions.question: 'Making the familiar strange' requires the researcher to:
options: A. bracket out prior assumptions and stay descriptive
B. judge each setting by personal morals
C. rely only on their common-sense views
D. avoid observing ordinary settings at all
questions.explanation: The first technique is descriptive and analytical, not evaluative — you suspend assumptions about what is normal.

questions.question: The phrase 'the anthropologist on Mars', viewing the familiar as if never seen, is credited to:
questions.explanation: Sacks's 'anthropologist on Mars' captures the detached observer stance; Highmore's own analogy was the detective.

questions.question: Gracia's thesis is that we laugh at something because in it we see:
options: A. the significance of the insignificant
B. the insignificance of the significant
C. the danger of the harmless
D. the sadness of the joyful
questions.explanation: Gracia proposes we laugh when we grasp the significance of the insignificant — and cry at the reverse.

questions.question: By contrast, Gracia says we cry at something because through it we grasp:
options: A. the insignificance of the significant
B. the significance of the insignificant
C. the humour of the ordinary
D. the order behind the chaos
questions.explanation: Tragedy makes us see that what we hold to be significant is, in the larger scheme, insignificant.

questions.question: For Gracia, comedy deals with the ordinary, whereas tragedy deals with subject matter that is:
options: A. momentous — love, death and betrayal
B. trivial — errands and small talk
questions.explanation: Tragedy's subject matter is momentous — love, death, betrayal, virtue, injustice and revenge.

questions.question: Which everyday example does Gracia give as too insignificant ever to be a tragedy?
questions.explanation: Gracia's own examples are the sale of a van, mail delivery and non-fat yogurt; the distractors are genuine tragic themes.

questions.question: Gracia argues comedy 'dates more easily than tragedy' because:
options: A. comedy leans on culture-specific customs
B. tragedy depends on passing fashions
C. comedy addresses universal human themes
D. tragedy is always about trivial matters
questions.explanation: Tragedy's shared human core (death, suffering, virtue) ages slowly, while comedy relies on culture-specific customs.

questions.question: The Seinfeld pitch 'a show about nothing' fits Gracia's argument because:
options: A. its significance lies in overlooked everyday life
B. it deliberately avoids all social content
C. it dramatises only momentous events
D. it proves the everyday has no meaning
questions.explanation: Seinfeld's characters never think their doings are significant; the series draws out overlooked everyday commonplaces.

questions.question: Participant observation, ethnography and focus groups are examples of:
questions.explanation: These are qualitative methods — they capture the depth and quality of participants' experience of the social world.

questions.question: The Australian census is used as an example of:
questions.explanation: The census is quantitative — a large-sample survey producing statistics, trends and snapshots of a changing society.

questions.question: The lecture argues that a person's class:
options: A. is not just wealth but also taste and status
B. is decided purely by annual income
C. has no genuine connection to one's lifestyle at all
D. is fixed permanently at birth
questions.explanation: The same income can carry very different tastes; class is not just wealth but also status and taste.

questions.question: The idea that taste and lifestyle act as a marker of status is the concept of:
questions.explanation: Taste as a status marker is cultural capital — the concept behind the 'who could sit on a monobloc' example.

questions.question: Ethan Zuckerman labelled the monobloc chair a:
questions.explanation: Zuckerman calls the monobloc a 'context-free object' — unlike most objects it gives no clue of time or place.

soci1010_wk2_meaning_of_everyday_life.ht.title: SOCI1010 W2 · The Meaning of Everyday Life
soci1010_wk2_meaning_of_everyday_life.ht.subject: Sociology
soci1010_wk2_meaning_of_everyday_life.ht.content: SOCI1010 Week 2 'The Meaning of Everyday Life' (A/Prof Selvaraj Velayutham) + essential reading Inglis, 'Modern Culture and Everyday Life' Ch.2. DEFINING: everyday life is NOT confined to important moments/events/festivities/holidays/the profane/'ordinary' people/private life; in its WIDE meaning it includes profane AND sacred, private AND public, all walks of life (COVID = a 'new normal'). SEVEN CHARACTERISTICS: (1) repetitive but punctuated by the unpredictable — repetition forms identity, 'we become who we are through acts of repetition' (Durkheim), and can enable creativity; (2) synonymous with habit — habit = action + attitude; Mauss 'techniques of the body' (squatting vs sitting mankind, people with/without chairs; bodily habits 'assembled by and for social authority'); Mauss coined HABITUS, developed by Bourdieu as 'durable dispositions' shaped by class & gender, taught by imitation; (3) spaces of familiarity — home as the privileged base; Giddens' ONTOLOGICAL SECURITY (trust in the world giving stability/continuity to identity); (4) the feel of 'normality'; (5) secular & democratic — no one escapes it, 'even the Queen'; (6) feels natural but is political (lecture room; gendered family home); (7) has a history — intellectual history (Goffman, Garfinkel, Durkheim, Simmel, Lefebvre, Bourdieu, Mauss, Douglas, Elias, Weber, Marx) and, per Lefebvre, emerges as a 'social category' with modernity (visible in 19th-c capitalism/industrialization; today exploded via social media). THE POLITICS OF WAITING: the bus stop as street furniture/corporate space (JCDecaux, Adshel)/social space; low-status, embodies social difference; unequal public spending (car-dependent Western Sydney); privatization/commercialization of public space; ads contested (Brandalism Project); counter-case = affordable/efficient/cuts congestion/climate. THE SOCIOLOGY OF THE QUEUE: an 'embryonic social system' (pattern of order, violation punishable); self-managed by the individual AND the queue-community; Goffman — the individual regulates their actions before others' eyes; a moral order / 'queue ethics'; types (physical, virtual, mobile, informal, regulated); Schwartz (1975); the Saarbrücken experiment — a single feeder line is faster and FEELS fairer than one-line-per-desk (fairness is designed). SITUATING THE EVERYDAY IN MODERNITY (Inglis): everyday activities are 'expressive of modernity'; method = DENATURALIZE the everyday ('a fish in its own cultural water'). Pre-modern (providence/religion/tradition) -> modern (progress/science/rationality); drivers = Enlightenment (17-18th c), industrialization, capitalism, the democratic state. MODERNIZATION (the process — weakening of traditional patterns) vs MODERNITY (the society born of industrialization/urbanization). Signature (Hall et al): rationality, routinization, market society, individualism. THE RATIONALIZATION OF EVERYDAY LIFE (Weber): modern West uniquely rational; ZWECKRATIONAL (efficient means to an end, e.g. business/profit) vs WERTRATIONAL (an ultimate moral/spiritual value). Protestant Ethic & the Spirit of Capitalism (1905) — capitalism's religious origins; the 'disenchantment of the world'. Authority: tradition/religion -> LEGAL-RATIONAL AUTHORITY (systematic application of rules) -> BUREAUCRACY ('control through regulations'); we obey the ROLE not the person (tax inspector, schoolteacher); officials as 'embodied rules'; bureaucracy colonizes everyday life. PROFESSIONALIZATION (only credentialed experts; the fake-doctor outrage). The IRON CAGE ('specialists without spirit, sensualists without heart'). Ritzer's McDonaldization: efficiency, predictability, calculability, dehumanization/control. RATIONALIZING EMOTIONS/MONEY/SPACE: Hochschild's FEELING RULES (airline staff drilled to be upbeat; emotion bureaucratized); Merton's ROLE AMBIVALENCE (doctor = detached scientist vs caring carer). Simmel's MONEY MENTALITY — money is impersonal & universalizing, judging by quantity not quality; relationships become monetary transactions (cashier, bank clerk); the 'have a nice day' veneer. Rationalizing space: Eichberg (pre-modern loose ball-games -> standardized rule-governed pitches for 'goal results'/'tension', commercialized); Lefebvre (car culture colonizes the city into 'geometric space'); Augé (motorways bypass places -> places become 'names/signs'). CULTURE & CHAOS (modernity is dualistic): Marx — 'all that is solid melts into air' (constant flux). Simmel — the metropolis bombards with stimuli, so the BLASÉ ATTITUDE blocks it out; the bigger the crowd the lonelier one feels; the 'leave me alone' city code. REVOLT INTO STYLE — rationalization (conform) vs individualization (cult of the unique self); style is a group-based 'individuality off the peg' (goths, subcultures, lifestyles); uniqueness is the flip side of sameness (the same designer dress). AUTHENTICITY & THE (POST/LATE) MODERN: INVENTED TRADITIONS (Hobsbawm & Ranger) — the Victorian 'traditional Christmas', 'timeless' Scottish tartan/bagpipes. TOURISM — the search for the authentic/exotic that destroys what it seeks (fishing village commodifies its culture); traveller vs tourist. The POST-TOURIST knowingly/ironically embraces the fake — post-modernity (Lyotard) / late modernity (Giddens); irony, knowingness, self-consciousness; pastiche/parody/bricolage (Jameson; Tarantino); Eco's 'As Barbara Cartland would put it, I love you madly'. Point: DENATURALIZE the everyday — our 'normal' is a peculiar, historically specific product of modernity (rationalization + chaos).

questions.question: In its wide meaning, everyday life includes:
options: A. sacred and profane, private and public alike
B. only the trivial, private and ordinary moments
C. just festivals, holidays and sacred events
D. exclusively the lives of ordinary people
questions.explanation: The wide definition spans profane and sacred, private and public, and people of all kinds.

questions.question: Which is offered as an example of a 'new everyday' or 'new normal'?
questions.explanation: Life under COVID becoming the 'new normal' shows how the everyday itself can be reshaped.

questions.question: The claim that 'we become who we are through acts of repetition' is credited to:
questions.explanation: For Durkheim, repetition is not mere boredom but key to the gradual formation of social identity.

questions.question: Mauss's 'techniques of the body' makes the point that:
options: A. even bodily habits are learned and socially shaped
B. bodily habits are purely biological instincts
C. the body has no real place in sociology
D. all humans move in exactly the same way
questions.explanation: Mauss showed that how we hold and use our bodies is assembled by and for social authority.

questions.question: The term 'habitus' was coined by Mauss and developed as 'durable dispositions' by:
questions.explanation: Bourdieu developed habitus as 'durable dispositions' — acquired, class- and gender-shaped ways of being.

questions.question: For Bourdieu, our habitus is most strongly shaped by:
questions.explanation: Habitus is strongly influenced by class and gender, reaching into eating, home decoration and taste.

questions.question: Giddens's 'ontological security' refers to:
options: A. trust in the world that stabilises identity
B. financial security against future loss
C. legal protection provided by the state
D. certainty that science alone explains everything fully
