C. speed the hepatic metabolism of drugs
D. raise the plasma protein binding of drugs
questions.explanation: P-gp throws drugs back out at the gut and blood-brain barrier (limiting absorption and CNS entry) and, when over-expressed in tumours, causes multidrug resistance.

questions.question: SSRIs increase serotonergic transmission by:
options: A. blocking serotonin reuptake at SERT
B. injecting more serotonin into synapses
C. synthesising extra serotonin in neurons
questions.explanation: SSRIs block the serotonin transporter (SERT), so released 5-HT lingers in the cleft and acts longer — amplifying the brain's own signalling rather than adding transmitter.

questions.question: Combining an SSRI with an MAOI risks serotonin syndrome because both:
questions.explanation: An SSRI blocks serotonin reuptake and an MAOI blocks its breakdown, so together they push synaptic serotonin dangerously high — agitation, hyperthermia, clonus.

cardiovascular_anatomy_mhhs2402_wk5.html.title: Anatomy of the Heart & Blood Vessels
cardiovascular_anatomy_mhhs2402_wk5.html.subject: Cardiovascular, Renal & Respiratory Systems
cardiovascular_anatomy_mhhs2402_wk5.html.content: Cardiovascular anatomy for MHHS2402 Week 5: mediastinum and pericardium, the four chambers and valves, the fibrous skeleton, coronary vessels, the conduction system and nerve supply, systemic vs pulmonary circulation, foetal circulation, the great vessels, and surface anatomy with valve auscultation.

questions.question: The sternal angle (angle of Louis) marks which vertebral level?
questions.explanation: The sternal angle marks the T4/T5 plane, the master surface landmark of the thorax.

questions.question: The heart sits within which subdivision of the mediastinum?
questions.explanation: The heart, pericardium and roots of the great vessels lie in the middle mediastinum.

questions.question: The single best clue for identifying the left ventricle in a cut section is its:
questions.explanation: The left ventricle has a markedly thicker, rounder myocardium, about three times the thin crescentic right ventricle.

questions.question: The natural pacemaker of the heart is the:
questions.explanation: The sinoatrial node in the right atrial wall sets the heart rate; its firing depolarises both atria.

questions.question: The coronary arteries arise from the aorta just above which valve?
questions.explanation: The coronary arteries arise from the aortic sinuses just above the aortic valve to supply the myocardium.

questions.question: At the sternal angle, the trachea divides into two bronchi at the:
questions.explanation: The trachea bifurcates at the carina at the sternal-angle level, where the aortic arch also begins.

questions.question: The tough outer layer of the pericardium that anchors the heart is the:
questions.explanation: The fibrous pericardium is dense connective tissue that anchors the heart and resists sudden overfilling.

questions.question: Sensory supply to the fibrous and parietal pericardium comes from the:
questions.explanation: The phrenic nerve (C3 to C5) is sensory to the pericardium, which underlies the referral of cardiac pain to the shoulder.

questions.question: The right border of the heart is formed almost entirely by the:
questions.explanation: The right border is formed almost entirely by the right atrium; the left border and apex belong to the left ventricle.

questions.question: The left atrium is most reliably identified by the entry of the:
questions.explanation: The left atrium receives the four pulmonary veins, which carry oxygenated blood, and has a mostly smooth wall.

questions.question: Which muscular structure is the give-away that you are viewing the right ventricle?
questions.explanation: The moderator band carries the right bundle branch to the anterior papillary muscle and is a right-ventricle signature.

questions.question: The chordae tendineae and papillary muscles function to:
questions.explanation: The chordae and papillary muscles tether the AV cusps so they cannot evert into the atrium when the ventricle contracts.

questions.question: The first heart sound (S1, 'lub') is produced by closure of the:
questions.explanation: S1 is the closure of the atrioventricular valves; S2 ('dub') is the closure of the semilunar valves.

questions.question: The left anterior descending artery is a branch of which coronary artery?
questions.explanation: The left coronary stem divides into the left anterior descending (LAD) and the circumflex arteries.

questions.question: Most cardiac veins drain into which structure before reaching the right atrium?
questions.explanation: The cardiac veins converge on the coronary sinus in the posterior AV groove, which empties into the right atrium.

questions.question: After the SA node, the electrical impulse next reaches the:
questions.explanation: The impulse passes from the SA node to the AV node, where it is briefly delayed before travelling down the bundle of His.

questions.question: The vagus nerve affects the heart mainly by:
questions.explanation: The vagus nerve is the parasympathetic brake, slowing heart rate and AV conduction with little effect on force.

questions.question: Compared with the systemic circulation, the pulmonary circulation operates at a pressure that is:
questions.explanation: Pulmonary pressures are about 25/10 mmHg, far lower than the systemic 120/80, matching the thin right ventricular wall.

questions.question: The first and largest branch of the aortic arch is the:
questions.explanation: The brachiocephalic trunk is the first arch branch and splits into the right common carotid and right subclavian.

questions.question: In the right atrium, the crista terminalis separates the pectinate wall from the smooth:
questions.explanation: The crista terminalis divides the smooth sinus venarum, the venous inflow region, from the rough pectinate part of the atrium.

questions.question: Besides anchoring the valves, the cardiac fibrous skeleton acts as an:
questions.explanation: The collagen rings electrically insulate the atria from the ventricles, so the AV node is the only conducting doorway.

questions.question: Semilunar valves need no chordae because their cup-shaped cusps:
questions.explanation: Retrograde blood fills the three pockets, which balloon together and seal, so the harder the backpush the tighter the seal.

questions.question: Coronary dominance is defined by which vessel gives rise to the:
questions.explanation: Dominance is defined by which vessel gives the posterior interventricular artery; the RCA does so in about 80 to 85 percent.

questions.question: The coronary arteries receive most of their blood flow during:
questions.explanation: During systole the contracting myocardium and open aortic cusps block the ostia, so coronaries fill mainly in diastole.

questions.question: An inferior myocardial infarction classically causes heart block because the RCA usually supplies the:
questions.explanation: The right coronary artery usually supplies the SA and AV nodes, so an inferior MI is a classic cause of complete heart block.

questions.question: The roughly 0.1 second delay at the AV node exists to:
questions.explanation: The AV delay lets atrial contraction top up ventricular filling before the ventricles contract, maximising stroke volume.

questions.question: Cardiac pain is referred to the left arm and jaw because heart afferents converge with somatic fibres from levels:
questions.explanation: The heart's sympathetic afferents (T1 to T5) share second-order neurons with somatic dermatomes, so pain is mislocated to the arm and jaw.

questions.question: Which capillary type has large pores and passes whole cells, as in bone marrow?
questions.explanation: Sinusoidal capillaries have an incomplete basement membrane and large pores, passing whole cells in bone marrow, liver and spleen.

questions.question: The main controllers of peripheral resistance and blood pressure are the:
questions.explanation: Arterioles have muscular walls that adjust calibre, making them the main controllers of peripheral resistance and blood pressure.

questions.question: The ductus arteriosus in the foetus connects the pulmonary trunk to the:
questions.explanation: The ductus arteriosus connects the pulmonary trunk to the aorta, diverting right-ventricular output away from the collapsed lungs.

questions.question: After birth, the foramen ovale becomes which adult structure?
questions.explanation: The foramen ovale seals to become the fossa ovalis; the ductus arteriosus becomes the ligamentum arteriosum.

questions.question: The carotid sinus at the carotid bifurcation functions as a:
questions.explanation: The carotid sinus is a baroreceptor sensing arterial stretch; the nearby carotid body is a chemoreceptor sensing O2, CO2 and pH.

questions.question: A portal system is defined as a venous circuit that runs blood between:
questions.explanation: A portal system interposes a second capillary bed, as in the hepatic portal vein carrying gut blood to the liver for first-pass processing.

questions.question: The mitral valve is best auscultated at which location?
questions.explanation: The mitral valve is heard at the apex in the left 5th intercostal space, midclavicular line, because flow is directed toward the apex.

questions.question: The azygos venous system provides a collateral channel linking the:
questions.explanation: The azygos system links the superior and inferior venae cavae along the posterior thoracic wall, a bypass if a cava is obstructed.

dna_replication_medi2200_wk5.html.title: DNA Replication
dna_replication_medi2200_wk5.html.subject: Human Cell & Molecular Biology
dna_replication_medi2200_wk5.html.content: Eukaryotic DNA replication: structure, semi-conservative principle, the four steps, and the polymerases/proofreading (MEDI2200 Wk5, Parts I-III).

questions.question: How does the sugar in DNA differ from the sugar in RNA?
options: A. it lacks a hydroxyl at the 2′ carbon
B. it carries an extra hydroxyl group
C. it uses uracil instead of thymine
D. it contains a phosphate in place of sugar
questions.explanation: DNA's sugar is 2′-deoxyribose, lacking the 2′-OH of ribose, which makes DNA chemically more stable.

questions.question: In DNA, adenine base-pairs with:
questions.explanation: Adenine pairs thymine via two hydrogen bonds; uracil replaces thymine only in RNA — a common trap.

questions.question: New DNA strands are synthesised in which direction?
questions.explanation: Nucleotides can only add to a free 3′-OH, so synthesis is always 5′→3′ on both strands.

questions.question: 'Semi-conservative' replication means each new double helix contains:
options: A. one original strand and one new strand
B. two entirely newly made strands
D. a patchwork of old and new bases
questions.explanation: Each parental strand is kept as a template, so every daughter duplex is half old and half new — not a patchwork.

questions.question: Okazaki fragments are made on the:
questions.explanation: The lagging strand runs opposite to fork movement, so it is built discontinuously as short Okazaki fragments.

questions.question: The primer that starts each new DNA strand is made of:
questions.explanation: Primase, an RNA polymerase, lays a short RNA primer that provides the 3′-OH DNA polymerase needs to begin.

questions.question: Which enzyme unwinds the double helix at the replication fork?
questions.explanation: MCM2-7 is the replicative helicase; topoisomerase relieves supercoiling but does not unwind the strands.

questions.question: DNA replication takes place during which phase of the cell cycle?
questions.explanation: Replication is confined to S phase, keeping it coupled to cell-cycle control.

questions.question: DNA ligase acts to:
options: A. join adjacent DNA fragments together
B. unwind the parental double helix
C. add the first RNA primer
D. proofread each new base added
questions.explanation: Ligase seals the nick between fragments by forming a phosphodiester bond between a 3′-OH and a 5′-phosphate.

questions.question: The lagging strand is made discontinuously because:
options: A. its template runs opposite to fork movement
B. its template runs the same way as the fork
C. it needs no RNA primer to begin
D. it is copied entirely before the leading strand
questions.explanation: Synthesis is 5′→3′ only; on the lagging template that direction points away from the fork, forcing short fragments.

questions.question: The 3′ exonuclease activity of a DNA polymerase:
options: A. removes a mismatched terminal nucleotide
B. adds nucleotides to the growing strand
C. unwinds the DNA ahead of the fork
D. lays down the initial RNA primer
questions.explanation: Proofreading backs up over a wrongly inserted base and excises it, cutting the error rate roughly 100–1000-fold.

questions.question: Which polymerase synthesises the leading strand?
questions.explanation: Pol ε (epsilon) makes the leading strand; Pol δ (delta) makes the lagging strand; Pol α primes.

questions.question: The lagging strand is synthesised mainly by:
questions.explanation: Pol δ (delta) extends the Okazaki fragments on the lagging strand; Pol ε handles the leading strand.

questions.question: PCNA raises replication efficiency by:
options: A. clamping the polymerase onto the DNA
B. cutting the RNA primer away
C. unwinding the helix at the fork
D. joining the finished fragments together
questions.explanation: PCNA is a sliding ring around the DNA that tethers the polymerase for high processivity.

questions.question: Replication protein A (RPA) functions to:
options: A. coat the exposed single strand
B. relieve supercoiling ahead of the fork
questions.explanation: RPA binds single-stranded DNA to protect it and stop the strands re-annealing before they are copied.

questions.question: Roughly how many origins of replication fire per eukaryotic cell cycle?
questions.explanation: Tens of thousands of origins are needed because forks move only ~2–3 kb/min and fire in staggered fashion.

questions.question: Topoisomerases are required during replication to:
options: A. relieve over-winding ahead of the fork
B. add nucleotides to the new strand
D. remove the RNA primers afterwards
questions.explanation: Unwinding over-winds the DNA ahead of the fork; topoisomerases nick a strand, let the strain unwind, then reseal.

questions.question: Primase is best classified as:
questions.explanation: Primase makes RNA de novo, so it is an RNA polymerase — the only replication enzyme that can start a strand from scratch.

questions.question: During lagging-strand maturation, the FEN1 endonuclease:
options: B. seals the final nick shut
C. adds the RNA primer first
questions.explanation: As Pol δ displaces the downstream fragment into a flap, FEN1 cuts it off; DNA ligase then seals the nick.

questions.question: A tumour with a Pol ε proofreading mutation becomes 'ultra-mutated' because losing 3′ exonuclease activity:
options: A. removes proofreading, so errors rise sharply
B. speeds replication far beyond normal
C. stops replication at every origin
D. deletes whole chromosome arms at once
questions.explanation: Proofreading normally cuts the error rate ~100-fold; without it, base-substitution mutations accumulate genome-wide.

questions.question: Why are RNA primers removed and replaced with DNA before ligation?
options: A. RNA is less stable and lower-fidelity
B. RNA cannot base-pair with the template
C. RNA blocks the helicase from unwinding
D. RNA carries no genetic information at all
questions.explanation: The finished genome must be all DNA: the temporary primers and Pol α's error-prone stretch are excised and rebuilt in DNA.

questions.question: A fully heavy-labelled DNA duplex replicates once in light medium. Each daughter duplex is:
options: A. one heavy strand paired with one light
B. two fully heavy strands paired together
C. two fully light strands paired together
D. one duplex all heavy, the other all light
questions.explanation: Semi-conservative replication keeps each old (heavy) strand and pairs it with a new (light) one — the classic Meselson–Stahl hybrid.

questions.question: Pol δ is slightly less accurate than Pol ε, yet lagging-strand fidelity stays high because of:
options: A. extra mismatch repair on that strand
B. Pol δ having no error rate at all
C. the leading strand copying it again
questions.explanation: The lower fidelity of Pol δ is counterbalanced by more active mismatch repair targeted to the lagging strand.

questions.question: Replication licensing ensures each origin fires only once per cycle by:
options: A. loading the helicase in G1, firing in S
B. destroying every origin after S phase
C. firing all origins at the exact same instant
D. loading the helicase only during mitosis
questions.explanation: MCM helicases load in G1 but can only fire in S, and firing blocks any reloading — so a fired origin cannot re-fire.

questions.question: What supplies the energy for adding each nucleotide during DNA synthesis?
options: A. cleavage of the incoming dNTP to dNMP
B. hydrolysis of a wholly separate ATP molecule
C. breakdown of the RNA primer
D. proton flow across the nuclear membrane
questions.explanation: Each incoming dNTP is hydrolysed to a dNMP plus pyrophosphate; releasing that pyrophosphate drives the addition — no separate ATP needed.

questions.question: Most DNA initially laid down by Pol α is later replaced because Pol α:
options: A. cannot proofread, so its DNA is error-prone
B. works far too slowly for the fork
C. can only copy the leading strand
D. adds RNA rather than DNA bases
questions.explanation: Pol α lacks 3′ exonuclease proofreading, so its stretch is relatively inaccurate and Pol δ replaces most of it.

questions.question: 'Strand-displacement synthesis' by Pol δ means Pol δ:
options: A. runs into the downstream fragment
B. skips right over the next fragment
C. removes the RNA primer itself
D. seals the nick without ligase
questions.explanation: On reaching the previous Okazaki fragment, Pol δ pushes into it and displaces its 5′ end as a flap, which FEN1 then cuts.

questions.question: Since forks move only ~2–3 kb/min, firing tens of thousands of origins mainly serves to:
options: A. finish the genome within one S phase
B. proofread the whole genome more thoroughly
C. lengthen the telomeres at each cycle
D. keep the two strands from re-annealing again
questions.explanation: A single fork would take far too long to copy a chromosome; thousands of origins provide the throughput to finish within S phase.

questions.question: Compared with an AT-rich region, a GC-rich region will:
options: A. need more energy to separate into strands
B. melt apart at a much lower temperature
C. contain no hydrogen bonds at all
D. replicate without any helicase needed
questions.explanation: C–G pairs have three hydrogen bonds versus two for A–T, so GC-rich DNA is more stable and harder to melt apart.

questions.question: During replication, each parental strand serves as:
options: A. a template for a new complementary strand
B. a primer for the opposite strand
C. an enzyme that joins fragments
D. a signal that ends the S phase
questions.explanation: Each old strand templates a new complementary strand by base-pairing, the basis of semi-conservative replication.

soci1010_wk4_researching_everyday_life.h.title: Researching Everyday Life — Ethnography & the Go-Along
soci1010_wk4_researching_everyday_life.h.subject: Sociology
soci1010_wk4_researching_everyday_life.h.content: SOCI1010 Week 4 on the methods of studying everyday life: wrapping up Garfinkel's ethnomethodology and Goffman's dramaturgy, the self-checkout as Weber's rationalisation, research design (deductive/inductive, quant/qual/mixed), ethnography (thick description, the two components, emic/etic, the positioned subject) and its history (Malinowski, the Chicago School), four case studies (Goffman's total institution, Willis, Wacquant, Venkatesh), and the week's reading — Kusenbach's go-along and its five themes.

questions.question: Which sociologist coined 'ethnomethodology' and used breaching experiments?
questions.explanation: Garfinkel introduced ethnomethodology in Studies in Ethnomethodology (1967) and used breaching experiments.

questions.question: A breaching experiment works by:
options: A. deliberately breaking a tacit rule to expose it
B. carefully obeying every social rule closely
C. surveying a very large random sample of people
D. running a controlled laboratory experiment
questions.explanation: Breaking an unwritten rule — like over-answering 'How are you?' — makes it suddenly visible.

questions.question: In Goffman's dramaturgy, a waiter relaxing out of role in the kitchen is on the:
questions.explanation: Back stage is where the performance relaxes; front stage is where one performs to the audience.

questions.question: The word 'ethnography' breaks down to mean, roughly:
options: A. writing about people or culture
questions.explanation: Ethno = people/culture, graphy = writing; ethnography means writing about people and culture.

questions.question: Which method best captures people's subjective, lived experience?
questions.explanation: Qualitative research prioritises meaning and lived experience; the census and polls are quantitative.

questions.question: Bronisław Malinowski's foundational ethnographic fieldwork was conducted in the:
questions.explanation: Malinowski studied the Trobriand Islands (1915–19); Goffman's PhD fieldwork was in the Shetlands.

questions.question: The 'go-along' method, as Kusenbach defines it, means the researcher:
options: A. accompanies an informant on an everyday outing
B. interviews an informant in a quiet office
C. mails a survey to many strangers
D. watches an informant on hidden camera
questions.explanation: A go-along walks or rides with the informant on their own routine trip, asking questions along the way.

questions.question: Which is one of Kusenbach's five themes the go-along is suited to explore?
questions.explanation: Kusenbach's five themes are perception, spatial practices, biographies, social architecture and social realms.

questions.question: The lecture frames the self-checkout mainly through which Weberian idea?
options: B. the sacred and the profane
questions.explanation: Self-checkouts illustrate rationalisation, the iron cage and the irrationality of rationality.

questions.question: A researcher watches a class with no prior hypothesis and builds a conclusion from what they see. This is:
questions.explanation: Building a general conclusion up from specific observations is inductive; deductive starts from a hypothesis.

questions.question: Knowing that a 'wink' carries a coded insider meaning while a 'blink' is just dust is the:
questions.explanation: The emic perspective is the insider's point of view that distinguishes a meaningful wink from a mere blink.

questions.question: Alongside participant observation, the second component of ethnography is:
options: B. running a large statistical survey
questions.explanation: The two components are participant observation and the recording and documenting of fieldnotes.

questions.question: Describing ethnographers as 'positioned subjects' captures the claim that they:
options: A. become part of the world they study
B. stay fully detached and objective the whole time
C. never enter the field at all
D. rely only on official statistics
questions.explanation: Ethnographers are the research tool; the work is experiential and subjective, so they join the world they study.

questions.question: The Chicago School's approach to studying the city is best summarised as:
options: A. treating the city as a 'social experiment'
B. surveying the whole city with mailed forms
C. avoiding the city street entirely
D. studying only rural farming villages
questions.explanation: Dissatisfied with the survey method, the Chicago School treated the city as a living social experiment studied first-hand.

questions.question: Which practice was central to Malinowski's method?
options: A. keeping daily diaries while living among people
B. sending a single brief questionnaire by mail
C. reading old records from a distance
D. running experiments in a laboratory
questions.explanation: Malinowski kept daily diaries, learned the language and stayed long-term in the field.

questions.question: Goffman's 'total institution' is defined by which feature?
options: A. an enclosed, formally administered, cut-off life
B. an open community free to come and go
C. a temporary weekend gathering of friends
D. an online forum with no physical site
questions.explanation: A total institution — asylum, prison, monastery, army camp — encloses similar people in a formally administered life.

questions.question: Willis's central explanation for why working-class 'lads' end up in working-class jobs is that:
options: A. the lads 'let themselves' through a counter-school culture
B. the lads simply lacked the natural ability
C. the teachers deliberately failed each of the lads
D. the economy offered them no jobs at all
questions.explanation: Willis argued the lads consciously reject school via a culture of resistance, steering themselves into working-class jobs.

questions.question: Wacquant trained as a boxer to honour which Bourdieu claim?
questions.explanation: Bourdieu's 'we learn by body' warrants embodied participation — the sociologist trains as a boxer to understand the gym.

questions.question: How did Venkatesh's Robert Taylor Homes research change after his first encounter?
options: A. he refocused from poverty onto the gang
B. he abandoned the whole research project entirely
C. he switched to a mailed survey
D. he studied only the police instead
questions.explanation: Held at first, then invited to 'live with people', Venkatesh refocused from poverty generally onto the gang.

questions.question: For authenticity, Kusenbach argues a go-along should ideally be:
options: A. natural, following a trip they'd take anyway
B. staged along a route chosen by the researcher
C. replaced entirely by a phone survey
D. done only inside a closed office
questions.explanation: Natural go-alongs track routine trips — same day, time and route — preserving authenticity.

questions.question: A key limit of the sit-down interview that the go-along overcomes is that it:
options: A. removes people from the place being discussed
B. always captures the whole environment perfectly well
C. is always faster than a go-along
D. needs no informant at all
questions.explanation: Interviews are static and pull informants out of place, hiding the pre-reflective, trivial detail a go-along reveals.

questions.question: Replacing 10 staffed lanes with 20 self-service machines is an example of:
questions.explanation: Reconfiguring the shop floor around self-checkout machines is the 'rationalisation of space'.

questions.question: Ross calls an overgrown house a 'jungle' eyesore while Jill calls the same house lovely. This shows:
options: B. everyone perceives a scene identically
C. words always carry a single fixed meaning
D. perception is purely biological, not social
questions.explanation: The same word carrying opposite meanings shows perception is filtered by pre-existing relevances — tastes and values.

questions.question: Tony times his walk and buys a lottery ticket for 'fun'. Under which theme does this fall?
options: A. spatial practices, since 'thickening' is unobservable
B. perception, since it involves the senses
C. biographies, since it recalls the past
D. social realms, since it is fully public
questions.explanation: Reframing a routine as fun or competition is a spatial practice — 'thickening' — that a static interview cannot observe.

questions.question: Tony recalling his post-war home when passing an old bungalow is which theme?
questions.explanation: A personal landmark triggering memory is the 'biographies' theme — the environment sparking one's own life story.

questions.question: Jill reading a 'rental' and a model's 'wonderful' house as a status map for herself is:
questions.explanation: Reading other houses as a status map to place oneself is 'comparing and positioning' within social architecture.

questions.question: Kusenbach argues the lone, transient observer suits the public realm because it rests on:
options: A. categoric, anonymous knowing rather than personal
B. personal knowing rather than anonymous
C. no knowing of others at all
D. purely statistical knowing of crowds
questions.explanation: In public space anonymity reigns, so conduct rests on categoric (anonymous) rather than personal knowing.

questions.question: Ethnography at home, the lecture says, makes the:
options: A. 'familiar unfamiliar' at home for sociology
C. no change to familiarity at all
D. only unfamiliar settings ever studied
questions.explanation: Anthropology abroad makes the unfamiliar familiar; sociology at home makes the familiar unfamiliar.

questions.question: Answering 'How are you?' with 'In regard to what — my health, my finances?' shows that:
options: A. order only appears orderly, recreated moment to moment
B. social order is completely fixed and permanent forever
C. order comes solely from written law
D. order needs no human effort at all
questions.explanation: The breach shows order is a fragile achievement, continually re-created by actors moment to moment.

questions.question: Goffman posed as an assistant in the asylum in order to capture:
options: A. the 'unofficial reality' from the patients' view
B. the official view held by the doctors
C. a purely statistical picture of the ward
D. the architecture of the hospital building
questions.explanation: Covert immersion gave Goffman the 'unofficial reality' seen from the patients' standpoint.

questions.question: Kusenbach's overall argument about the go-along relative to observation and interviews is that it is:
options: A. a hybrid whose strengths accumulate when combined
B. clearly superior to every other method
C. always worse than a sit-down interview
D. useful only for studying private homes
questions.explanation: Kusenbach argues not for the go-along's superiority but for combining methods to gather many kinds of knowledge.

soci1010_wk5_class_gender_bodies.html.title: Class, Gender & Bodies — The Sociology of the Body
soci1010_wk5_class_gender_bodies.html.subject: Sociology
soci1010_wk5_class_gender_bodies.html.content: Week 5 of Introduction to Sociology: the sociology of the body. Opens with a history of the toilet, then covers class (Marx, Weber, Bourdieu), embodiment (Foucault, Bourdieu, Goffman, Young), the sex-gender system and contemporary bodies (neoliberal self, Hockey's trainers/material culture, ageing and non-human bodies), integrating the Archer, Young and Hockey readings.

questions.question: Why open a lecture on class, gender and bodies with the toilet?
options: A. a mundane object reveals social organisation
B. toilets are the most important technology
C. plumbing history is the core of sociology
D. everyday objects have no social meaning
questions.explanation: It is the lecturer's trademark 'sociology of the banal' — a mundane object reveals how the body is socially organised.

questions.question: In Elizabeth Shove's practice theory, the learned ability to squat comfortably is a:
options: A. a competence — bodily skill and know-how
B. a material — the physical objects used
C. a meaning — the shared cultural idea
D. a wage — the money earned by it
questions.explanation: Competences are the skills and bodily know-how a practice needs; squatting is a learned competence (Shove).

questions.question: The lecture calls elimination a 'human leveller' yet insists the toilet is social because:
options: A. all eliminate, but toilets differ by class
B. everyone uses an identical toilet worldwide
C. the body escapes all social difference here
D. only the rich ever need a toilet
questions.explanation: The universal act — 'bodily democracy' — throws the class-layered differences of technology and meaning into relief.

questions.question: For Marx, the two great classes of capitalist society are distinguished by:
options: A. whether they make profits or earn wages
B. whether they live in cities or country
C. whether they are educated or not
D. whether they own a car or not
questions.explanation: Marx bases class on the split between those who make profits (bourgeoisie) and those who earn wages (proletariat).

questions.question: Marx's concept of 'surplus value' refers to:
options: A. the value a worker creates beyond their wage
B. the total wage a worker is paid
C. the money a firm spends on machines
D. the tax a worker pays the state
questions.explanation: Surplus value is the value workers create over and above their wage, which the owner appropriates.

questions.question: That Marxian exploitation is 'structural, not personal' means:
options: A. it is built into the relationship itself
B. it depends on how kind the boss is
C. it happens only with cruel employers
D. it disappears with a friendly manager
questions.explanation: Exploitation is the systemic appropriation of surplus value, so it operates whatever the individual boss's manner.

questions.question: Which everyday parallel does the lecturer use for Marx's alienation?
options: A. feeling an essay handed to GPT isn't yours
B. feeling proud of work you fully made
C. earning a completely fair wage for your labour
D. owning the tools you work with
questions.explanation: Alienation is losing a meaningful connection to what you produce; the GPT-essay feels external and not really yours.

questions.question: Weber defines the 'class' dimension of stratification chiefly as:
options: A. market-determined life chances from property and skills
B. the social honour granted by group membership
C. control of the political party machine
D. shared culture and lifestyle alone
questions.explanation: For Weber, class is market-determined life chances resting on property and marketable skills.

questions.question: Weber adds a dimension Marx omits: social honour granted for group membership. It is:
questions.explanation: Status is Weber's honour/prestige dimension, based on consumption and lifestyle — the axis Marx omits.

questions.question: Contrasting King Charles ('high status, little power') with a powerful CEO shows that:
options: A. status and power are separate axes
B. status and power always rise together
C. power alone determines all prestige
D. only the wealthy can hold status
questions.explanation: King Charles has high status but little power — prestige (status) and authority (power) are separate Weberian axes.

questions.question: Which statement best defines Bourdieu's 'habitus'?
options: A. internalised, embodied structures shaping perception
B. the money and assets a person owns
C. a conscious choice made freely each day
D. a purely genetic and inborn trait
questions.explanation: Habitus is the internalised, embodied social structures that shape what feels natural, tasteful or possible.

questions.question: A violinist who is not wealthy yet is widely revered holds mainly:
options: A. cultural capital and symbolic capital
B. economic capital and social capital
D. no capital of any kind
questions.explanation: Mastery of the violin is embodied cultural capital, and the reverence it earns is symbolic capital.

questions.question: The lecturer's shorthand 'who you know' corresponds to which of Bourdieu's capitals?
questions.explanation: Social capital is networks of influence and support — 'who you know', for example a LinkedIn network.

questions.question: Two students of equal ability differ: one assumes she should apply to the top university, one doesn't. This is:
options: A. Bourdieu's habitus, a felt sense of one's place
B. just simple random chance in the choosing process
C. a difference in raw natural ability
D. a purely rational cost-benefit choice
questions.explanation: Same scores, different disposition: habitus shapes what feels possible, so one applies to the top university and one does not.

questions.question: Archer's 'Class and Class Relations' deploys Marx, Weber and Bourdieu to challenge:
options: A. that Australia is a classless 'fair-go' society
B. that class no longer exists anywhere
C. that only Marx's theory is correct
D. that class is purely about income
questions.explanation: Archer marshals Marx, Weber and Bourdieu against the Australian myth of a classless 'fair-go' society.

questions.question: In The Birth of the Clinic, Foucault's 'medical gaze':
options: A. separates the body from the person as 'text'
B. treats the patient as one whole rounded person
D. cures the patient without any tools
questions.explanation: Under the medical gaze the person becomes a site of observable phenomena — a body separated from the person, a 'text to read'.

questions.question: Foucault would classify public-health messages like 'don't sit in the sun too long' as:
options: A. biopower — medical knowledge as bodily control
B. the moral consensus shared among all citizens
C. banal nationalism in daily life
D. pure repression by armed force
questions.explanation: Because medical discourse is authoritative, its rules regulate everyday conduct — biopower.

questions.question: Foucault's Panopticon produces disciplined conduct primarily because:
options: A. prisoners, unsure if watched, police themselves
B. guards physically restrain every prisoner
C. prisoners are never watched at all
D. the walls alone prevent any escape
questions.explanation: The watchtower design means the possibility of being watched is internalised, so prisoners come to police themselves.

questions.question: Bourdieu calls habitus 'history transformed into nature' to say that:
options: A. class dispositions feel innate though learned
B. dispositions are truly fixed by biology
C. habitus can be changed at will daily
D. history has no bearing on the body
questions.explanation: Habitus is 'forgotten history' — socially learned dispositions that come to feel innate.

questions.question: In Goffman's dramaturgical metaphor, the 'back stage' is where:
options: A. we are out of role and relax
B. we perform hardest for the audience
C. no one is ever allowed to enter
D. the role is enforced most strictly
questions.explanation: Back stage — the kitchen, say — is where the performer drops the mask; front stage is where we perform to the audience.

questions.question: Standing upright and meeting your eye is read by the lecturer as:
options: A. Goffman's impression management and Bourdieu's habitus
B. Marx's surplus value and his alienation
C. Weber's status and party dimensions
questions.explanation: Bearing is both a managed performance (Goffman) and a class disposition inscribed in the body (Bourdieu).

questions.question: Iris Marion Young argues 'throwing like a girl' is best understood as:
options: A. a socially produced, restricted style of movement
B. a purely biological and completely inborn natural limitation
C. a deliberate personal choice each time
D. a sign of weaker natural muscles
questions.explanation: Young rejects the biological explanation and argues the inhibited style is socially produced, not natural.

questions.question: Which best fits Young's 'restricted' or 'inhibited' modalities of movement?
options: A. motion sits in one part, not following through
B. motion flows through the whole entire body freely
C. movement is always fast and powerful
D. the body moves with no restriction
questions.explanation: Young's restricted modalities describe motion concentrated in one part that does not reach or follow through.

questions.question: Young builds her phenomenology of the 'lived body' on which two thinkers?
options: A. Merleau-Ponty and Simone de Beauvoir
questions.explanation: Merleau-Ponty supplies the lived body (the 'I can'); de Beauvoir supplies the woman's situation.

questions.question: The 'sex-gender system' argues that:
options: A. a biological difference tied to unequal order
B. biology has no real link to social order
C. gender and sex are exactly the same
D. society ignores all bodily difference
questions.explanation: The system 'translates' a biological difference into an 'order of value' — an unequal social order.

questions.question: Which axis does 'intersex' belong to, and which does 'nonbinary'?
options: A. intersex under sex; nonbinary under gender
B. intersex under gender; nonbinary under sex
C. both belong only to sexuality
D. both are purely a personal choice
questions.explanation: Intersex describes biological sex (anatomy, chromosomes, hormones); nonbinary describes gender identity.

questions.question: Which athlete does the lecture use for the sex-verification and testosterone story?
questions.explanation: Caster Semenya, an intersex woman, was subjected to sex-verification and testosterone scrutiny.

questions.question: The Norwegian handball team fined for wearing shorts illustrates:
options: A. gatekeeping that polices the binary for men
B. a fully neutral rule about athletic safety
C. a free choice made by the players
D. a rule with no gendered meaning
questions.explanation: The uniform rule enforces gendered display 'for the male audience' — gatekeeping that polices the binary.

questions.question: The 'toned body as cultural icon' is tied most directly to:
options: A. the logic of neoliberal capitalism and self-work
B. a full return to older religious asceticism
questions.explanation: The firm body signals willpower and self-care; neoliberalism makes the body a personal project of self-work.

questions.question: Which pairing correctly matches the early- and late-capitalist body?
options: A. early = discipline and asceticism; late = hedonism
B. early = hedonism; late = discipline and asceticism
C. both eras value only discipline
D. both eras value only hedonism now
questions.explanation: Early capitalism links the body to discipline, asceticism and production; late capitalism to hedonism and consumption.

questions.question: What is the central question of Hockey et al.'s study of trainers?
options: A. how trainers 'make' the individual as a prosthetic
B. how much a single pair of trainers costs
C. which brand of trainer sells best
D. when trainers were first invented
questions.explanation: Hockey et al. reverse the usual question to ask how the trainer 'makes' the individual as a bodily prosthetic.

questions.question: A generic old trainer that consumers begin to prize as a 'vintage' item has undergone:
questions.explanation: Singularisation is the process by which private meanings make a mass-produced object special and 'vintage'.

questions.question: Senator Wendy Davis's 'hot pink' trainers, worn for an 11-hour filibuster, came to:
options: A. resist and subvert gender, class and sexuality norms
B. reinforce every existing social norm
C. clearly have no political meaning at all now
D. signal only personal wealth and taste
questions.explanation: Through singularisation, the pink trainers came to resist and subvert gender, class and sexuality norms.

questions.question: Which is the lecture's example of 'non-human bodies' in everyday life?
options: A. socially-assistive robots in Japanese aged-care
B. wild animals in a national park
C. statues in an art gallery
D. cartoon characters in a film
questions.explanation: Socially-assistive robots — aged-care carers that converse and 'express emotion' — are the lecture's non-human bodies.

questions.question: The conclusion frames the body through three lenses. Which pairing is correct?
options: A. 'social phenomenon' paired with Bourdieu and Goffman
B. 'pure biology' paired with Marx and Weber
C. 'private matter' paired with Foucault alone
D. 'fixed object' paired with no theorist
questions.explanation: The body as social phenomenon = Bourdieu's habitus and Goffman's dramaturgy — one of the three lenses.

questions.question: An 'intersectional' understanding of the body, as the lecture uses it, means:
options: A. studying class, gender, race and ability as overlapping
B. studying each single social category in full isolation
C. ranking the categories by importance
questions.explanation: Intersectionality treats class, gender, race and ability as overlapping and mutually shaping, not separate.

pelvis_hip_lower_limb_mhhs2401_wk6.html.title: Pelvis, Hip Joint & the Lower Limb
pelvis_hip_lower_limb_mhhs2401_wk6.html.subject: Musculoskeletal System
pelvis_hip_lower_limb_mhhs2401_wk6.html.content: General organisation of the lower limb (regions, fascia, compartments, nerves, line of gravity); osteology of the hip bone, sacrum and proximal femur; the pelvic joints and their ligaments; the hip joint (articular surfaces, capsule, ligaments, blood supply, movements); and the clinical anatomy of hip dislocations and femoral fractures.

questions.question: Compared with the upper limb, the lower limb is designed mainly for:
questions.explanation: The lower limb is built for stability and weight-bearing, the opposite priority to the mobility-focused upper limb.

questions.question: The adult hip bone is formed by the fusion of which three bones?
questions.explanation: The hip bone forms from the ilium, ischium and pubis, which fuse at the acetabulum between ages 20 and 25.

questions.question: The hip joint is which type of synovial joint?
questions.explanation: The hip is a synovial ball-and-socket joint between the femoral head and the acetabulum, allowing movement in all planes.

questions.question: Which bone is the longest in the body?
questions.explanation: The femur is the longest bone in the body, ending in the hip joint above and the knee below.

questions.question: Which direction of acquired hip dislocation is the most common?
questions.explanation: Posterior dislocation is most common, as in a dashboard injury; the limb is then held flexed, adducted and internally rotated.

questions.question: In anatomical terms, the 'leg' refers specifically to which segment?
questions.explanation: The leg is only the knee-to-ankle segment containing tibia and fibula; the thigh is hip to knee.

questions.question: The three compartments of the thigh are the anterior, posterior and:
questions.explanation: The thigh has anterior (extensor), medial (adductor) and posterior (hamstring) compartments; the leg swaps the medial for a lateral one.

questions.question: The lateral thickening of the fascia lata forms which structure?
questions.explanation: The fascia lata thickens laterally into the iliotibial tract, a tension band running down to the tibia.

questions.question: The sciatic nerve, the largest nerve in the body, arises from which spinal levels?
questions.explanation: The sciatic nerve (L4 to S3) supplies the posterior thigh and the whole leg and foot; it is the largest nerve in the body.

questions.question: In standing, the line of gravity passes posterior to the hip and anterior to the:
questions.explanation: The line of gravity runs posterior to the hip and anterior to the knee and ankle, so passive ligament tension holds these joints.

questions.question: The sacrum is formed by how many fused vertebrae?
questions.explanation: The sacrum is five fused vertebrae forming a wedge that transmits body weight into the pelvic ring.

questions.question: The 'sitting bone' that gives origin to the hamstrings is the:
questions.explanation: The ischial tuberosity is the sitting bone and the origin of the hamstring muscles.

questions.question: Compared with the male pelvis, the female pelvis has a subpubic angle that is:
questions.explanation: The female subpubic angle is wide and rounded (over about 80 degrees) to admit the fetal head; the male angle is acute.

questions.question: The sacroiliac joint is classified as which type of joint?
questions.explanation: The sacroiliac joint is a weight-bearing plane synovial joint between the auricular surfaces of sacrum and ilium.

questions.question: The iliopsoas muscle inserts onto which part of the proximal femur?
questions.explanation: Iliopsoas inserts on the lesser trochanter; the greater trochanter takes gluteus medius, minimus and the deep rotators.

questions.question: The acetabular labrum contributes to hip stability by:
questions.explanation: The fibrocartilaginous acetabular labrum deepens the socket beyond a hemisphere so it grips the femoral head.

questions.question: The dominant blood supply to the femoral head and neck comes from the:
questions.explanation: The medial circumflex femoral artery, via the retinacular vessels, dominates the head and neck supply; its damage causes avascular necrosis.

questions.question: The highest point of the iliac crest lies at the level of which vertebra?
questions.explanation: The supracristal plane through the highest iliac crest sits at the L4 spinous process, the landmark for lumbar puncture.

questions.question: The sacrospinous ligament runs from the sacrum to the ischial spine and forms the:
questions.explanation: The sacrospinous ligament forms the lesser sciatic foramen; the sacrotuberous ligament forms the greater sciatic foramen.

questions.question: The strongest ligament restraining the sacroiliac joint is the:
questions.explanation: The interosseous sacroiliac ligament is the strongest restraint on the joint, permitting only slight gliding and rotation.

questions.question: A pathological decrease in the femoral angle of inclination is called:
questions.explanation: A decreased angle of inclination is coxa vara; an increased angle is coxa valga. The angle also falls with age.

questions.question: Shenton's line follows the femoral neck onto the superior margin of the:
questions.explanation: Shenton's line is a smooth curve from the inferior femoral neck to the superior obturator foramen; a break signals hip pathology.

questions.question: The strongest ligament in the body, resisting hyperextension of the hip, is the:
questions.explanation: The Y-shaped iliofemoral ligament from the AIIS is the strongest ligament in the body and resists hip hyperextension.

questions.question: The three capsular ligaments of the hip all tighten in which position, to lock the joint?
questions.explanation: The spiral ligaments all wind tight in extension, screwing the head into the socket for energy-free standing.

questions.question: The hip capsule leaves part of the femoral neck extracapsular because posteriorly it attaches only to the:
questions.explanation: Anteriorly the capsule reaches the intertrochanteric line, but posteriorly only the proximal neck, leaving the posterolateral neck extracapsular.

questions.question: The socket of the acetabulum is completed inferiorly across the notch by the:
questions.explanation: The transverse acetabular ligament bridges the acetabular notch, completing the socket rim inferiorly with the labrum.

questions.question: A transcervical femoral neck fracture is dangerous chiefly because it can cause:
questions.explanation: An intracapsular neck fracture can sever the retinacular branches of the medial circumflex femoral artery, causing avascular necrosis.

questions.question: An intertrochanteric fracture usually heals better than a neck fracture because it is:
questions.explanation: An intertrochanteric fracture is extracapsular, so it usually spares the head's blood supply and can be fixed internally.

questions.question: After a posterior hip dislocation, the limb is characteristically held:
questions.explanation: Posterior dislocation leaves the limb flexed, adducted and internally rotated, and often shortened.

questions.question: Developmental dysplasia of the hip is screened for at birth using which tests?
questions.explanation: The Ortolani and Barlow tests screen newborns for developmental dysplasia, since early acetabular remodelling can correct it.

questions.question: On a child's hip X-ray, the Y-shaped cartilage at the acetabulum is the:
questions.explanation: The triradiate cartilage is the growth plate where the three hip bones meet, not to be mistaken for a fracture.

gluteal_posterior_thigh_mhhs2401_wk6.htm.title: Gluteal Region & Posterior Thigh
gluteal_posterior_thigh_mhhs2401_wk6.htm.subject: Musculoskeletal System
gluteal_posterior_thigh_mhhs2401_wk6.htm.content: Muscles of the gluteal region (gluteus maximus/medius/minimus, TFL, and the deep lateral rotators — piriformis, obturator internus, gemelli, quadratus femoris); the gluteal vessels and sciatic nerve relative to piriformis; the safe quadrant for intramuscular injection; bony features of the femur, tibia and fibula; and the hamstrings of the posterior thigh with their actions and innervation.

questions.question: The main action of gluteus maximus at the hip is:
questions.explanation: Gluteus maximus is the powerful hip extensor, especially from a flexed position, as in rising from sitting or climbing.

questions.question: The sciatic nerve is best described as:
options: A. the largest nerve in the body
D. a branch of the femoral nerve
questions.explanation: The sciatic nerve is the largest nerve in the body and supplies the posterior thigh and the whole leg and foot.

questions.question: The hamstring muscles lie in which compartment of the thigh?
questions.explanation: The hamstrings occupy the posterior (flexor) compartment of the thigh.

questions.question: The safe quadrant for a gluteal intramuscular injection is the:
questions.explanation: The upper outer (superolateral) quadrant is injected because it lies over gluteus medius, well away from the sciatic nerve.

questions.question: The lateral malleolus at the ankle is a feature of which bone?
questions.explanation: The fibula forms the lateral malleolus, while the tibia forms the medial malleolus of the ankle.

questions.question: Gluteus medius and minimus are both supplied by which nerve?
questions.explanation: The superior gluteal nerve supplies gluteus medius, minimus and TFL; the inferior gluteal nerve supplies gluteus maximus alone.

questions.question: Gluteus maximus is supplied by which nerve?
questions.explanation: The inferior gluteal nerve supplies gluteus maximus alone; the abductors take the superior gluteal nerve.

questions.question: In single-leg stance, gluteus medius and minimus act mainly to:
questions.explanation: In stance, the abductors of the planted limb hold the pelvis level so the unsupported side does not drop.

questions.question: In a positive Trendelenburg sign, the pelvis drops on which side?
options: A. the side opposite the weak muscle
B. the same side as the weak muscle
questions.explanation: The pelvis drops on the side opposite the weak gluteus medius, because that healthy side is the one being lifted.

questions.question: The iliotibial tract is the shared tendon of gluteus maximus and the:
questions.explanation: The iliotibial tract is the shared insertion of gluteus maximus and tensor fasciae latae, ending on Gerdy's tubercle of the tibia.

questions.question: The six deep gluteal muscles act on the hip chiefly as:
questions.explanation: The deep group runs horizontally to the greater trochanter, so they laterally rotate the thigh.

questions.question: Piriformis is the key landmark of the gluteal region because it:
options: A. divides the greater sciatic foramen
questions.explanation: Piriformis passes through and divides the greater sciatic foramen, so every gluteal vessel and nerve is described relative to it.

questions.question: Most hamstrings share a common origin from the:
questions.explanation: The hamstrings arise from the ischial tuberosity; the short head of biceps femoris is the exception, from the linea aspera.

questions.question: Because they cross two joints, the hamstrings extend the hip and also:
questions.explanation: The hamstrings span hip and knee, so they extend the thigh at the hip and flex the leg at the knee.

questions.question: The popliteal fossa is the diamond-shaped hollow located:
options: B. in front of the elbow
questions.explanation: The popliteal fossa is the diamond behind the knee where the sciatic nerve splits and vessels pass to the leg.

questions.question: The sciatic nerve is really two nerves in one sheath, the tibial and the:
questions.explanation: The sciatic nerve carries a tibial and a common fibular (peroneal) division bundled together until they split near the knee.

questions.question: The greater trochanter of the femur is the insertion for gluteus medius, minimus and the:
questions.explanation: The greater trochanter takes gluteus medius, minimus and the deep lateral rotators; the gluteal tuberosity takes deep gluteus maximus.

questions.question: The gluteal fold is formed not by the muscle edge but by a fat pad over the:
options: A. inferior border of gluteus maximus
B. superior border of gluteus medius
D. iliac crest of the pelvis
questions.explanation: Gluteus maximus fibres run obliquely, so the horizontal fold is a fat-pad crease over its inferior border, not the muscle edge.

questions.question: Gluteus medius inserts on the lateral surface of the greater trochanter, and gluteus minimus on the:
questions.explanation: Gluteus medius inserts on the lateral surface of the greater trochanter and gluteus minimus on its anterior surface.

questions.question: Which structure leaves the greater sciatic foramen above piriformis?
questions.explanation: Only the superior gluteal nerve and vessels leave above piriformis; the sciatic, pudendal and inferior gluteal exit below.

questions.question: Piriformis syndrome causes buttock pain radiating down the leg because piriformis compresses the:
questions.explanation: A tight or variant piriformis can compress the sciatic nerve, often its fibular fibres, mimicking disc-related sciatica.

questions.question: Quadratus femoris inserts onto the quadrate tubercle on which femoral ridge?
questions.explanation: Quadratus femoris runs from the ischial tuberosity to the quadrate tubercle on the intertrochanteric crest as a pure lateral rotator.

questions.question: A gluteal injection placed too low and medial risks striking the:
questions.explanation: The sciatic nerve runs through the lower medial region below gluteus maximus, so a low, medial needle can strike it, causing foot-drop.

questions.question: Which hamstring inserts with the pes anserinus on the medial proximal tibia?
questions.explanation: Semitendinosus joins sartorius and gracilis at the pes anserinus; semimembranosus inserts on the medial tibial condyle.

questions.question: Biceps femoris rotates the flexed knee laterally because its tendon inserts on the:
questions.explanation: Biceps femoris inserts laterally on the fibular head, so it laterally rotates the tibia; the medial 'semis' rotate it medially.

questions.question: The short head of biceps femoris is unusual because it is supplied by the:
questions.explanation: The short head of biceps takes the common fibular division of the sciatic nerve, while the other hamstrings take the tibial division.

questions.question: From superficial to deep, the contents of the popliteal fossa are ordered:
questions.explanation: The order is nerve, then vein, then artery, with the popliteal artery deepest against the bone, making its pulse hard to feel.

questions.question: The common fibular nerve is most easily injured at the:
questions.explanation: The common fibular nerve winds around the fibular neck superficially, making it the most commonly injured lower-limb nerve, causing foot-drop.

questions.question: The popliteal artery is vulnerable in a posterior knee dislocation because it lies:
options: B. most superficial in the fossa
questions.explanation: The popliteal artery is the deepest structure, tethered against the joint capsule and femur, so a posterior dislocation can tear it.

questions.question: The main arterial supply to the femoral head anastomoses with the gluteal vessels and is the:
questions.explanation: The medial circumflex femoral artery is the main supply to the femoral head and anastomoses with the gluteal system around the hip.

questions.question: Nélaton's line runs from the ASIS to the ischial tuberosity; the tip of which structure normally lies on it?
questions.explanation: The greater trochanter tip should lie on Nélaton's line; if it rides above, the femur has shortened, suggesting fracture or dislocation.

circulatory_system_mhhs2402_wk7.html.title: MHHS2402 W7 · Circulation, Blood Pressure & Flow
circulatory_system_mhhs2402_wk7.html.subject: Cardiovascular, Renal & Respiratory Systems
circulatory_system_mhhs2402_wk7.html.content: MHHS2402 Week 7 (Butlin): haemodynamics — systemic/pulmonary circuits, five vessel types, wall structure and compliance, the arterial pressure waveform, MAP/PP, Poiseuille flow=ΔP/R with resistance ∝ 1/r⁴, MAP = CO × TPR, and local (regional) autoregulation (four theories, hyperaemia, the L-arginine–NO pathway), with a pointer to the online blood-constituents module.

questions.question: Leaving the heart, blood passes through the vessels in which order?
options: A. arteries, arterioles, capillaries, venules, veins
B. veins, venules, capillaries, arterioles, arteries
C. arteries, capillaries, arterioles, veins, venules
D. arterioles, arteries, capillaries, veins, venules
questions.explanation: Blood always runs arteries, then arterioles, then capillaries, then venules, then veins, in both circuits.

questions.question: Exchange of oxygen, nutrients and waste occurs across which vessels?
questions.explanation: Capillaries are one cell thick, the only place where oxygen, carbon dioxide, nutrients and waste cross the vessel wall.

questions.question: Pulse pressure is calculated as systolic pressure minus:
questions.explanation: Pulse pressure is simply the height of the arterial wave, the systolic pressure minus the diastolic pressure.

questions.question: Which vessels are the body's main adjustable controllers of blood flow?
questions.explanation: The small muscular arterioles set resistance and regional flow, acting as the body's adjustable taps.

questions.question: At rest, most of the body's blood volume is held in the:
questions.explanation: About 64 percent of blood volume sits in the compliant systemic veins, the mobilisable capacitance reservoir.

questions.question: William Harvey proved blood circulates using an argument based on:
options: A. the quantity of blood pumped
B. the colour of the blood
D. the shape of the heart
questions.explanation: Harvey showed the volume pumped per hour far exceeds what food could supply, so blood must be recirculated, not consumed.

questions.question: An artery is defined as a vessel that carries blood:
questions.explanation: An artery carries blood away from the heart regardless of oxygen, which is why pulmonary arteries can be deoxygenated.

questions.question: The middle coat of a vessel wall that sets its diameter is the:
questions.explanation: The tunica media of smooth muscle, elastin and collagen bears load and actively sets the vessel's diameter.

questions.question: The elastic aorta smooths the heart's pulsatile ejection into steady flow, an effect called:
questions.explanation: The Windkessel effect: the elastic aorta stores part of each stroke in systole and recoils in diastole, giving near-continuous capillary flow.

questions.question: Compliance of a vessel is defined as the change in volume divided by the change in:
questions.explanation: Compliance C equals change in volume over change in pressure; veins are far more compliant than arteries.

questions.question: Mean arterial pressure is best described as the:
options: A. time-average of the pressure wave
B. midpoint of systolic and diastolic
C. peak of the pressure wave
questions.explanation: MAP is the time-average of the whole pressure wave, sitting nearer diastolic because diastole lasts longer.

questions.question: Blood flow through a vessel equals the pressure gradient divided by the:
questions.explanation: Flow equals pressure difference over resistance, the fluid analogue of Ohm's law where pressure is the push and resistance the friction.

questions.question: In the electrical analogy for blood flow, blood flow corresponds to which electrical quantity?
questions.explanation: Flow is the analogue of current, pressure difference of voltage, and resistance of resistance in the fluid version of Ohm's law.

questions.question: Mean arterial pressure is approximately the product of cardiac output and:
questions.explanation: MAP is approximately cardiac output times total peripheral resistance, the master equation of blood pressure control.

questions.question: Autoregulation is a tissue's ability to keep its own blood flow steady despite changes in:
questions.explanation: Autoregulation holds local flow constant despite systemic pressure swings; it is strongest in the brain and coronary beds.

questions.question: The rise in blood flow to a muscle while it is active is called:
questions.explanation: Active hyperaemia is the flow rise driven by vasodilator metabolites during tissue activity; supply is matched to demand.

questions.question: Blood consists of plasma plus the formed elements, which are red cells, platelets and:
questions.explanation: The formed elements are red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets, suspended in the fluid plasma.

questions.question: By Poiseuille's law, resistance is inversely proportional to the vessel radius raised to the:
questions.explanation: Resistance varies as one over radius to the fourth power, so flow is proportional to the pressure gradient times radius to the fourth.

questions.question: If a vessel's radius is halved at constant pressure, its flow falls to about:
questions.explanation: Because flow scales with radius to the fourth power, halving the radius cuts flow to two to the fourth, or one sixteenth.

questions.question: Arterioles have the highest wall-thickness-to-radius ratio because this lets them:
options: A. clamp down to set resistance
D. conduct flow with no loss
questions.explanation: A thick wall on a narrow bore lets an arteriole generate a large pressure drop without tearing, so it can set resistance.

questions.question: The estimate MAP equals diastolic plus one third of pulse pressure is weighted toward diastole because:
questions.explanation: At rest the heart spends about two-thirds of each cycle in diastole, so the time-average weights the lower diastolic pressure more.

questions.question: On the aortic pressure wave, the incisura (small notch) is caused by:
questions.explanation: The incisura on the aortic wave marks aortic valve closure; the peripheral dichrotic notch has similar timing but arises from wave travel.

questions.question: Systolic pressure is higher in the radial artery than in the aorta because of:
questions.explanation: Reflected pressure waves add onto the forward wave in the stiffer peripheral arteries, augmenting the systolic peak.

questions.question: The steepest fall in mean pressure across the systemic circulation occurs at the:
questions.explanation: The arterioles carry most of the resistance, so the biggest pressure drop happens across them, making them the flow-control point.

questions.question: Using MAP equals cardiac output times resistance, septic shock lowers blood pressure chiefly by reducing:
questions.explanation: Septic and anaphylactic shock cause runaway vasodilation, dropping total peripheral resistance; hypovolaemic and cardiogenic shock drop cardiac output.

questions.question: In most essential hypertension, cardiac output is near normal but there is a chronic rise in:
questions.explanation: Essential hypertension usually has near-normal output with chronically raised total peripheral resistance from narrowed arterioles.

questions.question: The myogenic theory of autoregulation holds that a rise in pressure makes vascular smooth muscle:
questions.explanation: In the myogenic theory, stretch opens calcium channels so the smooth muscle contracts, raising resistance to oppose the pressure rise.

questions.question: Which substance, released as ATP is broken down, is a key local vasodilator in low oxygen?
questions.explanation: Adenosine, along with carbon dioxide, potassium and hydrogen ions, is released in low oxygen and dilates the local arterioles.

questions.question: Reactive hyperaemia is the surge of flow that occurs after:
questions.explanation: During occlusion metabolites accumulate and dilate the bed; when flow returns, the low-resistance bed lets a large compensatory surge through.

questions.question: The endothelium releases nitric oxide, which relaxes vascular smooth muscle by raising:
questions.explanation: NO activates guanylate cyclase, which converts GTP to cGMP, and cGMP relaxes the smooth muscle, causing vasodilation.

questions.question: Endothelial nitric oxide release is triggered mechanically by:
questions.explanation: Shear stress from blood flowing along the wall activates nitric oxide synthase, converting L-arginine to nitric oxide.

questions.question: Oxygen delivery to a tissue equals blood flow multiplied by the:
questions.explanation: Delivery equals flow times oxygen content, so when content falls, as in anaemia or CO poisoning, only raising flow can defend delivery.

questions.question: Carbon monoxide poisoning starves tissues despite an apparently normal blood pressure because it lowers:
questions.explanation: CO binds haemoglobin far tighter than oxygen, collapsing oxygen content even though flow and blood pressure look normal.

gene_expression_medi2200_wk6.html.title: Gene Expression — Transcription & Translation
gene_expression_medi2200_wk6.html.subject: Human Cell & Molecular Biology
gene_expression_medi2200_wk6.html.content: Gene expression from DNA to protein: RNA chemistry, gene structure, RNA polymerases, transcription initiation, RNA processing (cap/splice/poly-A), the genetic code, tRNA, and translation (MEDI2200 Wk6, Parts I-III).

questions.question: In which direction is a new RNA strand synthesised?
options: C. both ends at the same time
D. from the middle of the strand outward
questions.explanation: The only reactive site for chain growth is the free 3′-OH, so RNA is always extended 5′ → 3′.

questions.question: In RNA, adenine base-pairs with which base?
questions.explanation: RNA uses uracil in place of thymine, so A pairs U while C pairs G — each a purine with a pyrimidine.

questions.question: Which codon starts translation, and which amino acid does it specify?
questions.explanation: AUG is the start codon and codes for methionine; it also sets the reading frame.

questions.question: Which set lists the three stop codons?
questions.explanation: UAA, UAG and UGA are the three termination codons; none specifies an amino acid.

questions.question: Which eukaryotic RNA polymerase synthesises mRNA?
questions.explanation: RNA Pol II makes mRNA (plus snRNA and miRNA); Pol I makes pre-rRNA and Pol III makes tRNA.

questions.question: What molecule forms the 5′ cap added to eukaryotic mRNA?
questions.explanation: A 7-methylguanosine is added to the 5′ end via an unusual 5′-to-5′ linkage soon after transcription starts.

questions.question: Of the 64 codons, how many specify amino acids versus stop?
questions.explanation: Of 64 codons, 61 specify amino acids and 3 are stop codons — which is why the code is redundant.

questions.question: Which ribosomal site binds the incoming charged tRNA?
questions.explanation: The A site accepts the incoming charged tRNA; the P site holds the growing peptide; the E site is the exit.

questions.question: Which two subunits join to form the eukaryotic 80S ribosome?
questions.explanation: The small 40S and large 60S subunits, assembled in the nucleolus, join on the mRNA to form the 80S ribosome.

questions.question: Which part of a tRNA base-pairs with the mRNA codon?
questions.explanation: The anticodon — three bases in the anticodon loop — pairs the complementary codon; the amino acid attaches at the acceptor stem.

questions.question: How does ribose's 2′-OH group affect RNA compared with DNA?
options: A. it makes RNA more reactive and less stable
B. it makes RNA more stable and quite inert
C. it lets RNA store the archival copy
D. it stops RNA from ever base-pairing again
questions.explanation: The reactive 2′-OH, absent in DNA, makes RNA less stable — why DNA is the archival copy and mRNA is disposable.

questions.question: What distinguishes an exon from an intron?
options: A. exons stay in mature mRNA; introns are removed
B. introns stay in mature mRNA; exons are removed
C. exons are never transcribed in the first place
D. introns code directly for the final protein
questions.explanation: Both are transcribed, but introns are spliced out and the exons (expressed sequences) are joined for the mature mRNA.

questions.question: Why is the non-template strand called the 'coding' strand?
options: A. its sequence equals the RNA, T replacing U
B. it is the strand actually read by polymerase
C. it carries all the introns of the gene
D. it is always shorter than the template
questions.explanation: The template strand is read by the polymerase; the coding strand is named for matching the RNA sequence, with T in place of U.

questions.question: Compared with DNA polymerase, RNA polymerase:
options: A. needs no primer and proofreads only modestly
B. needs a primer and proofreads very tightly
C. cannot start a chain without a primer
D. copies DNA with perfect fidelity always
questions.explanation: RNA polymerase starts a chain without a primer and proofreads only modestly (~1 error per 10⁴ nt), acceptable for disposable transcripts.

questions.question: What forms the conserved core of a Pol II pre-initiation complex?
options: A. Pol II, TBP and the general transcription factors
B. Pol II, DNA ligase and a poly-A polymerase
C. Pol III, primase and a sliding clamp
D. Pol I, helicase and a single-strand binding protein
questions.explanation: The PIC core is RNA Pol II plus the TATA-binding protein and the general transcription factors; TBP nucleates the complex.

questions.question: In the first splicing step, the branch-point adenosine:
options: B. binds the 5′ cap of the transcript
C. adds the poly-A tail to the 3′ end
D. joins the two exons directly together
questions.explanation: The branch-point A attacks the phosphodiester bond at the 5′ splice site, cleaving the 5′ exon and forming a lariat intermediate.

questions.question: Which factor recognises the AAUAAA polyadenylation signal?
questions.explanation: CPSF binds the AAUAAA signal while CstF binds the downstream GU-rich sequence; poly-A polymerase then adds the tail.

questions.question: At which codon position is 'wobble' pairing tolerated?
questions.explanation: Pairing is strict at positions 1 and 2, but a purine–pyrimidine wobble is tolerated at the third position, aiding redundancy.

questions.question: How does the small subunit locate the start codon during initiation?
options: A. it scans the 5′ cap to the AUG
B. it binds straight onto the poly-A tail
C. it starts at the 3′ end reading back
D. it locks onto the branch-point adenosine first
questions.explanation: The 40S subunit with initiation factors and initiator tRNA-Met scans from the 5′ cap to the first AUG in a Kozak context.

questions.question: What powers each step of translation elongation, and how fast is it?
options: A. GTP hydrolysis, about 15 amino acids per second
B. ATP hydrolysis, about 2 amino acids per second
C. GTP hydrolysis, about 1 amino acid per minute
D. proton flow, about 50 amino acids per second
questions.explanation: Elongation factors spend GTP for each of the three steps; eukaryotic elongation runs at ~15 amino acids per second.

questions.question: When do DNA replication and most transcription occur in the cycle?
options: A. replication in S-phase; most transcription in G1
B. both entirely during mitosis itself
C. replication in G1; transcription in S-phase
D. both only during the G0 resting phase
questions.explanation: DNA is replicated in S-phase before division; transcription happens mainly in G1, after division, when the cell grows.

questions.question: Where does the energy for adding each nucleotide during transcription come from?
options: A. hydrolysis of the incoming rNTP to rNMP
B. hydrolysis of a separate ATP molecule
C. breakdown of the DNA template strand
D. cleavage of the 5′ cap structure
questions.explanation: Each incoming ribonucleotide triphosphate is hydrolysed to rNMP plus pyrophosphate; releasing pyrophosphate drives the addition.

questions.question: The death-cap toxin α-amanitin is lethal chiefly because it inhibits:
options: A. RNA polymerase II, halting mRNA synthesis
B. RNA polymerase I, halting rRNA synthesis
D. the ribosome, halting translation directly
questions.explanation: α-amanitin specifically blocks RNA Pol II; with mRNA synthesis shut down, protein production collapses.

questions.question: Which two activities does TFIIH bring to transcription initiation?
options: A. a DNA helicase and a CDK7 kinase
B. a ligase and an exonuclease
C. a primase and a sliding clamp
D. a poly-A polymerase and a capping enzyme
questions.explanation: TFIIH's helicase/ATPase opens the DNA into the open complex, and its CDK7 kinase phosphorylates Pol II to start elongation.

questions.question: Why is TATA-binding protein still needed at promoters lacking a TATA box?
options: A. it is a conserved PIC core component
B. it directly transcribes the first few bases
C. it splices the introns from the transcript
D. it adds the 5′ cap before elongation
questions.explanation: TBP is part of the universal PIC core; it nucleates the complex and positions the polymerase at TATA and TATA-less promoters alike.

questions.question: What is the main functional consequence of alternative splicing?
options: A. one gene can make several protein species
B. one gene can make only one protein
C. it permanently deletes the gene's exons
D. it stops the transcript from leaving the nucleus
questions.explanation: By choosing which exons to keep, alternative splicing lets one DNA sequence encode multiple related proteins.

questions.question: Saying the genetic code is 'redundant' (degenerate) means:
options: A. one amino acid can have several codons
B. one codon can code several amino acids
C. every amino acid has exactly one codon
D. most codons specify no amino acid
questions.explanation: With 61 coding codons for 20 amino acids, most amino acids are specified by several codons — one to six each.

questions.question: How does an aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase help drive later peptide-bond formation?
options: A. it joins amino acid to tRNA with ATP
B. it hydrolyses GTP inside the ribosome
C. it reads the codon in the A site
D. it removes the stop codon from mRNA
questions.explanation: Each synthetase charges its tRNA using ATP, forming a high-energy amino-acid–tRNA bond whose energy later drives peptide-bond formation.

questions.question: Why does a stop codon end translation even though it enters the A site?
options: A. no tRNA fits it, so eRF1 binds instead
B. a special tRNA delivers a stop amino acid
C. the ribosome reverses to the start codon
D. the mRNA cap is cleaved at that point
questions.explanation: No tRNA has an anticodon for a stop codon; instead release factor eRF1 recognises it in the A site and frees the polypeptide.

questions.question: Why do a 40S and a 60S subunit combine into an 80S ribosome, not a 100S one?
options: A. S values are sedimentation rates, not additive
B. some mass is lost when the subunits join
C. the mRNA subtracts twenty S units
D. one subunit shrinks during assembly
questions.explanation: The 'S' is a Svedberg sedimentation unit reflecting both mass and shape, so the values are not simply additive.

heart_physiology_mhhs2402_wk6.html.title: The Heart — Cardiac Cycle, Conduction & Output (MHHS2402 Wk6)
